lessons.title: What Software Project Management Is
lessons.content:
Imagine your family decides to hold a big wedding for your elder sister in three months. Nobody in the house is a professional cook, decorator or photographer, yet somehow, on the day, the hall is booked, 400 guests are fed, the stage is decorated, and the photographer arrives on time. That happens because someone, usually an uncle or your mother with a notebook, quietly plans who does what, by when, and with how much money, and keeps checking that it is all on track. That person is doing project management. Now replace the wedding with a food-delivery app, the cooks with programmers, and the notebook with a planning tool, and you have software project management, the subject of this whole course.

What a project is: the most widely used definition, from the Project Management Institute (PMI), says a project is a temporary effort undertaken to create a unique product, service or result. Temporary means it has a clear start and a clear end. Unique means you have not built exactly this thing before, so there is always some uncertainty. Building the bKash-style wallet feature for a new bank is a project. Answering customer calls every day at that bank is not a project; it is an operation, because it repeats forever with no planned end.

Project vs operation: operations keep the business running, projects change the business. A team that keeps a website online, fixes small bugs and answers support tickets is doing operations. A team asked to rebuild the website with a new design by December is running a project. Once the project ends, its result is handed over to operations. Many problems happen exactly at this handover, so a good manager plans it from the start.

Progressive elaboration: because a project is unique, you cannot know every detail on day one. You start with a rough picture and add detail as you learn. A client might first say, we want an app for ordering food. After a few meetings this becomes three apps (customer, rider and restaurant), with bKash and card payment, live rider tracking and ratings. Plans are refined step by step. This is not a failure of planning; it is how real projects work, and it is why later lessons treat plans as living documents.

Program and portfolio: a program is a group of related projects managed together because they share a goal. A bank's digital banking program might include a mobile app project, a new core banking interface project and a staff training project. A portfolio is the full collection of projects and programs an organisation chooses to invest in, selected to match its strategy. A project manager runs one project, a program manager coordinates several, and a portfolio manager decides which ones are worth doing at all. Lesson 03 shows how that choice is made with money calculations.

Why software projects are especially hard: building a bridge and building software are both projects, but software has extra difficulties. In his famous 1986 essay No Silver Bullet, Fred Brooks named four properties that make software hard by its nature. Complexity: even a medium app has thousands of parts that interact, and no two parts are alike. Conformity: software must fit around messy human rules, laws, other systems and old databases. Changeability: because software looks easy to change, everyone keeps asking for changes. Invisibility: you cannot see software the way you see a half-built wall, so it is hard to tell how much is really finished.

Invisibility in practice: on a building site, a manager can walk around and see that 7 of 10 floors are done. In software, a programmer may say the login feature is 90 percent done for three weeks in a row. The code exists, but nobody can see whether the hard last part is solved. That is why software project management invents ways to make progress visible: working demos, finished and tested features, burndown charts and earned value numbers, all of which you will learn in this course.

What success means: the classic answer is that a project succeeds if it finishes on time, within budget and delivers the agreed scope at acceptable quality. Modern managers add a fifth point: value. An app that was delivered perfectly on time but which nobody uses has not really succeeded. So we judge a project on two levels. Project success asks whether we delivered what we promised, the way we promised. Product success asks whether the thing we delivered actually helps users and the business.

Why projects fail: industry surveys over many years keep finding that a large share of software projects are late, over budget, cut features, or are cancelled. The causes are rarely that people cannot code. The usual culprits are unclear requirements, a client who keeps adding features, estimates that were really wishes, no handling of risks, poor communication, too few skilled people, and a manager who notices problems too late. Almost every one of these is a management failure, which is good news: management can be learned.

The project manager's job: a project manager, often shortened to PM, is responsible for getting the project's objectives achieved. Day to day this means planning the work, estimating time and cost, building and guiding the team, talking to clients and bosses, watching progress, spotting risks early, handling changes and conflicts, and finally closing the project properly. The PM usually does not write most of the code. Think of a cricket captain: the captain may not bowl every over, but sets the field, chooses bowlers, reads the match and changes plans when the situation changes.

Skills a PM needs: technical understanding, so engineers respect you and you can judge estimates; planning and numbers, for schedules and budgets; communication, because most of a PM's day is talking and writing; leadership and people skills, to motivate and resolve conflict; and judgement, to make decisions with incomplete information. In software, a PM who has written code before has a big advantage, because they can tell when a 2-day estimate is really a 2-week task.

The four Ps: Roger Pressman's textbook sums up what a software manager must manage with four words. People: the most important factor, because skilled, motivated people deliver and unhappy ones do not. Product: what is being built, its scope and its requirements. Process: the way of working, such as Waterfall or Scrum. Project: the plan, schedule, budget and tracking that tie the other three together. If you forget one P, the others suffer; a great process cannot save a project with no clear product.

Project manager vs product manager vs Scrum Master: these titles confuse many students. A project manager focuses on delivering a defined piece of work on time and budget. A product manager, or Product Owner in Scrum, decides what the product should be and which features matter most for users. A Scrum Master helps a Scrum team follow and improve its process and removes obstacles. In a small Bangladeshi startup one person may wear two of these hats, but the jobs are different. Lesson 18 returns to this.

The running example of this course: throughout these 25 lessons we will follow one invented project. MeghSoft, a software firm in Dhaka, has been asked by a client to build DhakaEats, a food-delivery system with a customer app, a rider app, a restaurant panel and payment through mobile wallets and cards. The client wants it live in 6 months. We will use DhakaEats to write a business case, a scope statement and a WBS, estimate it with function points and COCOMO, schedule it with a network diagram, track it with earned value, manage its risks, and finally close it.

A small worked feel for the numbers: suppose MeghSoft estimates DhakaEats needs about 30 person-months of work. A person-month is the work one person does in one month. If 5 developers work on it, a naive division says 30 / 5 = 6 months. But lesson 12 will show why 10 developers will not finish it in 3 months: new people need training, and more people means more communication. With 5 people there are 5 x 4 / 2 = 10 communication pairs; with 10 people there are 10 x 9 / 2 = 45. Simple arithmetic, but it explains many late projects.

Real-life example 1, a government e-service: imagine a ministry wants an online system where citizens apply for a trade licence. The deadline is set by a political announcement, the budget is fixed by a public tender, and dozens of offices must change how they work. The technical part, a web form and a database, is not the hardest part. The hard parts are agreeing on requirements across departments, training staff, migrating paper records, and handling the day the system goes live and thousands of people log in at once. Each of those is a project management problem.

Real-life example 2, a student team: five classmates build a final-year project in 12 weeks. Without management, they spend 8 weeks on a beautiful login screen and panic in the last month. With basic management they list the features, estimate each one, agree who does what, meet briefly every week, cut a nice-to-have feature when they fall behind, and demo a working app on time. Same people, same skills, very different result. You will use everything in this course directly in your final-year project (deep-cse-6-7).

How this course is organised: lessons 01-04 cover the big picture: life cycles and frameworks, choosing projects with money calculations, and stakeholders. Lessons 05-14 are the planning core: scope, WBS, estimation (including function points and COCOMO), scheduling, resources, cost and earned value. Lessons 15-16 cover risk. Lessons 17-19 cover agile management with Scrum and Kanban. Lessons 20-24 cover people, communication, quality, configuration and contracts. Lesson 25 covers monitoring, closing, and puts DhakaEats together from start to end.

What you already know and where it fits: in Software Engineering (deep-cse-4-4) you met process models, Scrum, a first critical path and basic COCOMO. In Operations Research (deep-cse-6-10) you did the full CPM and PERT mathematics. Here we will not repeat those from zero; we recap them quickly and focus on using them as a manager makes decisions.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: students often call any piece of work a project; remember the two tests, temporary and unique. Many think project management means drawing Gantt charts; charts are tools, the real job is decisions and people. Another mistake is thinking success only means on time and on budget, forgetting value. Typical exam questions: define a project and give its characteristics, distinguish project from operation and program from portfolio, explain why software projects are harder than other projects (Brooks's four properties), and list the responsibilities of a software project manager.

Recap: a project is a temporary, unique effort; operations repeat. Projects are refined by progressive elaboration and grouped into programs and portfolios. Software is hard to manage because of complexity, conformity, changeability and invisibility. Success means scope, time, cost, quality and real value. Most failures are management failures, and a project manager's job is to plan, track, communicate and decide. Next lesson: the life cycle every project passes through and the frameworks, like PMBOK, PRINCE2 and Scrum, that organise this work.
key_points: A project is a temporary effort to create a unique product, service or result; an operation repeats with no planned end.
Progressive elaboration means plans start rough and get detailed as the team learns.
A program groups related projects; a portfolio is all projects an organisation chooses to invest in.
Brooks named four essential difficulties of software: complexity, conformity, changeability and invisibility.
Success has two levels: delivering scope on time, on budget and at quality, and delivering real value to users.
Most project failures come from unclear requirements, bad estimates, unmanaged risk and poor communication, not from weak coding.
The project manager plans, estimates, leads, communicates, tracks and decides; it is different from a product manager or Scrum Master.
Communication pairs grow as n(n-1)/2, so doubling a team more than quadruples its conversations.
lessons.tip: From today, treat every group assignment as a tiny project: write down its end date, its budget (even if it is only your time) and its deliverables. You will be surprised how much calmer the deadline week becomes.
lessons.task: Pick something you did recently, like a class trip, a birthday party or a group assignment. On paper, answer: was it temporary and unique? Who were the stakeholders? What were the scope, deadline and budget? List two things that went wrong and say which of them was really a planning or communication problem.

quiz.q: Which of these is a project, not an operation?
options: Answering customer calls at a bank every day
Building a new mobile wallet feature by March
quiz.explain: Building the feature is temporary and unique with a clear end. The others repeat forever, so they are operations.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of Brooks's four essential difficulties of software?
quiz.explain: Brooks listed complexity, conformity, changeability and invisibility. Gravity is not one of them.

quiz.q: What is a portfolio?
options: The whole set of projects and programs an organisation chooses to invest in
quiz.explain: A portfolio is the full collection of projects and programs selected to match the organisation's strategy.

quiz.q: A team grows from 5 to 10 people. How many communication pairs are there now?
Progressive elaboration means:
options: Writing every detail of the plan on day one
Adding detail to plans step by step as more is learned
Cancelling a project when it is late
Adding more people to speed up work
quiz.explain: Because projects are unique, plans begin rough and become more detailed as the team learns.

lessons.title: Life Cycles, Process Groups and Frameworks
lessons.content:
Every cricket match has a shape: the toss, the first innings, the break, the second innings, the result. Every match is different, yet the shape stays the same, and that shape lets players, umpires and fans know what should happen next. Projects have a shape too. They begin, they get planned, work gets done and watched, and they end. In this lesson we study that shape, called the life cycle, and the well-known frameworks, PMBOK, PRINCE2 and Scrum, that describe how to manage a project through it.

Project life cycle: the project life cycle is the series of phases a project goes through from start to finish. A typical software project might have phases like concept, requirements, design, build, test and deploy. In an agile project the phases may repeat as short cycles. Whatever the phases are called, every project starts, does its work, and closes.

Project life cycle vs product life cycle: the product life cycle is much longer. A product such as a ride-sharing app is born, grows, matures with many updates, and one day is retired. During its life many projects happen: the first launch project, a project to add parcel delivery, a project to move to a new payment gateway. So a product life cycle contains many project life cycles. Students often mix these up in exams; remember that a project ends, a product can live for years.

The classic life cycle curve: in most projects, cost and staffing are low at the start, rise to a peak during the building and testing work, and fall sharply as the project closes. Two other lines go the other way. Uncertainty and risk are highest at the start, when you know least. The ability of stakeholders to influence the result without big cost is also highest at the start. As time passes, the cost of changing something rises. Changing a requirement in week 1 costs a conversation; changing it after launch can cost a rewrite. This one picture explains why early planning matters so much.

Phases and phase gates: a phase gate, also called a stage gate or kill point, is a review at the end of a phase where sponsors decide whether to continue, change direction, or stop. At the end of requirements, for example, the gate might ask: are requirements signed off, is the business case still good, are major risks under control? Stopping a doomed project at a gate is a success of management, not a failure, because it saves money that would have been wasted.

The five process groups: the PMI's PMBOK Guide organises project management work into five process groups. Initiating defines the project and gets authorisation to start. Planning sets scope, schedule, budget, risks and everything needed to do the work. Executing does the work: builds, tests, communicates, manages the team. Monitoring and Controlling measures progress against the plan and takes corrective action. Closing formally finishes the project or a phase, hands over results and records lessons learned.

Process groups are not phases: this is a classic exam trap. Process groups are kinds of activity, not steps in time. Inside a single phase, say the design phase of a big project, you still initiate the phase, plan it, execute it, monitor it and close it. Monitoring and controlling in particular runs across the whole project, wrapping around the others like a loop: plan, do, check, act. It resembles the Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle used in quality management.

The ten knowledge areas: older editions of PMBOK (up to the 6th) also sort the work by subject into ten knowledge areas. Integration ties everything together and handles change. Scope decides what is and is not included. Schedule manages time. Cost manages money. Quality makes sure the result meets requirements. Resource manages people and equipment. Communications makes sure information reaches the right people. Risk handles uncertainty. Procurement handles buying from outside. Stakeholder manages the people affected by the project. Notice that this course is roughly organised along these ten areas.

A simple way to remember them: scope, schedule and cost are the three sides of the famous triangle. Quality, resource and communications keep the work healthy. Risk, procurement and stakeholder deal with the outside world and uncertainty. Integration is the glue. A grid of 5 process groups by 10 knowledge areas gave the older guide its 49 processes in the 6th edition, for example Plan Risk Management (planning, risk) or Control Costs (monitoring, cost).

PMBOK 7 and principles: since the 7th edition (2021), PMBOK moved away from a long list of processes to a lighter, principle-based approach. It describes 12 principles, such as being a diligent steward, focusing on value, recognising systems thinking, demonstrating leadership, tailoring, building quality in, navigating complexity, optimising risk responses, embracing adaptability and enabling change. It also describes 8 performance domains: stakeholders, team, development approach and life cycle, planning, project work, delivery, measurement and uncertainty. The reason for the change was that agile and hybrid projects did not fit neatly into fixed process lists. The older process view is still widely taught and appears in exams, so learn both.

PRINCE2: PRINCE2 (PRojects IN Controlled Environments) began in the UK government and is popular in the UK, Europe and Australia, and with some international donor-funded projects. It is built on seven principles: continued business justification (the project must stay worth doing), learn from experience, defined roles and responsibilities, manage by stages, manage by exception (managers get tolerances, for example plus or minus 10 percent on cost, and only escalate if they will break them), focus on products (deliverables), and tailor to suit the project. It also has seven themes (business case, organisation, quality, plans, risk, change and progress; renamed practices in the 2023 edition) and seven processes from starting up a project to closing a project.

Manage by exception, worked: suppose a stage has a budget of 10 lakh taka with a tolerance of plus or minus 10 percent. The project manager may spend anywhere between 9 and 11 lakh without asking the project board. If a forecast shows 11.5 lakh, the tolerance is broken, so the manager raises an exception report and the board decides. This saves senior people from attending every small meeting, while keeping them in control of big decisions.

Scrum as a framework: Scrum is a lightweight framework for agile work, described in the Scrum Guide by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland. It does not try to cover contracts, budgets or procurement; it describes how a small team delivers value in short sprints with a few roles, events and artifacts. You met Scrum in Software Engineering (deep-cse-4-4, lesson 07) and lesson 18 takes it further from a manager's view. Many real organisations combine Scrum for the team's daily work with PMBOK or PRINCE2 ideas for budgets, contracts and governance.

Kinds of life cycle: frameworks describe four broad shapes. A predictive life cycle, like Waterfall, plans scope, time and cost up front and follows the plan phase by phase. An iterative life cycle repeats cycles to refine the product, for example building a rough version and improving it. An incremental life cycle delivers the product in usable pieces, such as releasing ordering first and live tracking later. An adaptive or agile life cycle is both iterative and incremental, with short cycles and scope that changes with feedback. A hybrid mixes them. Lesson 17 explains how to choose; for now, just know the life cycle is a choice, not a fixed rule.

Governance, who decides what: every framework separates the people who do the work from the people who make the big decisions. In PRINCE2 the project board has three roles: the executive, who owns the business case and holds the money; the senior user, who speaks for the people who will use the product; and the senior supplier, who speaks for the people building it. The project manager runs the project day to day within the limits the board sets. In PMBOK language the sponsor plays a similar role to the executive. Knowing who can approve what saves weeks of waiting.

Comparing them:PMBOK is a broad guide to what good project management involves; it says what areas to manage but not exactly how to run your project. PRINCE2 is a method: it says who does what and which documents and decisions are needed at each stage. Scrum is a team-level framework for building a product in short cycles. None is a law you must follow word by word. They are toolboxes.

Tailoring: every framework says you should tailor it. A 3-person, 6-week internal project does not need a 40-page risk plan and weekly board meetings. A 200-person national ID system does. Tailoring means choosing which processes, documents and meetings to use, and how formal to be, based on size, risk, team experience, the client and the law. Using every possible process on a small project is called over-engineering the management, and it wastes time just as badly as having no process.

Real-life example 1, a bank's mobile app: a bank in Dhaka wants a new app. The bank's governance demands phase gates: a business case approved by the board, requirements signed by compliance, a security review before launch. Inside the build phase, the vendor's team works in two-week Scrum sprints. At each gate, the project manager presents progress, budget and risks. This is a hybrid: PMBOK-style phases and gates around, Scrum inside. It is extremely common in banks, telecoms and government work.

Real-life example 2, DhakaEats at MeghSoft: for our running project, MeghSoft tailors a light process. Initiating: a one-page charter signed by the client. Planning: scope statement, WBS, estimate and a release plan. Executing: two-week sprints with demos to the client. Monitoring: a weekly status report with schedule, budget and top risks, and earned value each month. Closing: final acceptance, handover to the client's support team and a lessons-learned meeting. Four gates are agreed: after charter, after the first release plan, before beta, and before launch.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: confusing process groups with phases; thinking monitoring happens only at the end; believing PRINCE2, PMBOK and Scrum are competitors you must pick one of; and forgetting that a product life cycle contains many projects. Exams often ask you to list and explain the five process groups, name the ten knowledge areas, draw the cost and staffing curve over the life cycle, explain manage by exception, or compare PMBOK, PRINCE2 and Scrum.

Recap: a project life cycle is the sequence of phases from start to close, inside a longer product life cycle. Cost peaks in the middle, while uncertainty and the ability to change things cheaply are highest at the start. The five process groups are initiating, planning, executing, monitoring and controlling, and closing; they are activities, not phases. PMBOK lists ten knowledge areas and now also principles and performance domains; PRINCE2 gives principles, themes and processes with manage by exception; Scrum gives a light team framework. Always tailor. Next lesson: how a project gets chosen and started, with business cases and money calculations.
key_points: The project life cycle runs from start to close; a product life cycle is longer and contains many projects.
Cost and staffing peak in the middle; risk and cheap ability to change are highest at the start.
Phase gates are go, change or stop decisions at the end of a phase.
The five process groups are initiating, planning, executing, monitoring and controlling, and closing; they are not phases.
PMBOK's ten knowledge areas: integration, scope, schedule, cost, quality, resource, communications, risk, procurement, stakeholder.
PMBOK 7 adds 12 principles and 8 performance domains for agile and hybrid work.
PRINCE2 has seven principles including manage by stages and manage by exception with tolerances.
Frameworks are toolboxes; tailor them to the project's size, risk and context.
lessons.tip: Make a 5 by 10 grid on one page: process groups across, knowledge areas down. Fill a few cells with one example activity each. One page like that helps you answer half the theory questions in this course.
lessons.task: Take any project you know (a college fest, a website for a shop). Write one concrete activity for each of the five process groups. Then add one phase gate question you would ask before the project is allowed to continue.

quiz.q: When is the cost of changing a project decision usually lowest?
options: At the start of the project
quiz.explain: Early on little has been built, so changes cost little. The cost of change rises as the project progresses.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the five process groups?
quiz.explain: The five are initiating, planning, executing, monitoring and controlling, and closing. Coding is part of executing work, not a group.

quiz.q: In PRINCE2, a stage budget is 10 lakh taka with plus or minus 10 percent tolerance. The forecast is 11.5 lakh. What happens?
options: The manager raises an exception to the project board
The team works overtime without telling anyone
quiz.explain: The tolerance allows 9 to 11 lakh. 11.5 lakh breaks it, so under manage by exception the manager escalates to the board.

quiz.q: Which statement about process groups is correct?
options: They happen strictly one after another, once each
They can repeat inside each phase, and monitoring runs throughout
They are the same as SDLC phases
quiz.explain: Process groups are kinds of activity, not phases. Each phase can be initiated, planned, executed, monitored and closed.

quiz.q: Tailoring a framework means:
options: Always using every process it describes
Choosing which processes and how much formality fit the project
Buying a tool that implements it
quiz.explain: Tailoring adapts processes, documents and formality to the project's size, risk and context.

lessons.title: Project Initiation and the Business Case
lessons.content:
Imagine your family has 2 lakh taka saved. Your brother wants to buy a laptop for freelancing, your mother wants to repair the roof before the monsoon, and your father wants to start a small tea stall. You cannot do all three. Somebody has to ask: what does each cost, what does each give back, how soon, and how risky is it? Companies face exactly this choice with software projects, only with bigger numbers. This lesson is about how a project gets chosen and officially started: the business case, a few simple money calculations, and the project charter.

Why projects need to be selected: every organisation has more ideas than money and people. A bank might want a new app, a loan system upgrade, a chatbot and a data warehouse, all in the same year. Choosing badly means wasting money on projects that do not help, or starving the important ones. Project selection is usually done by senior management or a portfolio board, but project managers must understand it, because the reasons a project was chosen decide what counts as success.

The business case: a business case is a document that explains why a project is worth doing. It typically contains the problem or opportunity, the options considered (including doing nothing), the expected benefits, the costs, the timescale, the major risks, and a recommendation. Benefits can be tangible, which you can count in money, like saving 15 lakh taka a year in call-centre costs, or intangible, which are real but hard to price, like a better brand image. A business case is not written once and forgotten. In PRINCE2 continued business justification is a principle: if costs explode or benefits disappear, the project should be stopped.

Cost-benefit analysis: the core of a business case is comparing costs and benefits over time. Costs include development (salaries, tools, outsourcing), infrastructure (servers, cloud bills), and running costs after launch (support, maintenance, licences). Benefits include new income, cost savings and avoided losses. Because money arrives over several years, we use a few standard measures: payback period, return on investment, net present value and internal rate of return.

The DhakaEats numbers: for our running example, suppose the client will spend 60 lakh taka now (year 0) to build DhakaEats. The client expects net benefits, meaning extra income minus running costs, of 20 lakh in year 1, 30 lakh in year 2 and 35 lakh in year 3. We will use these numbers for every measure below so you can compare them.

Payback period: payback is the time taken to earn back the investment. Add the benefits year by year, keeping a running total starting at minus 60. After year 1 the total is minus 60 + 20 = minus 40. After year 2 it is minus 40 + 30 = minus 10. During year 3 we need 10 more lakh out of the 35 that year brings, so 10 / 35 = 0.29 of the year. Payback is about 2 + 0.29 = 2.29 years. Payback is easy to explain to anyone, but it has two weaknesses: it ignores everything after the payback point, and it treats taka next year the same as taka today.

Return on investment: a simple ROI is (total benefits minus total cost) divided by total cost. Over three years total benefits are 20 + 30 + 35 = 85 lakh. ROI = (85 minus 60) / 60 = 25 / 60, about 0.417, or 41.7 percent. This says each taka invested returns itself plus about 42 paisa over three years. Different companies define ROI slightly differently, for example per year, so always state the formula you used.

The time value of money: would you rather have 100 taka today or 100 taka in a year? Today, because you could put it in a bank and earn interest, and because prices rise. If the interest rate is 10 percent, 100 taka today becomes 110 taka in a year. Turning it around, 110 taka received next year is worth only 100 taka today. To bring a future amount back to today we divide by (1 + r) raised to the number of years, where r is the discount rate. That is called discounting, and the result is the present value.

Net present value, worked: let the discount rate be 10 percent. The discount factors are 1 / 1.1 = 0.909 for year 1, 1 / 1.21 = 0.826 for year 2, and 1 / 1.331 = 0.751 for year 3. Present values: 20 x 0.909 = 18.18, 30 x 0.826 = 24.79, 35 x 0.751 = 26.30 lakh. Their sum is 69.27 lakh. NPV = 69.27 minus 60 = 9.27 lakh. A positive NPV means the project earns more than the 10 percent the money could earn elsewhere, so it creates value. A negative NPV means you would be better off leaving the money in the safer alternative.

The discount rate matters: if the client's money costs more, say 12 percent, the present values drop to 17.86, 23.92 and 24.91, summing to 66.69, and the NPV falls to 6.69 lakh. Higher discount rates punish projects whose benefits come late. That is why risky, long projects often look worse under NPV than short ones.

Internal rate of return: the IRR is the discount rate at which the NPV becomes exactly zero. For DhakaEats it is about 17.8 percent, found by trying rates until the NPV is zero (spreadsheets do it with one function). If IRR is higher than the company's required rate of return, often called the hurdle rate, the project passes. IRR is popular with managers because it is a single percentage, but NPV is generally considered more reliable when comparing projects of different sizes.

Comparing two projects: suppose the same client could instead build a smaller loyalty-points system costing 40 lakh with benefits of 25, 15 and 10 lakh. Its payback is exactly 2 years (25 + 15 = 40), faster than DhakaEats. But its ROI is (50 minus 40) / 40 = 25 percent and its NPV at 10 percent is only about 2.64 lakh. Payback prefers the loyalty system; NPV and ROI prefer DhakaEats. This is a typical exam question, and the lesson is that the measure you choose changes the answer. Companies short of cash may prefer quick payback; others prefer the largest NPV.

Scoring models: not every benefit is money. A weighted scoring model lists criteria, gives each a weight, scores each project, and adds up. Suppose criteria are strategic fit (weight 0.4), financial return (0.3), risk, where a higher score means lower risk (0.2), and team readiness (0.1). DhakaEats scores 8, 6, 7 and 5: total 0.4 x 8 + 0.3 x 6 + 0.2 x 7 + 0.1 x 5 = 3.2 + 1.8 + 1.4 + 0.5 = 6.9. The loyalty system scores 6, 9, 5 and 6: total 2.4 + 2.7 + 1.0 + 0.6 = 6.7. DhakaEats wins narrowly. The weights must be agreed before scoring, otherwise people tune them to get the answer they wanted.

The sunk cost trap: money already spent and impossible to recover is a sunk cost. When deciding whether to continue a troubled project, only future costs and future benefits matter. Suppose 40 lakh has been spent, finishing needs 30 lakh more, and the finished system will bring benefits worth only 20 lakh in today's money. Continuing loses another 10 lakh, whatever was spent before. People hate to waste what they spent, so they keep going; good gates stop this.

Feasibility recap: before or alongside the business case, analysts check feasibility: technical (can we build it?), economic (is it worth it?), operational (will people use it and can the organisation run it?), schedule (can it be done in time?) and legal (is it allowed?). System Analysis & Design (deep-cse-4-6) covers feasibility studies in detail; here the point is that the business case leans on them.

The project charter: once a project is chosen, the sponsor issues a project charter. It is a short document, often one to three pages, that formally authorises the project and the project manager. It usually contains the project's purpose and objectives, high-level requirements and scope, major deliverables, key milestones, a summary budget, main risks and assumptions, key stakeholders, the name and authority of the project manager, and the sponsor's signature. Without a charter, a project manager may be asked to spend money or ask people for time with no official authority.

Good objectives: charter objectives should be SMART: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. Make a better food app is not an objective. Launch DhakaEats in Dhaka North and South with ordering, rider tracking and mobile-wallet payment by 30 June, supporting 5,000 orders per day, within 60 lakh taka, is.

Real-life example 1, a university portal: a private university is deciding between a new student portal (cost 30 lakh, saves staff time and reduces registration queues) and a new library system (cost 15 lakh). The portal's tangible saving is 13 lakh per year in staff hours; the library's is 4 lakh. With a 10 percent discount rate over three years, the portal has a positive NPV of about 2.3 lakh, while the library system's NPV is about minus 5 lakh on money alone. Yet the board still funds the library a year later because of an intangible benefit: accreditation requirements. Business cases combine numbers and judgement.

Real-life example 2, the charter that saved a project: a small software firm in Chattogram started building an ERP for a garments factory after a friendly phone call. No charter, no agreed scope. Three months later the factory owner said he had expected payroll too, and refused to pay. On the next project the firm insisted on a two-page charter signed by the owner, listing what was and was not included. When a similar argument came up, the signed list ended it in five minutes.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: forgetting the do-nothing option in a business case; ignoring running costs after launch; treating ROI and NPV as the same thing; forgetting to discount future money; and starting work before a charter is signed. Typical exam questions: compute payback, ROI and NPV from a table of cash flows; compare two projects and explain why measures disagree; list the contents of a business case or a project charter; and explain the time value of money.

Recap: projects are selected because resources are limited. The business case argues why a project is worth doing, with costs, benefits, options and risks. Payback tells how fast money returns, ROI how much, and NPV how much value is created after discounting; IRR is the rate where NPV is zero. Weighted scoring adds non-money criteria. The charter formally authorises the project and the manager, with SMART objectives. For DhakaEats: payback about 2.29 years, ROI about 41.7 percent, NPV at 10 percent about 9.27 lakh, IRR about 17.8 percent. Next lesson: the people around the project, stakeholders, and how organisations are structured to run projects.
key_points: A business case explains why a project is worth doing: problem, options including do nothing, benefits, costs, risks and a recommendation.
Payback period is the time to earn back the investment; DhakaEats pays back in about 2.29 years.
Simple ROI = (total benefits minus cost) / cost; DhakaEats gives about 41.7 percent over three years.
Discounting divides future money by (1 + r)^n; NPV is the sum of present values minus the investment.
At 10 percent, DhakaEats has NPV of about 9.27 lakh; IRR, the rate where NPV is zero, is about 17.8 percent.
Different measures can rank projects differently; payback favours quick returns, NPV favours total value.
Weighted scoring models add strategic and non-money criteria with agreed weights.
The project charter formally authorises the project and the project manager, with SMART objectives.
lessons.tip: Build the NPV table once in a spreadsheet: year, cash flow, discount factor, present value. Once you have done it by hand and in a sheet, every exam variant is just new numbers in the same table.
lessons.task: Invent a small project, like a tuition-booking app, costing 5 lakh taka now and bringing 2, 2.5 and 3 lakh in the next three years. Calculate the payback period, simple ROI and NPV at 10 percent with a calculator. Then decide whether you would approve it and write one SMART objective for its charter.

quiz.q: A project costs 60 lakh and returns 20, 30 and 35 lakh over three years. What is the payback period?
quiz.explain: After two years 50 lakh is back, 10 lakh remains. 10 / 35 = 0.29 of year 3, so about 2.29 years.

quiz.q: What does a positive NPV tell you?
options: The project earns more than the discount rate, so it creates value
The project pays back within one year
The project is cheaper than its competitors
quiz.explain: Positive NPV means discounted benefits exceed the investment at that discount rate.

quiz.q: At a 10 percent discount rate, what is the present value of 110 taka received one year from now?
quiz.explain: Present value = 110 / 1.1 = 100 taka.

quiz.q: Project X has a shorter payback but Project Y has a higher NPV. Which statement is right?
options: Payback and NPV always agree, so there is a calculation error
X must be chosen because payback is the only real measure
The choice depends on priorities: quick cash return or total value created
quiz.explain: Measures can disagree. Cash-poor firms may prefer quick payback; value-focused ones choose higher NPV.

quiz.q: Which document formally authorises a project and names the project manager?
quiz.explain: The charter, signed by the sponsor, authorises the project and gives the PM authority to use resources.

lessons.title: Stakeholders and Project Organization
lessons.content:
Think about building a new road in your neighbourhood. The engineers care about the design, the city corporation cares about the budget, the shopkeepers worry their shops will be blocked for months, rickshaw pullers want a smooth surface, and the local leader wants a ribbon-cutting before the election. If the road is perfect but the shopkeepers protest every day, the project still suffers. Software projects are the same. Many people are affected, and each one can help or hurt. These people are called stakeholders, and managing them is one of the most underrated skills in project management.

Who is a stakeholder: a stakeholder is any person, group or organisation that can affect the project, be affected by it, or believes it will be affected. That last part matters: someone who only thinks they will be harmed can still block you. Stakeholders can be inside the organisation (sponsor, project team, other departments, operations, finance, legal) or outside (customers, end users, vendors, regulators such as Bangladesh Bank for a payment app, and the general public).

DhakaEats stakeholders: for our running example, internal to MeghSoft we have the CEO, the project manager, developers, testers, designers and the finance team. On the client side there are the client's owner who pays (the sponsor), the client's operations manager who will run the service, and the customer support team. Outside are restaurant owners, riders, customers, the payment gateway and mobile-wallet providers, map service providers, and regulators for payments and data. Even competitors are stakeholders in a loose sense, because their moves can change your priorities.

Step one, identify: stakeholder identification should start in initiation, not after problems appear. Useful methods are brainstorming with the team, reading the charter and contracts, looking at the organisation chart, asking each stakeholder who else should be involved, and checking past similar projects. Missing an important stakeholder is dangerous; a classic case is forgetting the legal or compliance team until a week before launch.

The stakeholder register: the results are recorded in a stakeholder register, usually a simple table. For each stakeholder it lists name and role, contact, their interest in the project, their expectations, their influence, their current attitude (supportive, neutral, resistant), and how we plan to engage them. The register is a living document; people change jobs, and attitudes change as the project moves.

Power/interest grid: a quick way to decide how much attention each stakeholder needs is to place them on a 2 x 2 grid. One axis is power, meaning their ability to change the project; the other is interest, meaning how much they care. High power and high interest: manage closely, involve them in decisions and talk often. High power, low interest: keep satisfied, give them short summaries, don't flood them. Low power, high interest: keep informed, they often give useful feedback. Low power, low interest: monitor with minimal effort.

Placing DhakaEats stakeholders: the client owner has high power and high interest: manage closely with a weekly meeting and every release demo. MeghSoft's CEO has high power but, on a normal day, low interest in this one project: keep satisfied with a monthly one-page summary. Restaurant owners have low power individually but high interest: keep informed through pilot sessions and a feedback form. A map service provider has low interest in your small project and low power over its scope: monitor, mainly watching for pricing changes. The grid is a starting point; a regulator with low interest today can jump to high interest tomorrow.

Other models: the salience model looks at three attributes: power, legitimacy (is their claim appropriate?) and urgency (do they need attention right now?). A stakeholder with all three is a definitive stakeholder and must get attention first. You do not need to memorise every model; the idea is to prioritise attention instead of treating everyone equally.

Engagement levels: PMBOK suggests describing each stakeholder's engagement as one of five levels: unaware (does not know about the project), resistant (knows and opposes it), neutral (knows, neither supports nor resists), supportive (knows and supports) and leading (actively works to make it succeed). In a stakeholder engagement assessment matrix you mark C for current and D for desired. If the client's operations manager is currently resistant because she fears the new system will replace her staff, and you want her supportive, the gap tells you to plan conversations, training and maybe a role for her team in the new system.

Managing expectations: most stakeholder trouble comes from a gap between what someone expects and what they get. If the client owner silently expects a web version as well as the apps, they will feel cheated at the end even if every agreed feature works. So the stakeholder engagement plan says, for each key group, what they need to know, how often, through which channel, and who on the team owns the relationship. Good managers also say no early and politely, write decisions down, and bring bad news quickly. Stakeholders forgive a delay they heard about in week 4; they rarely forgive one they discover in week 20.

RACI matrix: once you know who is involved, you must be clear about who does what. A RACI matrix lists tasks down the side and people across the top, and each cell holds R, A, C or I. Responsible: does the work. Accountable: owns the outcome and signs off; there must be exactly one A per task. Consulted: gives input before the work is done, a two-way conversation. Informed: is told after decisions or progress, one-way.

RACI worked for DhakaEats: take the task integrate mobile-wallet payment. The backend developer is R. The tech lead is A, because one person must own it. The client's finance officer is C, because they know settlement rules. The payment provider's integration team is also C. The project manager and client owner are I. Now take the task approve release 1. The client owner is A, the project manager is R for preparing the release and arranging acceptance, the QA lead is C, and the riders' coordinator is I. A quick check of the matrix: every row has exactly one A, and no row is crowded with As or Rs. Two As on one row is the most common RACI mistake, because when two people own something, nobody owns it.

Organisation structures: how much authority a project manager has depends heavily on the organisation's structure. In a functional organisation people sit in departments (development, testing, sales), and each department head is the real boss. Projects cut across departments, and the project manager, if there is one, is a part-time coordinator with little authority. In a projectized organisation teams are formed around projects, the project manager is the boss, and people may have no department to return to when the project ends. Many software agencies are close to this.

Matrix organisations: most real organisations are in between, called matrix. People report to a functional manager and to a project manager at the same time. In a weak matrix the functional manager holds most power and the project manager acts as an expediter or coordinator. In a balanced matrix power is shared. In a strong matrix the project manager has most of the authority over the project, its budget and its people, often with a full-time role. Matrices use people efficiently, but they create two bosses, so conflicts over priorities are common and must be handled openly.

A worked comparison: imagine a developer at a bank's IT division is asked by the project manager to finish the DhakaEats-style integration this week, while the head of development asks her to fix a production bug. In a functional or weak matrix organisation, the head of development normally wins. In a strong matrix or projectized organisation, the project manager's priority usually wins. Knowing the structure in advance tells the project manager whom to talk to first, and when to escalate.

The PMO: a project management office is a unit that standardises how projects are managed. A supportive PMO provides templates, training and lessons from past projects, with low control. A controlling PMO requires compliance with its methods and reviews projects, with moderate control. A directive PMO directly manages projects, with high control. In Bangladesh, large banks, telecom operators and big software companies commonly have some form of PMO; small startups usually do not.

Sponsor, project manager and product owner: the sponsor provides the money and backing, owns the business case, approves big changes and removes organisational obstacles the project manager cannot. The project manager runs the project day to day. In agile work, the product owner decides what to build and in what order, representing customer value. A project fails quietly when the sponsor disappears after signing the charter; part of the manager's job is keeping the sponsor engaged with short, regular updates.

Real-life example 1, a hospital system: a software firm built an appointment and billing system for a private hospital in Dhaka. The doctors were not consulted because the hospital director said he would decide. At launch, senior doctors refused to use the new appointment screens because they did not match how they actually worked. The fix took two months. Had the doctors been placed correctly in the grid (high power, high interest) and consulted early, a few workshops would have avoided it.

Real-life example 2, an NGO field app: an NGO wanted an Android app for field workers in rural areas to record health visits. The project manager mapped stakeholders and noticed that field supervisors were resistant because the app would make their reporting visible. She moved them toward supportive by involving them in testing, showing that the app would save them two days of paperwork per month, and making them the first trainers. Adoption was smooth.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: identifying stakeholders too late; treating all stakeholders the same; putting two As in a RACI row; confusing Consulted (two-way, before) with Informed (one-way, after); and assuming the project manager has the same authority in every organisation. Exams often ask you to define stakeholder, draw and explain the power/interest grid, build a RACI matrix for a few tasks, compare functional, matrix and projectized structures, and describe the three kinds of PMO.

Recap: stakeholders are everyone who affects or is affected by the project. Identify them early and record them in a register. Use the power/interest grid to decide attention, and the engagement matrix to plan moving people from current to desired levels. RACI makes responsibilities clear, with exactly one Accountable per task. The project manager's authority grows from functional to weak, balanced and strong matrix to projectized. PMOs can support, control or direct. Above all, manage expectations: share bad news early, write decisions down, and keep the sponsor close, because a quiet sponsor is an early warning sign. Next lesson: deciding exactly what the project will and will not deliver, its scope.
key_points: A stakeholder is anyone who affects, is affected by, or believes they are affected by the project.
Identify stakeholders early and keep a living stakeholder register with interest, influence and attitude.
Power/interest grid: manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed, or monitor.
Engagement levels run from unaware and resistant through neutral to supportive and leading; plan to close current vs desired gaps.
RACI: Responsible does, Accountable owns (exactly one per task), Consulted gives input before, Informed is told after.
PM authority grows from functional through weak, balanced and strong matrix to projectized organisations.
A PMO can be supportive, controlling or directive.
The sponsor funds and backs the project; keeping the sponsor engaged is part of the PM's job.
lessons.tip: Whenever a new name appears in an email thread about your project, ask yourself where they sit on the power/interest grid. That one habit prevents many nasty surprises.
lessons.task: List 8 stakeholders of your university's online result system (students, parents, exam controller, IT staff, and so on). Place them on a power/interest grid. Then build a RACI matrix with 4 tasks (publish results, fix a wrong grade, change the login system, announce downtime) and check that every task has exactly one A.

quiz.q: A stakeholder with high power but low interest should usually be:
options: Kept informed in detail every day
quiz.explain: High power, low interest: keep them satisfied with short, relevant updates without overwhelming them.

quiz.q: In a RACI matrix, how many Accountable people should each task have?
quiz.explain: Exactly one A per task ensures someone clearly owns the outcome.

quiz.q: In which structure does the project manager usually have the MOST authority?
quiz.explain: In a projectized organisation teams are built around projects and the PM controls budget and people.

quiz.q: What is the difference between Consulted and Informed in RACI?
options: Consulted gives two-way input before work; Informed is told one-way after
Informed approves the work; Consulted does it
quiz.explain: Consulted people are asked for input before decisions; Informed people are kept updated afterwards.

quiz.q: A PMO that provides templates and training but does not enforce methods is:
quiz.explain: A supportive PMO offers help with low control. Controlling enforces compliance; directive manages projects directly.

lessons.title: Scope Management
lessons.content:
You hire a tailor to make a shirt for Eid. You agree on the cloth, the size, the price and the date. Then, two days before Eid, you ask: can you also add a pocket, change the collar and make a matching panjabi for my brother? The tailor can say yes, but either the price goes up, the delivery date moves, or the stitching gets sloppy. That simple story is the whole idea of scope management: agree clearly on what will be delivered, protect that agreement, and when it must change, change it on purpose, with the time and cost adjusted honestly.

What scope means: scope is the sum of the work and the results a project must deliver. There are two kinds. Product scope describes the features and functions of the thing being built: a customer can search restaurants, add items to a cart and pay with a mobile wallet. Project scope describes the work needed to deliver it, including things that are not features at all: requirements workshops, testing, training the client's support staff, writing user guides, deploying to servers. Many estimates go wrong because people count only product scope and forget the project work around it.

The scope management steps: PMBOK breaks scope work into a few steps. Plan scope management decides how scope will be defined, checked and controlled. Collect requirements finds out what stakeholders need. Define scope writes the detailed scope statement. Create WBS breaks the work into pieces (next lesson). Validate scope gets formal acceptance of finished deliverables from the customer. Control scope watches for changes and handles them through change control. The first four happen mostly in planning; the last two run throughout the project.

Collecting requirements, a recap: System Analysis & Design (deep-cse-4-6) and Software Engineering (deep-cse-4-4, lesson 08) taught how to gather and write requirements: interviews, workshops, questionnaires, observation, prototypes, use cases, user stories and acceptance criteria. From a manager's view, three extra points matter. First, talk to all key stakeholder groups, not just the person who pays. Second, separate needs from wishes early. Third, keep a requirements traceability matrix, a table linking each requirement to its source, its design element, its code and its test, so that nothing is lost and every change can be traced.

Traceability, a small example: requirement R7 says a customer can pay with a mobile wallet. In the matrix, R7's source is the client workshop on 12 February, it maps to the payment module design, to the code in the payment service, and to test cases T31 to T35. If the client later drops wallet payment, the matrix shows exactly which design, code and tests are affected. If a tester finds a test with no linked requirement, it may be testing a feature nobody asked for.

The scope statement: define scope produces the project scope statement, the main written agreement on what is included. A good statement contains: the project objectives; a product scope description; the major deliverables; acceptance criteria for each deliverable; exclusions, meaning what is explicitly not included; constraints, meaning fixed limits such as budget, deadline or required technology; and assumptions, meaning things believed true but not yet proven. Exclusions are the most underused part, and often the most valuable.

DhakaEats scope statement, in short: objective, launch a food-delivery service in Dhaka by 30 June within 60 lakh taka. Deliverables: an Android and iOS customer app, an Android rider app, a web restaurant panel, an admin dashboard, payment integration with one mobile wallet and card payment, user guides and two training sessions. Acceptance criteria: for example, an order can be placed, paid and tracked end to end, and the system handles 5,000 orders per day in a load test. Exclusions: no web version of the customer app, no grocery delivery, no loyalty points, no languages other than Bangla and English, no hardware for restaurants. Constraints: fixed launch date for a marketing campaign, client chose the payment provider. Assumptions: the client will supply restaurant data, map service costs stay within the quoted price.

Why exclusions save projects: the sentence no web version of the customer app looks boring. But four months later, if the client says, of course the web version was included, everyone has a website, the signed scope statement answers the question in one line. Without it, the argument turns into who remembers what from a meeting long ago. Assumptions help in the same way: if the client fails to supply restaurant data, the assumption was broken, so the resulting delay is not MeghSoft's fault.

The triple constraint: scope, time and cost are tied together, a relationship called the triple constraint or iron triangle. Quality usually sits in the middle. If one side changes, at least one other must change too, or quality suffers. Suppose the client adds live chat between customer and rider, estimated at 3 person-weeks. Options: extend the deadline by the time needed, add cost by bringing in another developer (if that actually helps; see lesson 12), drop or delay another feature of similar size, or squeeze it in with no change and accept lower quality, which usually means more bugs at launch. A good manager presents these options with numbers and lets the sponsor choose.

Scope creep: scope creep is the slow, uncontrolled growth of scope without matching adjustments to time, cost or resources. It rarely comes as one big change. It comes as many small requests, each sounding reasonable: one more filter on the search screen, a small change to the receipt, a quick report for the accounts team. Each takes hours; together they take weeks. The danger is not change itself, which is normal, but change without control.

Gold plating: gold plating is the team adding features or polish nobody asked for, usually with good intentions. A developer builds a beautiful animation for the order screen, or adds a dark mode because it seemed fun. It costs time, adds new places for bugs, and may not be wanted. Scope creep usually comes from the customer side, gold plating from the team side. Both are scope problems; the cure for both is to deliver what was agreed, and to propose extras through the change process.

Change requests: when someone wants to change scope, they submit a change request. The project manager, with the team, does an impact analysis: how much time, cost and risk will it add, which deliverables and tests are affected? Then the right authority, for big changes a change control board or the sponsor, approves, rejects or defers it. Approved changes update the scope baseline, schedule and budget. Lesson 23 covers change control in detail; the key idea here is that every change goes through one door.

A worked change: in month 3 the client asks for scheduled orders, letting customers order today for delivery tomorrow. Impact analysis: about 2 person-weeks of backend, 1 of app work, 1 of testing, and a new risk around restaurants forgetting future orders. Total 4 person-weeks; at a loaded cost of 1 lakh taka per person-month (about 4.3 weeks), that is roughly 0.93 lakh taka, and the release would slip by about one week with the current team. The client accepts the cost but not the delay, so the team moves the rider-rating feature to a later release to keep the date. The scope baseline, schedule and budget are updated and the client signs the change.

The scope baseline: once approved, the scope statement, the WBS and the WBS dictionary together form the scope baseline. A baseline is an approved version used for comparison. Later, every question about whether something is in scope, and every measurement of progress, is checked against the baseline. It can change only through formal change control.

Validate scope vs control quality: two processes that students mix up. Control quality is internal: the team and testers check that deliverables are correct, meeting quality requirements, before the customer sees them. Validate scope is external: the customer or sponsor formally inspects and accepts the completed deliverables. Usually quality control happens first, then scope validation. In agile projects, the sprint review is a natural place to validate scope, because the product owner sees working features and accepts or rejects them against the definition of done and acceptance criteria.

Scope in agile projects: in Scrum, scope is not frozen at the start. The product backlog holds everything that might be built, ordered by value, and the product owner can reorder it every sprint. So is scope control dead? No, it moves. Time and cost are usually fixed by the sprint length and team size, and scope becomes the flexible side of the triangle. Control now means that new ideas go into the backlog rather than straight into the current sprint, that the sprint goal is protected once a sprint starts, and that the product owner makes visible trade-offs: if live chat goes up, something else goes down. Lesson 17 shows how release plans and MoSCoW priorities keep this honest.

Real-life example 1, the e-commerce client: a Dhaka clothing brand hired a firm to build an online shop. The scope statement listed product catalogue, cart, cash-on-delivery and one card gateway, and excluded integration with the brand's old inventory software. During development the brand asked for that integration as part of the original price. Because exclusions were written and signed, the discussion became a normal change request with a price, and the relationship stayed friendly.

Real-life example 2, the student project: a team building a library app for their department kept agreeing to every suggestion from friends: book reviews, a chat feature, recommendations. By week 9 nothing was finished. Their supervisor made them write a one-page scope statement with must-have features and a list of exclusions. They finished search, issue and return, and fines, and put the extras in a future work section of their report. That is scope control in miniature.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: confusing product scope with project scope; writing no exclusions; treating any change as bad instead of controlling it; mixing up scope creep and gold plating; and confusing validate scope with control quality. Exam questions often ask you to define scope and the scope baseline, list the contents of a scope statement, explain the triple constraint with an example, distinguish scope creep from gold plating, and describe how a change request is processed.

Recap: scope is what the project delivers (product scope) and the work to deliver it (project scope). Collect requirements carefully and trace them. The scope statement records objectives, deliverables, acceptance criteria, exclusions, constraints and assumptions. Scope, time and cost are tied; changes must move at least one other side or quality pays. Control scope creep and avoid gold plating by sending every change through one change process. Validate scope means customer acceptance; control quality means internal correctness checks. Next lesson: breaking the scope into a work breakdown structure.
key_points: Product scope is the features of the result; project scope is all the work needed to deliver it, including testing, training and deployment.
A requirements traceability matrix links each requirement to its source, design, code and tests.
The scope statement lists objectives, deliverables, acceptance criteria, exclusions, constraints and assumptions.
Written exclusions and assumptions prevent many later disputes.
Triple constraint: changing scope, time or cost forces a change in another side, or quality suffers.
Scope creep is uncontrolled growth from requests; gold plating is the team adding unrequested extras.
Every change goes through a change request with impact analysis and approval, then updates the baseline.
Validate scope is formal customer acceptance; control quality is the internal correctness check that usually comes first.
lessons.tip: When writing any scope, force yourself to write at least five exclusions. If you cannot think of five things that are not included, you probably do not understand the scope yet.
lessons.task: Write a half-page scope statement for a small app you would like to build, such as a class routine app. Include two objectives, four deliverables, one acceptance criterion per deliverable, five exclusions, two constraints and two assumptions. Then imagine a friend requests a new feature and write a short impact analysis for it.

quiz.q: Training the client's support staff is part of:
quiz.explain: Training is work required to deliver the result, so it belongs to project scope even though it is not a product feature.

quiz.q: A developer adds a dark mode nobody requested. This is:
quiz.explain: Gold plating is the team adding unrequested features or polish.

quiz.q: Which part of the scope statement says what is explicitly NOT included?
quiz.explain: Exclusions list what is out of scope, which prevents later arguments.

quiz.q: The client adds a feature but refuses to change the deadline or budget, and the team accepts. According to the triple constraint, what is most likely to suffer?
quiz.explain: If scope grows while time and cost stay fixed, quality usually drops, for example through more bugs.

quiz.q: Validate scope means:
options: The customer formally accepts completed deliverables
quiz.explain: Validate scope is formal acceptance by the customer or sponsor; internal correctness checks are control quality.

lessons.title: Work Breakdown Structure
lessons.content:
How do you eat a whole cow? One bite at a time. It sounds silly, but it is exactly how big projects are planned. Nobody can estimate build a food-delivery system in one go. But anyone can estimate design the login screen or write the API that saves a cart. The work breakdown structure, or WBS, is the tool that turns a frightening, cloudy project into a tree of small, clear pieces that can be estimated, assigned, scheduled and tracked. It is often called the foundation of project planning, because almost everything else, the schedule, the budget, the risk list, is built on top of it.

What a WBS is: the WBS is a hierarchical decomposition of the total scope of work the project team must do to achieve the project objectives and create the deliverables. Hierarchical means it is a tree: the whole project at the top, major pieces below it, smaller pieces below those. Decomposition means breaking something into parts. Total scope means everything, including project management work, testing, training and deployment, not just features.

Why it matters: first, it makes scope visible and complete, so forgotten work is spotted early. Second, small pieces are much easier to estimate accurately than one big lump. Third, each piece can be given to one owner, which makes responsibility clear. Fourth, the schedule and budget are built by adding up the pieces, so they are grounded in real work. Fifth, progress can be tracked piece by piece, which fights the invisibility of software we met in lesson 01.

Work packages: the lowest level of a WBS is called a work package. A work package is small enough to estimate cost and duration reliably, to assign to one person or team, and to track. Work packages are deliverables or pieces of work, described with nouns, such as cart and checkout screens. The actions needed to produce them, such as design screen layouts or write unit tests, are activities, which come later in the activity list. In other words, the WBS says what; the activity list says how.

How small is small enough: a popular rule of thumb is the 8/80 rule: a work package should take at least 8 hours and no more than 80 hours of effort. Smaller than 8 hours and you are micromanaging; bigger than 80 hours, about two working weeks for one person, and it is hard to estimate and too long to wait before knowing whether it is on track. Another common guide is the reporting period rule: a work package should fit within one reporting period, such as one or two weeks. These are guidelines, not laws.

The 100 percent rule: the most important WBS rule says the WBS must include 100 percent of the work defined by the scope, and the children of any element must add up to exactly 100 percent of their parent, no more and no less. Missing work means it will be forgotten in the schedule and budget. Extra work, something under a parent that is not part of the scope, is gold plating hiding in your plan. Every level must be complete and must not overlap.

Deliverable-oriented vs phase-oriented: there are two common ways to organise the second level. A deliverable-oriented WBS uses the main products: customer app, rider app, restaurant panel, backend, and so on. A phase-oriented WBS uses life cycle phases: requirements, design, build, test, deploy. PMI recommends focusing on deliverables because a phase-oriented tree tends to hide what is actually being produced. In practice many software teams mix them: deliverables at level 2, and a few cross-cutting items like project management and testing as separate branches.

The DhakaEats WBS at level 2: 1 DhakaEats system. 1.1 Project management. 1.2 Requirements and design. 1.3 Customer app. 1.4 Rider app. 1.5 Restaurant panel. 1.6 Backend and payment integration. 1.7 Testing and quality assurance. 1.8 Deployment and training. Notice 1.1 Project management: planning, meetings, reporting and coordination are real work and must appear, or the budget will be short.

Going deeper: the customer app, 1.3, is broken into 1.3.1 Registration and login, 1.3.2 Restaurant search and menu, 1.3.3 Cart and checkout, 1.3.4 Order tracking. The numbering scheme, 1, 1.3, 1.3.3, is called the WBS code or code of accounts. It gives every piece a unique address, used later in the schedule, the budget, timesheets and the bug tracker, so everyone means the same thing when they say 1.3.3.

Worked 100 percent check: MeghSoft's team estimates effort in person-weeks for each level-2 branch: project management 10, requirements and design 12, customer app 30, rider app 14, restaurant panel 12, backend and payment 26, testing and QA 18, deployment and training 8. The total is 10 + 12 + 30 + 14 + 12 + 26 + 18 + 8 = 130 person-weeks. With about 4.3 weeks in a month, that is 130 / 4.3, roughly 30 person-months, which matches the rough figure from lesson 01. Under the customer app, the children are estimated at 4, 8, 10 and 8 person-weeks: 4 + 8 + 10 + 8 = 30, exactly the parent. If they had added to 34, either the parent estimate was wrong or a child contained extra work; both must be fixed.

Checking the 8/80 rule: cart and checkout, 1.3.3, is 10 person-weeks, about 400 hours at 40 hours a week. That is far above 80 hours, so it should be broken down further: 1.3.3.1 Cart screen, 1.3.3.2 Address and delivery options, 1.3.3.3 Payment screen, 1.3.3.4 Order confirmation and receipt, 1.3.3.5 Cart and checkout API. Each of these still might need splitting until pieces reach roughly two weeks of one person's work.

The WBS dictionary: a tree only shows names. The WBS dictionary is a companion document that describes each element in detail: the WBS code, a description of the work, the responsible person, the deliverables, acceptance criteria, assumptions and constraints, related activities and milestones, estimated cost and effort, and links to requirements. For 1.3.3.3 Payment screen, the entry might say: owner Rafi, includes wallet and card options, excludes saved cards, acceptance when a test payment succeeds in the sandbox and failure messages appear for declined payments, estimate 60 hours, depends on 1.6 payment API.

Control accounts and planning packages: on larger projects, the manager picks some WBS elements above work packages as control accounts, points where scope, budget and actual cost are measured for earned value (lesson 14). A planning package sits under a control account when the work is known to exist but not yet detailed. This connects to rolling wave planning: near-term work is broken down to work packages now, while work far in the future is left at a higher level and detailed later, as information arrives. Rolling wave planning is progressive elaboration in action.

From WBS to activities and milestones: once the WBS is stable, each work package is broken into activities, the actual tasks with durations. For 1.3.3.1 Cart screen, activities might be design cart layout (2 days), implement cart screen (4 days), connect to cart API (2 days) and write widget tests (1 day). Milestones are significant points with zero duration, like requirements signed off, beta released, or go-live. Activities and milestones become the input to the network diagram in lesson 10.

WBS in agile projects: Scrum teams rarely draw a formal WBS, but they decompose in the same spirit. A product is split into epics, large chunks of value such as order tracking; epics are split into features or user stories such as as a customer I can see my rider on a map; stories are split into tasks during sprint planning. The 100 percent idea still helps: if the backlog has no stories for deployment, monitoring or training, that work is missing from the plan just as surely as in a Waterfall project. Agile teams also keep stories small enough to finish inside one sprint, which plays the same role as the 8/80 rule.

WBS, OBS and responsibility: the WBS can be crossed with the organisation breakdown structure, or OBS, which shows the teams and people. Where a WBS element meets a team, you get an assignment. Laid out as a grid, this is a responsibility assignment matrix, and the RACI chart from lesson 04 is the most common kind. For DhakaEats, the backend team owns 1.6, the mobile team owns 1.3 and 1.4, and the QA team owns 1.7, with the project manager accountable for 1.1. Every work package should have exactly one owner.

How to build a WBS in practice: gather the scope statement and requirements; invite the people who will do the work, because they know what it involves; start top-down from the main deliverables, or bottom-up by brainstorming all tasks on sticky notes and grouping them; check the 100 percent rule at each level; stop decomposing when pieces meet your size rule; number everything; write the dictionary; and review it with the client against the scope statement. Templates from similar past projects speed this up a lot, which is one reason PMOs keep them.

Real-life example 1, a hospital website: a team building a hospital's website started their WBS with pages: home, doctors, departments, contact. On review, the project manager asked where content writing, photographs of doctors, Bangla translation, server setup and staff training were. None were in the tree, yet together they took nearly a third of the final effort. Adding them before the budget was signed saved an embarrassing conversation later.

Real-life example 2, a family house: building a two-storey house in Rajshahi uses a WBS without anyone calling it that: foundation, structure, roof, electrical, plumbing, finishing. Under electrical: wiring, switches and sockets, meter connection. The contractor prices each piece, the family pays by milestone, and anyone can see that plumbing is done but finishing is not. Software just needs the same discipline.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: listing activities (verbs) instead of deliverables (nouns) in the WBS; forgetting project management, testing, documentation and training; violating the 100 percent rule with gaps or overlaps; decomposing too far, into one-hour tasks; and confusing the WBS with the schedule, which it is not, since a WBS has no dates or order. Exams often ask you to draw a WBS for a given system, explain the 100 percent rule, define work package and WBS dictionary, compare deliverable and phase-oriented WBS, and explain rolling wave planning.

Recap: the WBS breaks the total scope into a tree of deliverables, down to work packages small enough to estimate, assign and track, commonly 8 to 80 hours. The 100 percent rule says children must add up exactly to their parent, with nothing missing or extra. Codes give each piece an address; the dictionary describes it. Control accounts measure performance; rolling wave planning details near work first. From work packages come activities and milestones for scheduling. For DhakaEats, 8 branches total 130 person-weeks, about 30 person-months. Next lesson: how to estimate those pieces well, and why estimates go wrong.
key_points: The WBS is a hierarchical decomposition of the total scope, including management, testing, training and deployment.
Work packages are the lowest WBS level: small enough to estimate, assign to one owner and track.
