The 8/80 heuristic: a work package should take about 8 to 80 hours of effort.
The 100 percent rule: children must add up exactly to their parent, with no missing or extra work.
Deliverable-oriented WBS is recommended; many software teams mix deliverables with cross-cutting branches.
WBS codes (1.3.3) give each element a unique address; the WBS dictionary describes each element in detail.
Rolling wave planning details near-term work now and future work later.
The WBS lists deliverables (what); activities and milestones (how and when) come from it for scheduling.
lessons.tip: Draw your first WBS with sticky notes on a wall or table. Moving notes around is much faster than editing a document, and it makes missing pieces jump out.
lessons.task: Build a three-level WBS for a college cultural fest website with online registration. Number every element, include project management and testing branches, give each work package an hour estimate, and check that every parent equals the sum of its children. Mark any work package bigger than 80 hours and split it.

quiz.q: What does the 100 percent rule say?
options: Every task must be 100 percent finished before the next starts
The children of a WBS element must add up to exactly 100 percent of the parent's work
100 percent of the budget must be spent
Every team member must be used 100 percent of the time
quiz.explain: The rule ensures the WBS covers all scope with no gaps and no extra work at every level.

quiz.q: Which is the best name for a work package in a deliverable-oriented WBS?
quiz.explain: Work packages are deliverables described with nouns. Actions like write code are activities.

quiz.q: A work package is estimated at 400 hours. Under the 8/80 heuristic, what should you do?
quiz.explain: 400 hours is far above 80, so it is too big to estimate and track well; split it further.

quiz.q: Which document describes each WBS element's work, owner, acceptance criteria and estimate?
quiz.explain: The WBS dictionary gives the detailed description of every WBS element.

quiz.q: Rolling wave planning means:
options: Detailing near-term work now and future work later as information arrives
Planning everything in full detail on day one
Repeating the same plan every month
Letting the team plan without the manager
quiz.explain: It is progressive elaboration: decompose what is close, keep distant work at a higher level until more is known.

lessons.title: Estimation Fundamentals and Techniques
lessons.content:
Ask a friend how long it takes to get from Mirpur to Motijheel and they might say 40 minutes. Ask again at 9 a.m. on a weekday in the rain and they will laugh and say, who knows, maybe two hours. The distance did not change; the uncertainty did. Software estimation is the same. A good estimate is not a single magic number pulled from the air; it is a judgement about a range of possible outcomes, made with methods that reduce bias and that get better as you learn more. This lesson covers why estimates go wrong and the main techniques managers use to make them better.

What we estimate: in software projects we usually estimate three things. Size: how big is the product, in lines of code, function points (lesson 08), use cases or story points. Effort: how much work, in person-hours, person-days or person-months. Duration: how much calendar time, which depends on effort, how many people work in parallel, and dependencies. Cost mostly follows from effort, because salaries are the largest cost in software. Lesson 09 shows formal models linking size to effort and duration.

Estimate, target and commitment: Steve McConnell's book Software Estimation separates three ideas that people mix up. An estimate is a prediction of how long or how much something will take. A target is a desired business goal, such as we must launch before Eid. A commitment is a promise to deliver by a certain date with certain functionality. Problems begin when a target is presented as an estimate: the boss says we need it by Eid, so the estimate becomes Eid. A healthy conversation compares the estimate with the target, and if they do not fit, adjusts scope, resources or the date before making a commitment.

Why estimates go wrong: requirements are unclear or keep changing; people forget whole categories of work (testing, meetings, deployment, bug fixing); estimators are optimistic; pressure from bosses or clients pushes numbers down; the team has never done this kind of work before; and estimates are given as single numbers that hide uncertainty. Psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky named a related bias the planning fallacy: people underestimate their own task times even when they know similar tasks took longer in the past.

The cone of uncertainty: early in a project, estimates are naturally very uncertain. Steve McConnell, building on Barry Boehm's research, describes this as a cone. At the initial concept stage, the real effort can be anywhere from about 0.25 times to 4 times the estimate. When the product definition is approved the range narrows to roughly 0.5x to 2x; when requirements are complete, about 0.67x to 1.5x; when the user interface design is complete, about 0.8x to 1.25x; and with a detailed design, about 0.9x to 1.1x. The cone does not narrow by itself: it narrows only when the team makes decisions that remove uncertainty.

Using the cone, worked: if DhakaEats is estimated at 30 person-months at the concept stage, the real effort could plausibly fall between 30 x 0.25 = 7.5 and 30 x 4 = 120 person-months. After requirements are complete, the range is about 20 to 45. This is why giving a client a fixed price at concept stage is very risky, and why many contracts are split: a small paid discovery phase first, then a firm price after requirements are clear.

Top-down and bottom-up: a top-down estimate looks at the whole project and estimates it at once, often by comparing to similar past projects or by using a model. It is fast and good early, but can miss details. A bottom-up estimate estimates each work package from the WBS and adds them up, like we did with the 130 person-weeks in lesson 06. It is slower but more detailed and usually more accurate once the WBS exists. Good managers do both and investigate if they disagree by a lot.

Estimation by analogy: compare the new project with completed ones whose actual effort you know, then adjust for differences. If MeghSoft's previous grocery-delivery app took 24 person-months and DhakaEats has about 25 percent more features plus a new rider app, an analogy estimate might be around 30 person-months. Analogy works only when you keep records of actual effort from past projects; many companies do not, which is one of the cheapest improvements a PMO can make.

Expert judgement and Wideband Delphi: expert judgement means asking experienced people. It is the most common technique in practice, but single experts can be biased. The Delphi method, developed at the RAND Corporation, reduces this by asking several experts to estimate anonymously, sharing the results, and repeating. Wideband Delphi, a version popularised by Boehm, adds discussion: the coordinator presents the task, experts estimate privately, the results are shown without names, the people with the highest and lowest numbers explain their reasoning, and everyone estimates again. Usually after two to four rounds the range narrows and hidden assumptions come out.

Planning poker: agile teams use a quick game version of Wideband Delphi. Each member holds cards with numbers like 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 20, 40 and 100 (a Fibonacci-like scale; the gaps grow because bigger items are less certain). The product owner reads a user story, everyone picks a card secretly, and all cards are shown together. If one person shows 3 and another 13, they explain: maybe the 13 knows the payment provider's sandbox is unreliable. Then the team votes again. The value is less in the number and more in the conversation that exposes misunderstandings. Story points are relative units of size, not hours; lesson 17 shows how velocity turns them into forecasts.

Three-point estimation: instead of one number, ask for three: optimistic O (if everything goes well), most likely M, and pessimistic P (if many things go wrong, but not a disaster). Two formulas are common. The triangular mean is (O + M + P) / 3. The beta or PERT mean is (O + 4M + P) / 6, which gives the most likely value more weight. The PERT standard deviation is approximated by (P minus O) / 6. You saw the probability side of PERT in Operations Research (deep-cse-6-10, lesson 16); here we focus on using it.

Three-point worked: integrating the mobile-wallet payment is estimated at O = 6 days, M = 10 days, P = 20 days. Triangular mean = (6 + 10 + 20) / 3 = 12 days. PERT mean = (6 + 40 + 20) / 6 = 66 / 6 = 11 days. Standard deviation = (20 minus 6) / 6 = 14 / 6, about 2.33 days. Notice the mean is above the most likely value of 10: because things can go much worse than they can go better, the distribution is skewed to the right. A single-number estimate of 10 days would be beaten less than half the time.

Adding estimates: suppose three tasks happen one after another: payment integration (O 6, M 10, P 20), order history (O 5, M 8, P 11) and receipts (O 3, M 5, P 7). PERT means are 11, 8 and 5 days, total 24 days. Standard deviations are 2.33, 1.00 and 0.67. You might think the total standard deviation is 2.33 + 1 + 0.67 = 4, but if the tasks are independent, variances add, not standard deviations. Variances: 2.33 squared is 5.44, plus 1, plus 0.44, total 6.89. The total standard deviation is the square root of 6.89, about 2.62 days. Some tasks run late while others run early, and they partly cancel.

Turning that into a range: if the total roughly follows a normal distribution, about 68 percent of outcomes fall within one standard deviation of the mean, and about 95 percent within two. So the three tasks will finish in 24 plus or minus 2.62 days with about 68 percent confidence, and roughly between 18.8 and 29.2 days with about 95 percent confidence. Presenting 24 days, likely between 21 and 27 is far more honest, and more useful, than saying 24 days.

Buffers, Parkinson and the student syndrome: managers sometimes pad every task estimate secretly. That backfires because of two human habits. Parkinson's law says work expands to fill the time available: give someone 10 days for a 6-day task and it will take 10. The student syndrome says people start working seriously only near the deadline, wasting the safety time at the start. A better practice is to estimate tasks honestly near their mean and keep a visible shared buffer at the end of the project or of each release. Lesson 11 shows how critical chain scheduling does this.

Habits that improve estimates: break work down small (lesson 06); include all categories of work, including testing, reviews, meetings and deployment; let the people who will do the work estimate; use more than one method and compare; give ranges, not single points; record actual effort and compare with estimates after each project; re-estimate as the cone narrows; and never let a target silently replace an estimate. Reference class forecasting, also from Kahneman's work, formalises the analogy idea: look at how long the class of similar projects actually took, and start from there instead of from your hopeful inside view.

Real-life example 1, the bank integration: a vendor estimated 2 weeks to connect a bank's app to a new payment switch, based on the switch's documentation. Nobody asked for a three-point estimate. The sandbox turned out to be down often and the documentation was outdated. It took 7 weeks. An honest pessimistic estimate of 6 to 8 weeks, with a buffer, would have let the bank plan its marketing correctly instead of cancelling a launch event.

Real-life example 2, a student team: five students used planning poker for their final-year project. On the story upload photos of a damaged road to report it, votes were 3, 3, 5, 3 and 13. The student who voted 13 explained that phones produce big images that must be compressed and that the free cloud storage tier had a size limit. Nobody else had thought of it. The team re-voted 8, split the story into two, and avoided a nasty surprise in week 10.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: treating targets as estimates; giving single-point estimates; adding standard deviations instead of variances; forgetting non-coding work; and padding secretly. Exams often ask you to explain the cone of uncertainty, compute triangular and PERT estimates and standard deviations, describe Wideband Delphi or planning poker, compare top-down with bottom-up, and explain Parkinson's law and the planning fallacy.

Recap: estimate size, effort and duration; keep estimates, targets and commitments separate. Uncertainty is huge early, from 0.25x to 4x at concept, and narrows only as decisions are made. Use top-down and bottom-up, analogy, Wideband Delphi and planning poker. Three-point estimates give a mean and a standard deviation; for tasks in sequence, add means and add variances. Give ranges and keep visible shared buffers. Next lesson: measuring software size by its functions, with function point analysis.
key_points: Estimate size, effort and duration; cost mostly follows from effort.
An estimate is a prediction, a target is a business wish, a commitment is a promise; don't let targets replace estimates.
The cone of uncertainty runs from about 0.25x to 4x at concept and narrows only as decisions remove uncertainty.
Use top-down and bottom-up estimates together, plus analogy from recorded past projects.
Wideband Delphi and planning poker gather independent estimates, then discuss the extremes and re-estimate.
Triangular mean = (O + M + P) / 3; PERT mean = (O + 4M + P) / 6; PERT standard deviation = (P minus O) / 6.
For independent tasks in sequence, means add and variances add; standard deviations do not simply add.
Give ranges and keep visible shared buffers; secret padding is eaten by Parkinson's law and student syndrome.
lessons.tip: For one week, write down how long you think each of your study tasks will take, then record how long it actually took. Most people discover they underestimate by 30 to 50 percent, and knowing your own bias is the first step to better estimates.
lessons.task: Pick three tasks from a real assignment. For each, write O, M and P in hours. Compute the PERT mean and standard deviation of each, then the total mean and total standard deviation (add the variances, then take the square root). Write the total as a range with about 95 percent confidence and compare it with what actually happens.

quiz.q: A task has O = 6, M = 10, P = 20 days. What is the PERT (beta) mean?
Three independent tasks in sequence have standard deviations 2.33, 1.00 and 0.67 days. The total standard deviation is about:
quiz.explain: Variances add: 5.44 + 1 + 0.44 = 6.89; the square root is about 2.62 days.

quiz.q: At the initial concept stage, the cone of uncertainty says actual effort may range roughly from:
quiz.explain: McConnell's cone shows about 0.25x to 4x at the concept stage, narrowing as decisions are made.

quiz.q: Work expands to fill the time available is known as:
quiz.explain: Parkinson's law describes work stretching to fill the given time, which is why hidden padding gets wasted.

quiz.q: Why do planning poker teams reveal their cards at the same time?
options: So the first number spoken does not anchor everyone else's estimate
Because the Scrum Master must approve each card
So the highest number wins automatically
quiz.explain: Simultaneous reveal keeps estimates independent; then the extremes explain their reasoning.

lessons.title: Function Point Analysis
lessons.content:
How big is a house? You could count the bricks, but a house built with small bricks would look bigger than the same house built with large ones. Builders instead measure floor area in square feet, which tells you how much house you get, whatever the bricks. Software has the same problem. Counting lines of code is like counting bricks: the same feature might be 50 lines in one language and 300 in another, and a careless programmer writes more lines than a skilled one. Function point analysis measures software by what it does for the user, like square feet for software.

Why not lines of code: LOC is easy to count after the code exists, but it has serious problems for project managers. You cannot count lines before the code is written, which is exactly when you need the estimate. LOC depends on the language and coding style. It rewards verbose code: a programmer who writes a function in 20 lines looks less productive than one who writes the same thing in 60. And it ignores non-code work like design. Function points were created to fix these problems by measuring functionality from the requirements, before coding starts.

History: Allan Albrecht at IBM introduced function points in 1979. The International Function Point Users Group, IFPUG, founded in 1986, maintains the most widely used counting rules, and the method is also standardised as ISO/IEC 20926. Other function point methods exist, such as COSMIC (ISO/IEC 19761), which suits real-time and embedded software better, but IFPUG is the version most often taught and asked in exams.

The boundary and the user view: before counting, you draw the application boundary, the line between the software you are measuring and the outside world: users and other systems. Then you count only what is visible from the user's point of view: data the system stores, and the ways data moves in and out across the boundary. Internal technical details, like which database or framework you use, do not count. This is what makes function points independent of technology.

The five components: IFPUG counts five types of things. Two are data functions. An internal logical file, ILF, is a group of related data that the application maintains, like the orders file or the restaurants file in DhakaEats. An external interface file, EIF, is a group of data the application uses but which is maintained by another application, like map data from a map service. Three are transaction functions. An external input, EI, brings data in from outside and usually updates an ILF, like placing an order or registering. An external output, EO, sends data out with some processing, such as calculations or derived data, like a restaurant's monthly sales report. An external inquiry, EQ, is a simple retrieval with no calculations, like looking up an order's status.

EO vs EQ, the classic confusion: both send data out. The test is whether processing logic is involved. If the output contains calculated totals, derived data or updates something, it is an EO. If it just retrieves and shows stored data, it is an EQ. Viewing a restaurant's menu is an EQ. A rider's weekly earnings statement that adds up deliveries and bonuses is an EO.

Complexity weights: each item is rated low, average or high complexity, using counts of data element types (DETs, roughly unique user-recognisable fields) and record element types or file types referenced (RETs or FTRs). Then each rating has a fixed weight. For EI: low 3, average 4, high 6. For EO: low 4, average 5, high 7. For EQ: low 3, average 4, high 6. For ILF: low 7, average 10, high 15. For EIF: low 5, average 7, high 10. Notice the stored data files have the largest weights, because maintaining data is a big part of what software does.

Counting DhakaEats, external inputs: the team lists 12 EIs, such as register customer, log in, add to cart, place order, rate rider, restaurant updates menu, rider updates delivery status and admin adds restaurant. Rated: 5 low, 5 average, 2 high. Points: 5 x 3 + 5 x 4 + 2 x 6 = 15 + 20 + 12 = 47.

External outputs and inquiries: 6 EOs, such as order receipt with totals and VAT, restaurant sales report, admin daily summary and rider earnings statement: 2 low, 3 average, 1 high, giving 2 x 4 + 3 x 5 + 1 x 7 = 8 + 15 + 7 = 30. 8 EQs, such as search restaurants, view menu, view order status and view order history: 4 low, 3 average, 1 high, giving 4 x 3 + 3 x 4 + 1 x 6 = 12 + 12 + 6 = 30.

Files: 6 ILFs: users, restaurants, menu items, orders, riders and payments. Rated 2 low, 3 average, 1 high: 2 x 7 + 3 x 10 + 1 x 15 = 14 + 30 + 15 = 59. 3 EIFs: map service data, payment gateway data and SMS gateway data: 2 low and 1 average, giving 2 x 5 + 1 x 7 = 10 + 7 = 17.

Unadjusted function points: add them all. UFP = 47 + 30 + 30 + 59 + 17 = 183. This number measures how much functionality DhakaEats provides to its users, regardless of whether it is written in Kotlin, Dart or Java.

The value adjustment factor: the classic IFPUG method then adjusts for general system characteristics. There are 14 of them: data communications, distributed data processing, performance, heavily used configuration, transaction rate, online data entry, end-user efficiency, online update, complex processing, reusability, installation ease, operational ease, multiple sites, and facilitate change. Each is rated from 0 (no influence) to 5 (strong influence). Their sum is the total degree of influence, TDI, which ranges from 0 to 70. Then VAF = 0.65 + 0.01 x TDI, which ranges from 0.65 to 1.35, so the adjustment can change the count by at most 35 percent either way.

Adjusted FP, worked: DhakaEats is online, needs fast responses at lunch and dinner peaks, has many online updates and runs on many devices, so the team rates the 14 characteristics and gets TDI = 42. VAF = 0.65 + 0.01 x 42 = 0.65 + 0.42 = 1.07. Adjusted function points = UFP x VAF = 183 x 1.07 = 195.81, about 196 FP. Note that newer IFPUG practice treats the VAF as optional, and the ISO version counts unadjusted points only, because many organisations found it better to handle technical factors in the effort model instead. Exams still commonly ask for it, so know both.

From function points to effort: function points measure size, not effort. To get effort you need productivity, ideally from your own history: how many function points does your team deliver per person-month? Suppose MeghSoft's past projects averaged about 6.5 FP per person-month. Effort = 196 / 6.5, about 30.2 person-months, which agrees nicely with the bottom-up WBS estimate of 130 person-weeks, about 30 person-months, from lesson 06. When two independent methods agree, confidence rises. When they disagree a lot, it is a signal to look for missing work or wrong assumptions.

From function points to lines of code: sometimes you need a LOC estimate, for example to feed a COCOMO model (lesson 09). Backfiring converts FP to LOC using an average number of lines per function point for a language. Published tables exist, but the ratio varies a lot between sources and teams, so the best ratio is your own. If MeghSoft's history shows about 50 lines of Kotlin per function point, DhakaEats is about 196 x 50 = 9,800 lines, roughly 9.8 KLOC. Treat backfired numbers as rough.

Strengths and weaknesses: function points are independent of language, can be counted from requirements before coding, are understandable by non-programmers (clients recognise inputs, outputs and files), and allow fair comparisons of productivity across projects. On the other hand, counting needs training and judgement, takes time on big systems, and does not capture algorithmic difficulty well; a tiny screen that calls a complex pricing algorithm may count as just one simple input. Certified counters exist precisely because consistency is hard.

Other sizing methods: use case points, proposed by Gustav Karner in 1993, size a system from its use cases and actors, weighted by complexity, then adjust for technical and environmental factors. Story points, used by agile teams, are relative sizes agreed within one team; they are excellent for that team's planning but cannot be compared between teams, because one team's 5 is not another's 5. Object points and feature counts also exist. The common idea: measure what the user gets, then convert to effort using real history.

Real-life example 1, comparing vendors: a government agency received two bids for a citizen-services portal. Vendor A planned only 15 person-months of effort; Vendor B planned about 60. An independent consultant counted about 450 function points from the requirements. Vendor A's plan implied 450 / 15 = 30 FP per person-month, while the agency's own past projects had delivered around 7 to 9. Vendor B's plan implied 450 / 60 = 7.5, right in that range. Vendor A had clearly not understood the scope, and a cheap bid would have turned into a late, expensive argument. Function points gave the buyer an objective size to judge bids.

Real-life example 2, measuring improvement: a software company in Dhaka counted function points on every finished project for two years. When they adopted automated testing and code review, their delivered FP per person-month rose by about a fifth, and defects per hundred FP fell. Because function points do not change with coding style, the comparison was fair; counting lines would have hidden the improvement, since the cleaner code was actually shorter.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: counting technical things like database tables instead of user-recognisable data groups; confusing EO and EQ; counting EIFs as ILFs; forgetting that VAF ranges from 0.65 to 1.35; and treating FP as effort. Exams usually give a table of counts with complexities and ask for UFP, then give 14 ratings or a TDI and ask for VAF and adjusted FP, sometimes followed by effort from a productivity figure. Practise the weight table until it is automatic, and always show each multiplication, because examiners give marks for the working, not just the final number.

Recap: function points measure software size by user-visible functionality, independent of language. Count five components: EI, EO, EQ, ILF and EIF, each weighted by complexity (EI 3/4/6, EO 4/5/7, EQ 3/4/6, ILF 7/10/15, EIF 5/7/10). Sum to get UFP. Optionally apply VAF = 0.65 + 0.01 x TDI with TDI from 14 characteristics. DhakaEats: UFP 183, TDI 42, VAF 1.07, about 196 FP, about 30 person-months at 6.5 FP per person-month. Next lesson: COCOMO models that turn size into effort and schedule.
key_points: Function points measure size by functionality visible to the user, independent of programming language.
Five IFPUG components: external inputs, external outputs, external inquiries, internal logical files and external interface files.
EO involves calculation or derived data; EQ is a simple retrieval with no processing.
Weights (low/average/high): EI 3/4/6, EO 4/5/7, EQ 3/4/6, ILF 7/10/15, EIF 5/7/10.
VAF = 0.65 + 0.01 x TDI, where TDI is the sum of 14 characteristics rated 0 to 5, so VAF ranges from 0.65 to 1.35.
DhakaEats: UFP 183, VAF 1.07, about 196 FP.
Effort = FP / productivity from your own history; DhakaEats at 6.5 FP per person-month needs about 30 person-months.
FP can be counted from requirements and compared across projects, but needs training and misses algorithmic complexity.
lessons.tip: Memorise the weight table as three rows of the same pattern: inputs and inquiries 3-4-6, outputs one higher 4-5-7, and files much heavier, internal 7-10-15 and external 5-7-10.
lessons.task: Take a simple app you use, such as a bus-ticket booking app. List its EIs, EOs, EQs, ILFs and EIFs, rate each as low, average or high, and compute UFP. Then rate the 14 characteristics quickly, compute VAF and adjusted FP, and estimate effort assuming 8 FP per person-month.

quiz.q: A rider's weekly earnings statement that adds up deliveries and bonuses is counted as:
quiz.explain: It sends data out with calculations, so it is an EO, not a simple EQ retrieval.

quiz.q: If TDI = 42, what is the VAF?
What is the possible range of the IFPUG value adjustment factor?
quiz.explain: TDI runs from 0 to 70, so VAF = 0.65 + 0.01 x TDI runs from 0.65 to 1.35.

quiz.q: Map data supplied and maintained by an outside map service is counted as:
quiz.explain: Data used by the application but maintained by another application is an EIF.

quiz.q: An application has 196 FP and the team delivers 7 FP per person-month. Effort is about:
quiz.explain: Effort = 196 / 7 = 28 person-months.

lessons.title: COCOMO Models
lessons.content:
A doctor can estimate a child's adult height from the child's current height, age and parents' heights, using a formula built from thousands of measured children. It will not be exact for any one child, but it is a useful, unbiased starting point. COCOMO is the same idea for software: a set of formulas, built by Barry Boehm from data on many real projects, that turn software size into estimated effort and schedule. In Software Engineering (deep-cse-4-4, lesson 23) you met basic COCOMO. Here we go further: intermediate COCOMO, COCOMO II, the schedule equation, and how a manager should use these numbers.

What COCOMO is: COCOMO stands for COnstructive COst MOdel. Boehm published the first version in his 1981 book Software Engineering Economics, based on 63 projects. It is called constructive because the model is open: you can see every formula and every factor, unlike black-box tools. The original model, now called COCOMO 81, has three levels: basic, intermediate and detailed. COCOMO II, published around 2000, updated it for modern development practices.

The three project modes: COCOMO 81 classifies a project into one of three modes. Organic: a small, experienced team working on a familiar kind of software with flexible requirements, like an in-house business application. Semi-detached: a medium mix, with some team experience and some rigid requirements, like a new transaction-processing system. Embedded: tight hardware, software and regulatory constraints, little room to relax requirements, like flight control or a payment switch with strict standards.

Basic COCOMO formulas: effort E = a x (KLOC)^b person-months, and development time D = c x E^d months, where KLOC is thousands of delivered lines of source code. The constants are: organic a = 2.4, b = 1.05, c = 2.5, d = 0.38; semi-detached a = 3.0, b = 1.12, c = 2.5, d = 0.35; embedded a = 3.6, b = 1.20, c = 2.5, d = 0.32. Average staff = E / D people. Productivity = KLOC / E.

Basic COCOMO worked for DhakaEats: lesson 08 gave about 9.8 KLOC by backfiring. Treating it as organic: E = 2.4 x 9.8^1.05, about 26.4 person-months. D = 2.5 x 26.4^0.38, about 8.7 months. Average staff = 26.4 / 8.7, about 3 people. If we wrongly treated it as semi-detached: E is about 38.7 person-months and D about 9.0 months. As embedded: E is about 55.7 person-months and D about 9.1 months. The mode choice changes effort hugely, so it must be justified, not picked to get a nice number.

A comparison at larger size: for 32 KLOC, organic gives about 91 person-months over about 13.9 months, an average of about 6.6 people. Embedded gives about 230 person-months over about 14.3 months. Notice something interesting: the schedule barely changes between modes, but effort more than doubles. Harder projects need more people working in parallel, not much more calendar time.

Diseconomy of scale: the exponent b is greater than 1 in every mode. That means doubling the size more than doubles the effort. For organic, 2^1.05 is about 2.07, so twice the code needs about 2.07 times the effort; for embedded, 2^1.20 is about 2.30. The reason is that bigger systems need more communication, more integration, more coordination and more testing of interactions. This is one mathematical reason why splitting a big system into smaller, independent releases often saves effort.

Intermediate COCOMO: basic COCOMO uses size alone. Intermediate COCOMO adds 15 cost drivers grouped into four kinds: product attributes (required reliability RELY, database size DATA, product complexity CPLX), computer attributes (execution time constraint, main storage constraint, platform volatility, turnaround time), personnel attributes (analyst capability ACAP, applications experience AEXP, programmer capability PCAP, platform experience, language experience) and project attributes (modern programming practices, use of software tools TOOL, required development schedule SCED). Each driver is rated from very low to extra high, and each rating maps to a multiplier near 1. Their product is the effort adjustment factor, EAF.

Intermediate formulas: effort E = a x (KLOC)^b x EAF, where the exponents b are the same as basic but the coefficients a differ: organic 3.2, semi-detached 3.0, embedded 2.8. Some typical multipliers: RELY high 1.15 and very high 1.40; CPLX high 1.15; ACAP high 0.86, meaning strong analysts reduce effort by 14 percent; PCAP high 0.86; TOOL high 0.91. A multiplier above 1 increases effort; below 1 decreases it.

Intermediate worked for DhakaEats: nominal effort = 3.2 x 9.8^1.05, about 35.2 person-months. MeghSoft rates RELY high (money moves through the app, 1.15), CPLX high (real-time tracking and payments, 1.15), ACAP high (0.86) and PCAP high (0.86), with all others nominal at 1.00. EAF = 1.15 x 1.15 x 0.86 x 0.86, about 0.98. Adjusted effort = 35.2 x 0.98, about 34.4 person-months. The high reliability and complexity push effort up; the capable team pulls it back down. Without the strong team, the estimate would be about 35.2 x 1.15 x 1.15, roughly 46.5 person-months.

COCOMO II: by the 1990s, development had changed: reuse, components, object-oriented languages, iterative processes and rapid prototyping. COCOMO II offers models for different stages: an application composition model for early prototyping, an early design model with 7 effort multipliers, and a post-architecture model with 17 effort multipliers. Size can be measured in thousands of source lines or derived from function points. The core equation is PM = A x Size^E x (product of effort multipliers), with A = 2.94 in the COCOMO II.2000 calibration.

Scale factors: instead of three fixed modes, COCOMO II computes the exponent from five scale factors: precedentedness PREC (have we built something like this before?), development flexibility FLEX, architecture and risk resolution RESL, team cohesion TEAM, and process maturity PMAT. E = B + 0.01 x (sum of scale factors), with B = 0.91. At nominal ratings the five values are 3.72, 3.04, 4.24, 3.29 and 4.68, summing to 18.97, so E = 0.91 + 0.1897, about 1.10. Better ratings lower the exponent: a team that has done similar work, has a clear architecture and works well together suffers less diseconomy of scale.

COCOMO II worked: with Size 9.8 KSLOC, all effort multipliers nominal and E = 1.0997: PM = 2.94 x 9.8^1.0997, about 36.2 person-months. The schedule equation is TDEV = C x PM^F with C = 3.67 and F = 0.28 + 0.2 x (E minus 0.91), which gives F = 0.28 + 0.2 x 0.1897, about 0.318. TDEV = 3.67 x 36.2^0.318, about 11.5 months. Average staff about 36.2 / 11.5, roughly 3.1 people.

What counts as a line: COCOMO 81 counts delivered source instructions, meaning code that is actually shipped as part of the product, not comment lines and not throwaway test scaffolding. COCOMO II counts logical source lines with a standard checklist. Reused or adapted code is not counted at full size: the models convert it into an equivalent number of new lines, depending on how much of its design, code and tests must be changed and how well the team understands it. That is why reusing MeghSoft's grocery-app modules, discussed below, really does shrink the estimate, but not to zero, because adapting and testing reused code still costs effort.

The schedule warning: every model above says DhakaEats nominally needs roughly 8.7 to 11.5 months, while the client wants 6. Boehm's research suggests that compressing a schedule below about 75 percent of the nominal value is extremely risky, often called the impossible zone, because adding people stops helping (lesson 12). Even the most optimistic nominal of 8.7 months gives 0.75 x 8.7, about 6.5 months, as the realistic minimum, and 6 / 8.7 is only about 69 percent. This is exactly what models are for: an early, objective warning. MeghSoft responds by reusing the login, cart and payment modules from its earlier grocery app, which cuts new code, and by agreeing with the client that reports and rider ratings will come in release 1.1 a few weeks after launch.

Using models wisely: the constants were calibrated on old data from other organisations, so the absolute numbers can be off by a large margin for your team. The real power comes from calibration: fit a and the multipliers to your own completed projects. Use models as a sanity check against bottom-up and analogy estimates, as a way to discuss trade-offs (what if we use a less experienced team? what if reliability must be very high?), and as an early warning when a deadline is unrealistic. Never present a model output with more precision than the inputs justify; 34.4 person-months really means roughly 30 to 40.

Real-life example 1, a tender evaluation: a ministry asked bidders for a 14-month delivery of a large records system. An evaluator sized it at about 60 KLOC, semi-detached. Basic COCOMO gives E = 3.0 x 60^1.12, about 294 person-months, and D = 2.5 x 294^0.35, about 18.3 months. A 14-month deadline is about 76 percent of nominal, right at the edge of the impossible zone. The evaluator recommended phasing the project into two releases, which later proved wise when the first release itself ran several weeks late.

Real-life example 2, team experience: a startup compared two staffing options for a fintech app in COCOMO II: a team of experienced developers who had built payment systems before, and a cheaper team new to the domain. Rating precedentedness, team cohesion and application experience differently changed the effort estimate by more than 40 percent. Even with higher salaries, the experienced team came out cheaper overall and faster, a conclusion the founders had not expected.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: using lines of code that include comments or generated code inconsistently; choosing the mode to get a desired answer; mixing basic and intermediate coefficients (2.4 vs 3.2 for organic); forgetting that D uses E, not KLOC; and quoting results with false precision. Exams typically give KLOC and a mode and ask for E, D, average staff and productivity, or give cost driver ratings and ask for EAF and adjusted effort. Know the constant table and practise with a calculator that can do powers, and always state which mode and which model level you used before writing any number.

Recap: COCOMO turns size into effort and schedule. Basic: E = a x KLOC^b, D = 2.5 x E^d, with organic 2.4 and 1.05, semi-detached 3.0 and 1.12, embedded 3.6 and 1.20 (d = 0.38, 0.35, 0.32). Intermediate multiplies by an EAF from 15 cost drivers with a = 3.2, 3.0, 2.8. COCOMO II uses PM = 2.94 x Size^E x product of EMs, with E = 0.91 + 0.01 x sum of five scale factors, and TDEV = 3.67 x PM^F. Exponents above 1 mean diseconomy of scale. For DhakaEats the models give about 26 to 36 person-months and 8.7 to 11.5 months nominal, warning that 6 months needs reuse and phased scope. Next lesson: turning activities into a network and finding the critical path.
key_points: COCOMO turns size into effort and schedule; Boehm published COCOMO 81 in 1981 and COCOMO II around 2000.
Basic: E = a x KLOC^b, D = 2.5 x E^d; organic 2.4/1.05/0.38, semi-detached 3.0/1.12/0.35, embedded 3.6/1.20/0.32.
Exponents above 1 cause diseconomy of scale: doubling size more than doubles effort.
Intermediate COCOMO multiplies by an effort adjustment factor from 15 cost drivers, with a = 3.2, 3.0, 2.8.
COCOMO II: PM = 2.94 x Size^E x product of effort multipliers, E = 0.91 + 0.01 x sum of five scale factors.
COCOMO II schedule: TDEV = 3.67 x PM^F, F = 0.28 + 0.2 x (E minus 0.91).
Compressing a schedule below about 75 percent of nominal is considered extremely risky.
Calibrate models to your own history and use them as sanity checks and early warnings, not exact answers.
lessons.tip: Make a one-line spreadsheet with KLOC, a, b, c, d and formulas for E, D and staff. Changing the mode or a driver and watching the numbers move teaches the model faster than memorising it.
lessons.task: Estimate a 20 KLOC hospital appointment system with basic COCOMO in all three modes. Compute E, D and average staff for each. Then choose the mode you think fits, justify it in two sentences, and say whether a 9-month deadline is realistic using the 75 percent rule.

quiz.q: In basic COCOMO, which mode has a = 2.4 and b = 1.05?
quiz.explain: Organic uses a = 2.4, b = 1.05; semi-detached 3.0 and 1.12; embedded 3.6 and 1.20.

quiz.q: Why does doubling size more than double effort in COCOMO?
options: Because programmers get slower with age
Because the exponent is above 1, reflecting extra communication and integration
It does not; effort grows linearly
quiz.explain: With b > 1, effort grows faster than size: the diseconomy of scale.

quiz.q: Intermediate COCOMO drivers RELY = 1.15 and ACAP = 0.86, others nominal. What is the EAF?
quiz.explain: EAF is the product of multipliers: 1.15 x 0.86 = 0.989, about 0.99.

quiz.q: In COCOMO II, what determines the exponent E?
quiz.explain: E = 0.91 + 0.01 x sum of scale factors (PREC, FLEX, RESL, TEAM, PMAT).

quiz.q: A model gives a nominal schedule of 10 months. The client demands 6 months. What does the 75 percent rule suggest?
options: 6 months is well below 7.5 months and extremely risky; reduce or phase scope
6 months is easy if more people are added
Any schedule is achievable with overtime
quiz.explain: 75 percent of 10 months is 7.5 months; 6 months is deep in the very risky zone, so scope or plan must change.

lessons.title: Activity Planning and Network Diagrams
lessons.content:
Making a pot of morog polao for guests: you cannot fry the chicken before you buy it, and you cannot serve before the rice is cooked. But while the rice soaks, someone can fry onions, and while the chicken simmers, someone else can make the salad. Some steps must wait for others; some can run side by side. If you want to know the earliest time dinner can be served, you have to find the longest chain of steps that must happen one after another. That chain is the critical path, and finding it for a software project is the subject of this lesson.

From WBS to activities: lesson 06 broke DhakaEats into work packages. Now each work package is turned into activities, the scheduled pieces of work with a duration, resources and dependencies. For a short exam-sized example we will work at a higher level, treating each big chunk as one activity, measured in weeks. On a real project you would do the same steps with dozens or hundreds of smaller activities, usually inside a tool such as MS Project, Jira's timeline or a spreadsheet.

Milestones: a milestone is a significant point or event with zero duration, such as requirements signed off, beta released or go-live. Milestones do not consume time or resources; they mark moments to check progress and often trigger payments in contracts. A schedule without milestones is hard for clients and sponsors to follow.

Dependency types: the most common relationship is finish-to-start (FS): B cannot start until A finishes, like testing a module after it is built. Start-to-start (SS): B cannot start until A starts, like writing user guides that can begin once development begins. Finish-to-finish (FF): B cannot finish until A finishes, like documentation that cannot be completed until the last feature is completed. Start-to-finish (SF) is rare: B cannot finish until A starts, like the old payment system that must keep running until the new one starts. About nine in ten software dependencies are FS.

Leads and lags: a lag is a forced waiting time added to a dependency. If the client needs 1 week to review designs before development starts, that is FS with a 1-week lag. A lead lets the successor start early: testers start writing test cases 2 weeks before coding finishes, an FS with a 2-week lead, which is the same as a negative lag. Leads and lags let you model reality without inventing fake activities.

Kinds of dependency by origin: mandatory dependencies, also called hard logic, are required by the nature of the work: you cannot test code that does not exist. Discretionary dependencies, also called soft or preferred logic, are choices based on best practice: we prefer to finish the design before coding. These are the first ones to relax when you need to speed up (lesson 11). External dependencies involve outside parties: the payment provider must issue sandbox credentials. Internal dependencies are within the project's control.

Activity-on-node: the standard way to draw a network today is activity-on-node (AON), also called the precedence diagramming method. Each activity is a box (node), and arrows show dependencies. The older activity-on-arrow method put activities on arrows and sometimes needed dummy activities; you may still see it in some textbooks, but AON is what modern tools use and is easier to read.

The DhakaEats network: here are the activities, durations in weeks, and predecessors. A Requirements and design, 4, none. B Backend core and APIs, 8, after A. C Customer app, 9, after A. D Rider app, 6, after A. J Rider onboarding material, 1, after D. E Restaurant panel, 5, after B (it needs the APIs). F Payment integration, 4, after B. G Integration and system testing, 4, after C, J, E and F. H Beta with pilot restaurants, 3, after G. I Training and go-live, 2, after H.

Forward pass: the forward pass computes each activity's early start (ES) and early finish (EF) from left to right. ES is the largest EF among its predecessors (0 for the first); EF = ES + duration. A: 0 to 4. B, C and D all start at 4: B ends 12, C ends 13, D ends 10. J: 10 to 11. E and F start at 12 (after B): E ends 17, F ends 16. G must wait for all of C (13), J (11), E (17) and F (16), so ES = 17 and EF = 21. H: 21 to 24. I: 24 to 26. The project's earliest finish is 26 weeks, about 6 months.

Backward pass: the backward pass computes late finish (LF) and late start (LS) from right to left. For the last activity, LF = project finish. For others, LF is the smallest LS among successors; LS = LF minus duration. I: LF 26, LS 24. H: LF 24, LS 21. G: LF 21, LS 17. E: LF 17, LS 12. F: LF 17, LS 13. C: LF 17, LS 8. J: LF 17, LS 16. D: LF = LS of J = 16, so LS = 10. B: LF = smallest of E's LS 12 and F's LS 13, so 12, and LS = 4. A: LF = smallest of B 4, C 8, D 10, so 4, and LS = 0.

Total float: total float (or slack) = LS minus ES (or LF minus EF). It is how long an activity can be delayed without delaying the project. A, B, E, G, H and I have 0. F has 13 minus 12 = 1 week. C has 8 minus 4 = 4 weeks. D has 10 minus 4 = 6 weeks, and J also has 16 minus 10 = 6 weeks.

The critical path: the critical path is the longest path through the network, and its activities have zero total float (when the deadline equals the earliest finish). Here: A, B, E, G, H, I with durations 4 + 8 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 26 weeks. Any delay on these delays go-live. Surprised that the restaurant panel is critical and the customer app is not? That is the value of the calculation: intuition says the customer app is the main thing, but the panel waits for the backend APIs, which makes its chain the longest.

Free float: free float is how long an activity can be delayed without delaying the early start of any successor. Free float = smallest ES of successors minus EF. C: 17 minus 13 = 4, same as its total float. F: 17 minus 16 = 1. But D: its successor J has ES 10 and D's EF is 10, so D's free float is 0, even though its total float is 6. If D slips by 2 weeks, the project is fine, but J must also move 2 weeks later, using up J's float. D and J share the same 6 weeks of float along their chain. J's free float is 17 minus 11 = 6.

Near-critical paths: F has only 1 week of float. A path with very little float is near-critical: a small delay makes it critical. In DhakaEats, payment integration depends on an external provider's sandbox, so a 2-week delay there is quite possible; it would push G to start at week 18 and go-live to week 27. Good managers watch near-critical paths almost as closely as the critical path, and do not trust a schedule just because only one path is red.

Negative float: what if the client insists on go-live at week 25, one week earlier than the earliest finish? Start the backward pass from LF = 25 instead of 26. Every activity on the critical path then gets LS minus ES = minus 1: negative float. Negative float is a loud alarm: the plan, as drawn, cannot meet the deadline, and the critical activities must together be shortened by 1 week, or the deadline or scope must change. Tools show negative float in red for exactly this reason.

How managers use this: the critical path tells you where to put your best people and where to focus risk management. Float tells you where you have room to move people or absorb small problems: the customer app team, with 4 weeks of float, could lend a developer to the critical restaurant panel for a while if their skills fit. A change request that adds 2 weeks to C costs no schedule; the same request on E costs 2 weeks. Lesson 11 uses these ideas for compressing and building the schedule.

Recap of the method from Operations Research: you learned the full mathematics in deep-cse-6-10, lesson 15, including AON drawing rules and the algorithms. The manager's addition is judgement: durations are estimates (lesson 07), so the critical path can change as work proceeds; recompute it whenever actuals arrive. A schedule computed once at the start and never updated is fiction.

Real-life example 1, a university admission system: the IT office had to open online admission on a fixed date. Their network showed the critical path ran through the payment gateway contract with a bank, an external dependency, not through any coding. The manager started the contract process in week 1 instead of week 6, and the system opened on time. Teams that only think about code often miss that the longest chain is paperwork.

Real-life example 2, a Pohela Boishakh campaign: a marketing team needed a new app feature for a Pohela Boishakh promotion. Their network revealed that app store review, which can take days, sat on the critical path at the very end with no float. They added a 1-week lead to submit a version earlier for review, and kept a fallback that could switch the campaign on remotely. The feature went live on the morning of the festival.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: thinking the critical path is the shortest path; forgetting to take the maximum EF in the forward pass and the minimum LS in the backward pass; confusing total and free float; treating all dependencies as mandatory; and ignoring near-critical paths. Exams usually give an activity table and ask you to draw the AON network, do forward and backward passes, list ES, EF, LS, LF and float, identify the critical path and project duration, and sometimes say what happens if one activity is delayed.

Recap: break work packages into activities, add milestones, and record dependencies (FS, SS, FF, SF), leads and lags, and whether each is mandatory, discretionary or external. Draw an AON network. The forward pass gives ES and EF and the project duration; the backward pass gives LS and LF. Total float = LS minus ES; free float = earliest successor ES minus EF. The critical path is the longest path, with zero float. For DhakaEats: A-B-E-G-H-I, 26 weeks, with payment integration near-critical at 1 week of float. Next lesson: turning the network into a real schedule and compressing it when needed.
key_points: Activities come from work packages; milestones are zero-duration checkpoints.
Dependencies: finish-to-start (most common), start-to-start, finish-to-finish and start-to-finish; leads and lags adjust timing.
Mandatory dependencies come from the work itself; discretionary ones are choices that can be relaxed; external ones involve outsiders.
Forward pass: ES = max EF of predecessors, EF = ES + duration; backward pass: LF = min LS of successors, LS = LF minus duration.
Total float = LS minus ES; free float = earliest ES of successors minus EF.
The critical path is the longest path, with zero float; it sets the earliest finish.
DhakaEats critical path A-B-E-G-H-I takes 26 weeks; payment integration is near-critical with 1 week of float.
Recompute the critical path as actual progress arrives; it can move.
lessons.tip: When doing a forward or backward pass by hand, write ES and EF above each box and LS and LF below it. Most exam mistakes come from forgetting to take the maximum at merge points going forward and the minimum at burst points going backward.
lessons.task: Draw the DhakaEats network on paper from the activity table in this lesson and repeat the forward and backward passes yourself. Then change the payment integration from 4 to 7 weeks and recompute: what is the new duration and critical path?

quiz.q: Testers start writing test cases 2 weeks before coding finishes. This is modelled as:
quiz.explain: A lead lets the successor start before the predecessor finishes; it is a negative lag.

quiz.q: In the forward pass, an activity with predecessors finishing at weeks 13, 11, 17 and 16 has an early start of:
quiz.explain: ES is the maximum EF of all predecessors: 17.

quiz.q: Activity D has ES 4, LS 10, EF 10, and its only successor starts early at week 10. What are its total and free float?
quiz.explain: Total float = 10 minus 4 = 6. Free float = 10 minus 10 = 0, so delaying D pushes its successor.

quiz.q: Which statement about the critical path is correct?
options: It is the shortest path through the network
It is the longest path, and delays on it delay the project
It always contains the most expensive activities
quiz.explain: The longest path sets the minimum project duration; its activities have zero float.

quiz.q: We prefer to finish design before coding, though it is not strictly necessary. This is a:
quiz.explain: Discretionary (soft) logic comes from preference or best practice and can be relaxed to save time.

lessons.title: Schedule Development and Compression
lessons.content:
Your exam is in 10 days and you have 12 days of study planned. You have three honest choices: study more hours each day (that costs sleep, the price of crashing), start the next chapter before fully finishing the current one (risky, you may need to come back, that is fast-tracking), or skip a chapter (cutting scope). Pretending 12 days of work will fit in 10 without any change is not a choice; it is how students fail. Project managers face this exact problem when a deadline is tighter than the network says. This lesson turns the network from lesson 10 into a real schedule and shows the honest ways to shorten it.

From network to schedule: the network gives the logic and the durations. A schedule adds real calendar dates, working days, holidays, resource availability and milestones. The output is usually shown as a Gantt chart, a milestone chart, and a schedule baseline. Lesson 10 found DhakaEats needs 26 weeks of working time; now we must check it against the calendar and the client's wishes.

Gantt charts: a Gantt chart, named after Henry Gantt who popularised it in the 1910s, lists activities down the left side and shows each as a horizontal bar on a timeline. Modern Gantt charts also show dependency arrows, milestones as diamonds, the critical path in a different colour, and progress as a filled part of each bar. Their strength is that anyone, even a non-technical client, can read them instantly. Their weakness is that complex dependencies are harder to see than in a network diagram, and large charts become walls of bars. Many teams use both: the network to calculate, the Gantt chart to communicate.

Calendars and working days: 26 weeks of work is not automatically 26 calendar weeks. If MeghSoft works 5 days a week, 26 weeks is 130 working days. Public holidays, especially the Eid holidays, which can close offices for several days, must be removed. If the project crosses Eid-ul-Fitr and Eid-ul-Adha and other national holidays, 130 working days might stretch to 28 or 29 calendar weeks. A schedule built without the calendar can be wrong by weeks, and in Bangladesh where the major holidays move with the lunar calendar each year, you must check the actual dates every time.

The schedule baseline: once the schedule is agreed, it is saved as the schedule baseline, the approved version against which progress is measured. When things change, you update the current schedule but keep the baseline, so you can say we planned to finish backend at week 12, we actually finished at week 13. Changing the baseline itself needs formal approval through change control. Without a baseline, every slip quietly disappears.

The compression problem: the client now says the marketing campaign has been moved and go-live must happen in 24 weeks, not 26. The network says 26. There are two classic techniques to shorten a schedule without cutting scope: crashing and fast-tracking. Both work only on the critical path; shortening a non-critical activity saves nothing, because the critical path still determines the finish.

Crashing: crashing means adding resources, such as more people, overtime or paid tools, to shorten critical activities, at extra cost. Each activity has a normal duration and cost, and a crash duration and cost, the shortest possible with extra resources. The cost slope = (crash cost minus normal cost) / (normal duration minus crash duration), the extra cost per week saved. You crash the cheapest critical activity first, one week at a time, and recompute the critical path after each step, because other paths can become critical.

Crashing DhakaEats, the data: on the critical path A-B-E-G-H-I, the team prices three options. B Backend: normal 8 weeks at 6 lakh taka, crash 6 weeks at 10 lakh (two extra specialists and paid overtime), slope (10 minus 6) / (8 minus 6) = 2 lakh per week. E Restaurant panel: normal 5 weeks at 2.5 lakh, crash 4 weeks at 4 lakh, slope 1.5 lakh per week. G Integration testing: normal 4 weeks at 4 lakh, crash 3 weeks at 5.5 lakh, slope 1.5 lakh per week. A, H and I cannot be crashed: requirements need client meetings, the pilot needs 3 real weeks with restaurants, and training dates are fixed.

Crashing step by step: step 1, the cheapest slopes are E and G at 1.5 lakh. Crash E by 1 week. E now runs weeks 12 to 16. But F, payment integration, also ends at week 16, so G still starts at 16: the project is now 25 weeks, and F has become critical too, with zero float. Step 2, now crashing E again is impossible (it is at its crash limit), and crashing only E would not help anyway, because F is also critical. G sits on every path, so crash G by 1 week at 1.5 lakh. G runs weeks 16 to 19, H 19 to 22, I 22 to 24. The project is 24 weeks. Total extra cost: 1.5 + 1.5 = 3 lakh taka. Notice that now two parallel critical paths exist, through E and through F, which makes the schedule more fragile: a slip on either delays go-live.

Why not crash B? B costs 2 lakh per week, more than E or G. But B sits before both E and F, so after step 1, crashing B by a week would shorten both critical paths at once for 2 lakh, while the only alternative that shortens both is G at 1.5 lakh. Always compare the cost of shortening all critical paths together, not just one activity. That is the logic exam questions test.

Crashing limits: adding people to software work does not shorten it in a straight line. New people need onboarding, more people need more communication, and some work cannot be split. Brooks's law, lesson 12, warns that adding people to a late software project can make it later. Crash estimates in software must come from the people who will do the work, and the most reliable forms of crashing are often overtime for short periods, buying a ready-made component, or adding a specialist for a well-separated task, not doubling a team.

Fast-tracking: fast-tracking means doing activities in parallel that were planned in sequence, usually by relaxing discretionary dependencies. For DhakaEats, the team could start backend work after 3 weeks of requirements instead of 4, using a start-to-start relationship with a 3-week lag. That could save a week at little direct cost. The price is risk: if requirements change in week 4, some backend work may need rework. Fast-tracking only works on discretionary dependencies; you cannot test code before it is written, however hard you fast-track.

Crash or fast-track: crashing costs money but adds little risk if the extra resources are effective. Fast-tracking costs little money but adds the risk of rework. A typical approach is to fast-track first where the overlap is safe, then crash the cheapest critical activities, and if that still does not meet the date, go back to the sponsor with the remaining option: reduce or phase scope. Promising a date that neither technique can reach is not optimism; it is planning to fail.

PERT probability, recap and use: you learned in Operations Research (deep-cse-6-10, lesson 16) how to estimate the chance of finishing by a date. Suppose the critical activities of the 26-week plan have standard deviations A 0.5, B 1.0, E 0.67, G 0.67, H 0.33 and I 0.33 weeks. The variances add: 0.25 + 1.0 + 0.45 + 0.45 + 0.11 + 0.11, about 2.37, so the path's standard deviation is about 1.54 weeks. The chance of finishing within 27 weeks: z = (27 minus 26) / 1.54, about 0.65, giving about 74 percent. Within 28 weeks: z is about 1.30, about 90 percent. So a manager could tell the client: 26 weeks is our expected date; to be 90 percent confident, plan for 28.

A warning about PERT: the calculation above looks only at the single critical path. When several paths with similar lengths merge, like G waiting for C, J, E and F, the chance that at least one of them runs late is higher than for any single path. This merge bias makes simple PERT probabilities too optimistic. Monte Carlo simulation, lesson 16, handles this better by simulating thousands of possible projects.

Critical chain: Eliyahu Goldratt proposed the critical chain method in his 1997 book Critical Chain. It attacks Parkinson's law and the student syndrome from lesson 07. Steps: estimate each task aggressively, near a 50 percent chance of finishing, removing the hidden safety from each task; take into account resource dependencies, not only logical ones, so the longest chain considering who does what is the critical chain; add a single project buffer at the end of the critical chain, often about half the safety removed from the tasks; add feeding buffers where non-critical chains join the critical chain; and track buffer consumption instead of task due dates. If the buffer is being eaten faster than work is being completed, act.

Critical chain worked: suppose DhakaEats' six critical activities had padded estimates totalling 26 weeks, and the team believes about a third of that is safety. Aggressive estimates total about 26 x 2/3, roughly 17.3 weeks. Half of the removed 8.7 weeks goes into a project buffer of about 4.3 weeks, giving a plan of about 21.7 weeks plus feeding buffers on side chains. Individual tasks will often overrun their aggressive estimates, which is expected and not punished; the shared buffer absorbs it. Many teams find this reduces total time because safety is no longer wasted task by task.

The schedule as a living document: every week, actual progress replaces estimates, the critical path is recomputed, and forecasts are updated. Agile teams achieve the same effect with fixed-length sprints and release burnup charts (lesson 17). Either way, a schedule that is not updated stops being a tool and becomes decoration on the wall.

Real-life example 1, a telecom launch: a telecom operator needed a new recharge-offer feature live before a cricket series. The network gave 9 weeks; the series began in 7. The team fast-tracked UI design with backend work, crashed testing by bringing in two experienced testers from another product for two weeks, and cut one low-value report from the first release. They went live with a day to spare. All three levers were used, and none of them alone would have been enough.

Real-life example 2, a student thesis: a student had 8 weeks to submit but a plan of 10. Crashing meant working weekends for two weeks; fast-tracking meant writing the literature review while experiments ran instead of after. Together they saved two weeks without dropping any chapter. The student also kept a visible buffer of three days before submission, which was used up when the lab server failed for two days.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: crashing non-critical activities; forgetting to recompute the critical path after each crash; crashing beyond the crash limit; fast-tracking mandatory dependencies; using PERT probabilities as if merge bias did not exist; and ignoring holidays. Exams often give a crashing table and ask for the minimum-cost schedule for a target duration, ask to compute cost slopes, explain crashing versus fast-tracking, compute a PERT probability, or describe critical chain buffers.

Recap: a schedule adds calendars, resources and milestones to the network and is communicated with Gantt charts and saved as a baseline. To shorten a schedule, crash (add resources at cost, cheapest slope first, recheck the critical path each step) or fast-track (overlap discretionary dependencies at the risk of rework), or reduce scope. DhakaEats was crashed from 26 to 24 weeks for 3 lakh taka by crashing E and G. PERT gives probabilities but is optimistic at merges. Critical chain moves safety into shared buffers. Next lesson: resources, levelling, and why adding people is not a magic fix.
key_points: A schedule adds calendars, holidays, resources and milestones to the network; it is saved as a baseline.
Gantt charts communicate the schedule; network diagrams are better for calculating it.
Crashing adds resources to critical activities; cost slope = (crash cost minus normal cost) / (normal minus crash duration).
Crash the cheapest critical activity first, one step at a time, and recompute the critical path after each step.
DhakaEats: crashing E and G by one week each cut 26 weeks to 24 for 3 lakh taka, leaving two parallel critical paths.
Fast-tracking overlaps discretionary dependencies, saving time at the risk of rework.
PERT probability uses the critical path's variance but is optimistic where paths merge.
Critical chain uses aggressive task estimates with project and feeding buffers and tracks buffer consumption.
lessons.tip: In crashing problems, draw a small table with columns step, activity crashed, new duration, extra cost, critical paths. Writing the critical paths in every row stops the most common mistake: crashing an activity that is no longer the bottleneck.
lessons.task: Using the DhakaEats network, suppose the client now wants 23 weeks. B can be crashed by up to 2 weeks at 2 lakh per week, E and G are already at their limits. Find what to crash, the new critical paths, and the total extra cost compared with the 26-week plan. Then write one fast-tracking idea that could avoid part of that cost.

quiz.q: An activity normally takes 5 weeks for 6 lakh and can be crashed to 4 weeks for 7.5 lakh. Its cost slope is:
quiz.explain: (7.5 minus 6) / (5 minus 4) = 1.5 lakh per week saved.

quiz.q: Why does crashing a non-critical activity not shorten the project?
options: Because non-critical activities cannot be crashed
Because the critical path still sets the finish date
Because crashing only works on milestones
quiz.explain: Only the longest path determines duration; shortening another path changes nothing.

quiz.q: Starting backend work before requirements are fully finished is an example of:
quiz.explain: Fast-tracking overlaps activities planned in sequence, adding the risk of rework.

quiz.q: The critical path has variance 2.37 weeks squared and expected length 26 weeks. The standard deviation is about:
quiz.explain: The standard deviation is the square root of the variance: about 1.54 weeks.

quiz.q: In critical chain scheduling, where does the safety time go?
options: Into shared project and feeding buffers
quiz.explain: Safety is stripped from tasks and pooled into a project buffer and feeding buffers that are tracked.

lessons.title: Resource Allocation and Brooks's Law
lessons.content:
One woman can have a baby in nine months, but nine women cannot have a baby in one month. Fred Brooks used this joke to make a serious point: some work simply cannot be split among more people. A schedule that looks perfect on paper fails if it needs seven developers in a week when you only have six, or if it assumes that doubling the team halves the time. This lesson is about resources: who is needed when, what to do when demand exceeds supply, and why people and months are not interchangeable.

What resources are: in project management, resources are everything the work consumes: people with particular skills, equipment like test phones and servers, facilities like a meeting room, materials, and money. In software, people are by far the most important and the most limited resource. A resource calendar records when each resource is available, including leave, holidays and other project commitments. Many schedules fail because they assume a senior developer is available full time when she also supports two other projects.

Skills matter, not just headcount: six developers are not six interchangeable units. One knows payment APIs, two are strong in Flutter, one is a backend specialist, two are juniors. A skills matrix lists people down the side and skills across the top, rating each person's level. It shows who can work on what, where the team is thin, and who needs training. In DhakaEats, the matrix shows only Rafi knows the payment provider's API well. That is a risk worth noticing.

The bus factor: the bus factor, or truck factor, is the number of people who would need to disappear (go on leave, quit, fall sick) before the project stalls because nobody else knows something vital. A bus factor of 1 means one person holds critical knowledge alone. Raising it means pair programming, code reviews, documentation and rotating tasks. For DhakaEats, the manager pairs a second developer with Rafi on payment integration, accepting a little slowdown now to avoid a disaster later.

Resource loading and histograms: after scheduling, add up how many units of each resource each activity needs in each period. Drawn as a bar chart over time, this is a resource histogram. Peaks above the available level show over-allocation: the plan asks for more people than exist. Deep valleys show under-use: people idle or pulled onto other work.

DhakaEats loading: MeghSoft has 6 developers for this project. From the lesson 10 network: B Backend needs 3 developers from week 4 to week 12; C Customer app needs 2 developers from week 4 to 13; D Rider app needs 2 developers from week 4 to 10; E Restaurant panel needs 2 from week 12 to 17; F Payment needs 1 from week 12 to 16. Adding up: weeks 4 to 10, B + C + D = 3 + 2 + 2 = 7 developers. Weeks 10 to 12: 3 + 2 = 5. Weeks 12 to 13: C + E + F = 2 + 2 + 1 = 5. Weeks 13 to 16: E + F = 3. Weeks 16 to 17: 2. The first block needs 7 but only 6 exist: over-allocated by one developer for 6 weeks.

Resource smoothing: smoothing adjusts activities within their float so that resource peaks fall, without changing the project end date. Rider app D has 6 weeks of total float, shared with J. D needs 2 developers for 6 weeks, which is 12 developer-weeks. Suppose the work can reasonably be done by one developer over 12 weeks (an assumption the team must confirm; not all work splits this way). D then runs from week 4 to week 16 with 1 developer, and J runs from 16 to 17, which still meets J's late finish of 17. New loading: weeks 4 to 10, 3 + 2 + 1 = 6. Weeks 10 to 12, 3 + 2 + 1 = 6. Weeks 12 to 13, 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 6. Weeks 13 to 16, 2 + 1 + 1 = 4. Weeks 16 to 17, 2. The peak is now exactly 6, the go-live date is unchanged, and D's float has been used up, so D has become critical.

Resource levelling: levelling is stronger: it resolves over-allocation even if the end date must move. Suppose a developer leaves and only 5 remain. No arrangement within float can fit the work into 26 weeks with 5 people during the busiest weeks, so some activity must be delayed beyond its float, and the project end slips. Levelling usually extends the schedule, which is why the rule is: try smoothing first, level only when you must, and tell the sponsor the date impact clearly.

Why levelling changes the critical path: after smoothing or levelling, activities that had float may have none, and a chain of activities that share one person becomes a hidden critical path even though there is no logical dependency between them. This is exactly what critical chain (lesson 11) means by resource dependencies. A schedule that only checks logic and ignores who does what is usually too optimistic.

Multi-project conflicts: in matrix organisations, the same person is often shared across projects. If Rafi is needed on DhakaEats payments in weeks 12 to 16 and on a bank project's audit fixes in weeks 14 to 15, someone must decide priority. Good organisations resolve this at the portfolio level, with a shared resource plan, instead of letting two project managers fight over a developer's calendar every Monday.

Brooks's law: in his 1975 book The Mythical Man-Month, Fred Brooks stated: adding manpower to a late software project makes it later. Brooks managed IBM's OS/360, one of the largest software projects of the 1960s, and saw this first hand. The book's title attacks the idea that effort measured in person-months can be traded freely between people and months. Ten people for one month is not the same as one person for ten months.

Why Brooks's law happens: three reasons. First, ramp-up: new people need time to learn the code, tools, domain and team habits, and during that time they produce little. Second, training cost: existing team members must spend time explaining things, so their own output drops. Third, communication overhead: more people means more coordination. And some tasks are simply sequential: if a bug investigation requires one person's chain of reasoning, ten people cannot do it faster.

Communication paths worked: with n people, each pair is a possible communication channel, and the number of pairs is n x (n minus 1) / 2. With 5 people: 5 x 4 / 2 = 10. With 8: 8 x 7 / 2 = 28. With 12: 12 x 11 / 2 = 66. With 20: 20 x 19 / 2 = 190. Team size grew 4 times from 5 to 20, but communication paths grew 19 times. That is why large projects split into small teams with clear interfaces, so that most communication happens inside teams of five to nine people.

Brooks's law worked: DhakaEats is late. Four person-months of work remain, 4 developers are on it, and the deadline is 1 month away: on paper, exactly enough, but the team is already behind its pace. The manager adds 4 new developers. In the first month, newcomers mostly learn and contribute almost nothing, while each old developer spends about a quarter of their time helping them. Work done in month 1: 4 x 0.75 = 3 person-months. One person-month is still left, so the project finishes later than if the newcomers had never joined and the original 4 had simply done the remaining 4 person-months themselves. The new people only start paying back in month 2, which is after the deadline.

When adding people does help: Brooks's law is a warning, not an absolute. Adding people works better early in a project, when there is time to ramp up; when the work splits into independent pieces with clear interfaces; when the new people are experienced in the technology and domain; and when you add them to a separate, well-defined task instead of to the middle of the hardest part. A tester added for regression testing, or a specialist who builds an isolated module, can help even late.

Team size and structure: research and practice suggest small teams communicate best; Scrum recommends teams of 10 or fewer people. Larger efforts use several small teams, each owning a component or feature area, coordinated through clear interfaces, shared standards and a few integration points. Conway's law, an observation by Melvin Conway, notes that systems tend to mirror the communication structure of the organisations that build them, which is another reason to design teams and architecture together.

Other resource decisions: should we use full-time staff, contractors or an outsourced team? Can expensive specialists be scheduled only for the weeks their skills are needed? Do we need a dedicated test device lab? Should two juniors be paired with one senior? Each choice changes cost, risk and quality. Lesson 24 looks at outsourcing; lesson 20 at motivating the people you have.

Real-life example 1, a late banking release: a bank vendor was three weeks behind with two weeks left before a regulatory deadline. Management added six developers from another project. The original team spent the next week explaining the code; two newcomers accidentally broke the build twice; the release slipped by a month. On the next project, the same vendor instead kept the team stable, cut two low-priority features, and added only one experienced tester. That release was on time.

Real-life example 2, a family wedding kitchen: cooking biryani for 300 guests, adding a fifth cook halfway through does not help much if all the pots are already on the fire and only the head cook knows the spice mix. Adding a helper earlier to chop onions and wash rice, a separate and well-defined task, helps a lot. The same logic applies to software teams.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: assuming person-months can be divided freely; ignoring resource calendars and leave; confusing smoothing with levelling; forgetting that smoothing uses up float; and treating Brooks's law as meaning never add anyone. Exams often ask you to draw a resource histogram from a schedule, level or smooth it, compute communication paths, state and explain Brooks's law with its three causes, and explain the mythical man-month.

Recap: resources include people, equipment, facilities and money; people and their skills matter most. Use resource calendars, skills matrices and the bus factor to see real capacity. Resource histograms reveal over-allocation. Smoothing moves activities within float without changing the end date; levelling resolves conflicts even if the end date slips. Brooks's law: adding people to a late software project makes it later, because of ramp-up, training cost and communication paths that grow as n(n minus 1)/2. Add people early, to separable work, with experienced newcomers. Next lesson: turning effort and resources into a budget.
key_points: Resources include people, equipment, facilities and money; in software, skilled people are the key constraint.
Resource calendars, skills matrices and the bus factor reveal real capacity and knowledge risk.
A resource histogram shows demand over time; peaks above availability mean over-allocation.
Smoothing shifts activities within float without moving the end date; levelling may move the end date.
DhakaEats needed 7 developers with 6 available; stretching the rider app within its float smoothed the peak to 6.
Brooks's law: adding people to a late software project makes it later.
Causes: ramp-up time, training cost for existing staff, and communication paths n(n minus 1)/2.
Adding people helps most early, on separable work, with experienced newcomers.
