lessons.tip: Whenever someone suggests adding people to fix a delay, ask three questions: how long will they take to become productive, who will train them, and is there a separate piece of work they can own? The answers usually tell you whether it will help.

With only 4 people available, find the over-allocated weeks and try to smooth the plan without moving the end date.

quiz.q: How many communication paths does a team of 12 people have?
Resource smoothing differs from resource levelling because smoothing:
options: Never changes the project end date and works within float
Adds new people to the team
quiz.explain: Smoothing only moves activities within their float, so the end date stays the same; levelling may push it out.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a reason behind Brooks's law?
options: Existing staff spend time training newcomers
Communication overhead grows with team size
New people always write worse code than old ones
quiz.explain: Brooks's causes are ramp-up, training cost and communication overhead, not that newcomers are worse programmers.

quiz.q: A bus factor of 1 for the payment module means:
options: One bus is needed for the team
Only one person holds vital knowledge, so losing them would stall the work
quiz.explain: Bus factor counts how many people must be lost before the project stalls; 1 is a serious risk.

quiz.q: When is adding people to a software project most likely to help?
options: One week before the deadline on the hardest task
When the newcomers have never used the technology
Early, on separable work with clear interfaces, using experienced people
quiz.explain: Brooks's law is a warning; early additions to independent work by experienced people can genuinely help.

lessons.title: Cost Management and Budgeting
lessons.content:
When a family plans Eid shopping, the father may say: we have 30,000 taka. Clothes for everyone, 18,000. Food for the feast, 8,000. Gifts, 3,000. And 1,000 kept aside in case prices are higher than expected. Then, while shopping, someone keeps checking how much has been spent. That is cost management in miniature: estimate what each part costs, add it up into a budget, keep a reserve for surprises, and watch spending against the plan. Software projects do the same thing with bigger numbers, and with one special feature: most of the money is people's time.

Why cost management matters: a project that runs out of money stops, however good its code is. For a software company like MeghSoft, cost overruns eat profit; for a client, they mean asking the board for more money, which damages trust. Cost management covers four steps: plan how costs will be managed, estimate costs, determine the budget, and control costs during the project. This lesson covers the first three; lesson 14, earned value, covers control.

Types of cost: direct costs are clearly caused by this project: salaries of the DhakaEats developers, test devices bought for it, the map service bill. Indirect costs are shared across projects: office rent, electricity, HR and accounts staff, the company's internet line. Fixed costs do not change with the amount of work, such as a yearly tool licence. Variable costs grow with work, such as cloud server bills that rise with testing load or SMS charges per message. Sunk costs, from lesson 03, are already spent and should not drive future decisions.

The loaded rate: when estimating people costs, using salary alone underestimates badly. A developer costs the company their salary plus bonuses and benefits, plus a share of office space, equipment, software, management and support staff. The loaded rate includes all of this. Worked: MeghSoft's average developer salary is 65,000 taka a month. Bonuses and benefits add about 15 percent, and office, equipment and overhead add about 40 percent of salary. Loaded cost = 65,000 x (1 + 0.15 + 0.40) = 65,000 x 1.55 = 100,750 taka, so about 1 lakh taka per person-month. This is the figure we used for change requests in lesson 05.

Estimate classes: cost estimates become more accurate as the project is better defined, mirroring the cone of uncertainty. PMBOK describes a rough order of magnitude (ROM) estimate, made early in initiation, with a typical range of minus 25 to plus 75 percent; and a definitive estimate, made once work is well defined, with a range of about minus 5 to plus 10 percent. Notice the asymmetry: early estimates are far more likely to be too low than too high. A ROM estimate of 30 lakh might really mean anywhere from 22.5 to 52.5 lakh.

Cost estimating techniques: the same techniques as effort estimation apply: analogy (what did a similar project cost?), parametric (cost per function point times number of function points, or COCOMO effort times loaded rate), bottom-up (cost each work package and add up) and three-point estimates for uncertain items. Vendor quotes cover purchased items. Reserve analysis decides how much contingency to hold. In software, the biggest step is converting effort to cost with the loaded rate; the second biggest is not forgetting non-labour costs.

Non-labour costs for DhakaEats: the team lists cloud servers for development and testing, 1.8 lakh for six months; test devices, a range of cheap and expensive Android phones and two iPhones, 1.2 lakh; third-party services like maps and SMS during development and testing, 1.5 lakh; tools and licences such as design software and a crash-reporting service, 0.8 lakh; and travel and training sessions for restaurants and riders, 0.7 lakh. Total non-labour: 1.8 + 1.2 + 1.5 + 0.8 + 0.7 = 6 lakh taka.

Cost aggregation: costs are estimated at the work-package level and rolled up through the WBS to control accounts and then to the project. Labour: about 30 person-months from lessons 06 to 09, at 1 lakh each, gives 30 lakh. Adding non-labour, the total of all work packages is 30 + 6 = 36 lakh taka. Because costs are tied to WBS codes, the manager can later see that, for example, 1.6 Backend and payment is overspending while 1.4 Rider app is on budget.

Contingency reserve: contingency reserves are money set aside for identified risks, the known unknowns. From the risk analysis we will do in lessons 15 and 16, the team identifies risks like the payment sandbox being unreliable, or a key developer leaving, and estimates their expected cost. MeghSoft sets a contingency reserve of 4 lakh taka, about 11 percent of the work cost. The project manager can usually use contingency when the identified risks occur, within agreed rules.

The cost baseline: the cost baseline is the approved, time-phased budget, including contingency reserves but excluding management reserve. For DhakaEats: 36 lakh of work plus 4 lakh contingency equals a cost baseline of 40 lakh taka. Time-phased means spread over the schedule, so you know how much should have been spent by each date. This baseline is what earned value compares against.

Management reserve: management reserve is money for unknown unknowns, problems nobody could have foreseen. It is not part of the cost baseline and is controlled by management, not the project manager; using it usually needs a change approval. MeghSoft's management adds a 2 lakh management reserve, so the total project budget is 40 + 2 = 42 lakh taka. The client price, 60 lakh in lesson 03, is a separate figure: it must cover this budget plus sales costs, tax, warranty support and profit.

Contingency vs management reserve, the classic exam point: contingency covers identified risks, is inside the cost baseline, and is used by the project manager. Management reserve covers unidentified risks, is outside the baseline but inside the total budget, and needs management approval. In short: work packages plus contingency equals cost baseline; cost baseline plus management reserve equals project budget.

The S-curve: plot cumulative planned cost against time and you usually get an S shape: slow at the start when few people work on requirements, steep in the middle when the full team builds, and flat at the end during beta and training. For DhakaEats, planned monthly work costs are 4, 6, 7, 8, 7 and 4 lakh over six months, so the cumulative planned values are 4, 10, 17, 25, 32 and 36 lakh. Lesson 14 compares actual spending and earned value against exactly this curve.

Cash flow: a budget says how much; cash flow says when money moves. MeghSoft's contract says the client pays 20 percent at signing, 30 percent at beta, 40 percent at go-live and 10 percent after a three-month warranty. On the 60 lakh price, that is 12 lakh at the start, 18 lakh at beta near the end of month 5, 24 lakh at go-live and 6 lakh later. But by the end of month 4, MeghSoft has spent about 25 lakh while receiving only 12. The company must fund a gap of about 13 lakh from its own cash. Many small software firms in Bangladesh get into trouble not because projects lose money but because cash runs out mid-project. Milestone payments tied to frequent, small deliverables reduce this risk.

Budgeting in agile projects: when a stable team works in fixed sprints, cost becomes very predictable: cost per sprint = number of people x loaded rate x sprint length. DhakaEats needs about 30 person-months over 6 months, so on average about 5 people. A 2-week sprint is about 2 / 4.3 of a month, so one sprint costs about 5 x 1 lakh x 0.47, roughly 2.33 lakh taka, and 13 sprints in 26 weeks cost about 30 lakh, matching the labour estimate. Agile budgets therefore fix the team and the time, and let the product owner decide which backlog items that money buys, which is the inverted triangle you will meet in lesson 17.

Controlling costs, a preview: cost control means tracking actual costs against the baseline, understanding why they differ, forecasting the final cost, and acting early. Timesheets coded to WBS elements, monthly invoices from cloud providers and purchase records feed the actual cost figures. The key insight of the next lesson is that comparing actual cost with planned cost alone is misleading: you must also know how much work has actually been done.

The cost of change and of poor quality: costs are not only spent on planned work. Fixing problems late is expensive: a requirement misunderstanding caught in a design review costs a meeting, while the same misunderstanding discovered after launch costs redesign, recoding, retesting and lost trust. That is why the cost of reviews, prototypes and early testing is usually money well spent. Lesson 22 measures this as the cost of quality.

Real-life example 1, the forgotten cloud bill: a startup in Dhaka budgeted carefully for developers but treated cloud hosting as small. During load testing for a big launch, they left large test servers running for three weeks and received a bill several times larger than their monthly estimate. After that, they gave every cloud resource a WBS tag, set budget alerts, and reviewed the bill weekly. Variable costs need active watching.

Real-life example 2, the fixed-price lesson: a firm quoted a fixed price for a school-management system using salaries only, not loaded rates. Halfway through, the accounts showed that office rent, equipment and the HR team's time had not been covered anywhere, and the project would lose money even if delivered on time. On later quotes, they used a loaded rate and added explicit contingency and management reserve lines, and their profit became predictable.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: using salaries instead of loaded rates; forgetting non-labour costs; treating ROM estimates as precise; mixing contingency and management reserve; and confusing budget with cash flow. Exams often ask you to compute a loaded rate, build a budget from work-package costs with reserves, explain the cost baseline and S-curve, state the ROM and definitive ranges, and distinguish direct from indirect and fixed from variable costs.

Recap: cost management plans, estimates, budgets and controls costs. Use loaded rates, about 1 lakh per person-month at MeghSoft, and include non-labour costs. Estimates narrow from ROM (minus 25 to plus 75 percent) to definitive (minus 5 to plus 10). Roll costs up the WBS: DhakaEats work packages 36 lakh, plus contingency 4 lakh gives a cost baseline of 40 lakh, plus management reserve 2 lakh gives a budget of 42 lakh. The time-phased baseline forms an S-curve: 4, 10, 17, 25, 32, 36. Watch cash flow, not just totals, and agree milestone payments that keep the vendor's cash gap small, ideally tied to small, frequent deliverables. Next lesson: earned value management, which measures cost and schedule performance together.
key_points: Cost management plans, estimates, budgets and controls costs; in software, people's time is most of the cost.
Direct vs indirect and fixed vs variable costs; sunk costs should not drive decisions.
Loaded rate = salary plus benefits and overhead; MeghSoft's is about 1 lakh taka per person-month.
ROM estimates range about minus 25 to plus 75 percent; definitive estimates about minus 5 to plus 10 percent.
Work package costs plus contingency reserve make the cost baseline; adding management reserve gives the project budget.
Contingency covers identified risks and is used by the PM; management reserve covers unknowns and needs management approval.
The cumulative time-phased baseline usually forms an S-curve.
Cash flow timing matters: milestone payments can leave the vendor funding a large gap mid-project.
lessons.tip: When you build any budget, write it as a pyramid: work packages at the bottom, then contingency, then cost baseline, then management reserve, then total budget. Drawing the pyramid makes the reserve questions in exams almost automatic.
lessons.task: Build a budget for a 3-month college website project with 2 developers at a salary of 50,000 taka per month. Add 15 percent benefits and 40 percent overhead to get the loaded rate, add 50,000 taka of non-labour costs, a 10 percent contingency and a 5 percent management reserve on the cost baseline. Show the cost baseline and the total budget, and sketch the monthly S-curve.

quiz.q: A developer's salary is 65,000 taka a month, with 15 percent benefits and 40 percent overhead. What is the loaded rate?
Work packages cost 36 lakh, contingency is 4 lakh and management reserve is 2 lakh. What is the cost baseline?
quiz.explain: Cost baseline = work packages + contingency = 40 lakh. Adding management reserve gives the 42 lakh budget.

quiz.q: Which statement about management reserve is correct?
options: It is part of the cost baseline
It covers identified risks and the PM uses it freely
It is the same as contingency
It covers unknown unknowns and needs management approval to use
quiz.explain: Management reserve is outside the cost baseline, for unforeseen problems, controlled by management.

quiz.q: The typical range of a rough order of magnitude estimate is:
quiz.explain: PMBOK gives about minus 25 to plus 75 percent for ROM estimates made early.

quiz.q: Office rent shared by all of a company's projects is a:
quiz.explain: Costs shared across projects, like rent and HR, are indirect costs.

lessons.title: Earned Value Management
lessons.content:
Imagine your mother gives you 1,000 taka to buy ten items from the bazar, and after an hour you phone to say you have spent 600 taka. Is that good or bad? You cannot tell. If you have bought eight items, you are doing great. If you have bought only three, something is wrong. And if you were supposed to be home already, you are also late. To judge progress you need three numbers: what you planned to have done by now, what you have actually done, and what it actually cost. Earned value management, or EVM, is exactly this idea, made precise, and it is one of the most useful tools a project manager has.

Why plan versus actual is not enough: suppose by the end of month 3, DhakaEats planned to spend 17 lakh and has actually spent 18 lakh. A naive reading says we are 1 lakh over budget, not bad. But the real question is how much work those 18 lakh bought. If the team finished more work than planned, overspending might be fine. If it finished less, the situation is much worse than 1 lakh. EVM adds the missing piece: the value of work actually completed, measured in the same units as the budget.

The three basic numbers: planned value (PV) is the budgeted cost of the work scheduled to be done by a given date; it comes from the time-phased baseline, the S-curve of lesson 13. Earned value (EV) is the budgeted cost of the work actually completed by that date: for each finished piece of work, you earn the amount that was budgeted for it, not what it actually cost. Actual cost (AC) is what was really spent on the work done. Budget at completion (BAC) is the total planned budget for all the work. All four are in money, so they can be compared directly.

The DhakaEats data: BAC for the work packages is 36 lakh taka (contingency is tracked separately in this example). The planned cumulative values from lesson 13 are 4, 10, 17, 25, 32 and 36 lakh by months 1 to 6. At the end of month 3, PV = 17 lakh. The manager adds up the budgets of all work actually completed: requirements and design fully done, most of the backend, part of the customer app. Their budgets add to EV = 15 lakh. Timesheets and invoices show AC = 18 lakh.

Variances: schedule variance SV = EV minus PV = 15 minus 17 = minus 2 lakh. Negative means behind schedule: 2 lakh worth of planned work has not been done yet. Cost variance CV = EV minus AC = 15 minus 18 = minus 3 lakh. Negative means over budget: the work done should have cost 15 but cost 18. Notice that both variances start with EV: earned value is the hero of the method. Positive variances are good, negative are bad.

Performance indices: indices express the same ideas as ratios, which is handy for comparing projects of different sizes. Schedule performance index SPI = EV / PV = 15 / 17, about 0.88: the team is progressing at about 88 percent of the planned rate. Cost performance index CPI = EV / AC = 15 / 18, about 0.83: each taka spent is producing only about 83 paisa of planned value. An index of 1 means on plan; above 1 is better than plan, below 1 is worse.

Reading the four quadrants: SPI below 1 and CPI below 1, as here, is the worst case: behind schedule and over budget. SPI above 1 with CPI below 1 often means the team is spending extra, such as overtime, to stay ahead. SPI below 1 with CPI above 1 can mean the team is understaffed: cheap but slow. Both above 1 means ahead and under budget, which is great, though a manager should still check the estimates were not padded.

Forecasting the final cost: the estimate at completion (EAC) predicts the total cost at the end. The most common formula assumes current cost efficiency continues: EAC = BAC / CPI = 36 / 0.833, about 43.2 lakh. The estimate to complete (ETC) is what remains to be spent: ETC = EAC minus AC = 43.2 minus 18 = 25.2 lakh. The variance at completion (VAC) = BAC minus EAC = 36 minus 43.2 = minus 7.2 lakh: the project is heading for a 7.2 lakh overrun.

Other EAC formulas: if the overrun so far was a one-off that will not repeat, for example an unexpected tool licence, use EAC = AC + (BAC minus EV) = 18 + (36 minus 15) = 39 lakh. If both cost and schedule problems will keep hurting, for example because schedule pressure will force expensive overtime, use EAC = AC + (BAC minus EV) / (CPI x SPI) = 18 + 21 / (0.833 x 0.882), about 18 + 28.6 = 46.6 lakh. Choosing a formula is a judgement about why the variance happened. Showing all three gives sponsors a realistic range: about 39 to 47 lakh.

The to-complete performance index: TCPI asks how efficient the team must be from now on to finish within a target. To finish within BAC: TCPI = (BAC minus EV) / (BAC minus AC) = (36 minus 15) / (36 minus 18) = 21 / 18, about 1.17. The team must produce 1.17 taka of value per taka spent for the rest of the project, while so far it has managed only 0.83. A TCPI that much higher than the current CPI means finishing within the original budget is unrealistic; the manager should plan with the reserves or a revised budget instead of hoping.

What this means for DhakaEats: the cost baseline included a 4 lakh contingency, so up to 40 lakh is covered by known-risk money. Management reserve adds 2 more, up to 42. The most likely forecast, 43.2 lakh, exceeds even that. So in month 3, not month 6, the manager must act: find the cause (in this case, the payment sandbox problems and rework in the backend), propose corrective actions (pair Rafi with a second developer, stop gold plating in the customer app, defer a report), and inform the sponsor with numbers. The earlier the warning, the more options remain.

Measuring earned value fairly: EV depends on how you credit partly finished work. The 0/100 rule gives no credit until a work package is complete: strict and honest, good for small packages. The 50/50 rule gives 50 percent when work starts and 50 percent when it finishes. The 20/80 rule gives 20 and 80. Weighted milestones give credit at defined checkpoints, such as design approved, code reviewed, tests passed. Subjective percent complete, where people say we are 70 percent done, is the least reliable, because of the 90-percent-done syndrome from lesson 01. Example: the cart API package is budgeted at 2 lakh and has started but not finished. Under 0/100, EV is 0; under 50/50, EV is 1 lakh. Small work packages make the choice of rule matter less.

Earned schedule: SV is measured in money, which is odd for schedule, and at the end of a late project SV always returns to zero because eventually all work is earned. Walt Lipke's earned schedule method fixes this by asking: at what time should the current EV have been earned? EV = 15 lies between the PV of 10 at month 2 and 17 at month 3, so earned schedule ES = 2 + (15 minus 10) / (17 minus 10), about 2.71 months. The actual time is 3 months, so the project is about 0.29 months, roughly 1.2 weeks, behind. SPI(t) = 2.71 / 3, about 0.90, and a simple forecast duration is 6 / 0.90, about 6.6 months.

EVM in agile projects: agile teams can use story points as the measure of earned value. Suppose the DhakaEats release plan holds 300 story points with a labour budget of 30 lakh over 13 sprints. After 5 sprints, the team has completed 100 points, and spent 12 lakh. EV = 100 / 300 x 30 = 10 lakh. PV = 5 / 13 x 30, about 11.5 lakh. CPI = 10 / 12, about 0.83; SPI = 10 / 11.5, about 0.87. The same conclusions follow, provided only fully done stories count and the backlog total is kept updated when scope changes.

Limits of EVM: EVM measures progress against the plan, not whether the plan was right, and not quality: a team can earn value by finishing code that is full of bugs. It needs a good WBS, a time-phased baseline and accurate actual costs coded to work packages, which small teams often lack. And it is only as honest as the EV measurement. Used well, it is an early warning system; used carelessly, it produces precise-looking numbers about imprecise things.

Real-life example 1, a government portal: on a large portal project, monthly reports said spent 45 percent of budget, on track. When an auditor introduced EVM, it showed EV was only 30 percent of BAC while AC was 45 percent: CPI about 0.67. The project was heading for a 50 percent overrun. Because this was found at the 45 percent point, the ministry could cut scope and re-plan instead of discovering the problem when the money ran out.

Real-life example 2, the household renovation: a family budgets 3 lakh to repaint and re-tile their flat over 6 weeks. After 3 weeks, they planned to have spent 1.5 lakh; they have spent 1.6 lakh, which looks fine. But only the painting is done, worth 1 lakh of the plan. EV = 1, PV = 1.5, AC = 1.6: SPI about 0.67 and CPI about 0.63. EAC = 3 / 0.63, about 4.8 lakh. Seeing this, they choose cheaper tiles for the kitchen before it is too late.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: using AC instead of EV in variances; mixing up which is divided by which in SPI and CPI (always EV on top); thinking negative SV in money is in days; using EAC = BAC / CPI when the variance was a one-off; and ignoring that EVM says nothing about quality. Exams almost always give PV, EV, AC and BAC, then ask for SV, CV, SPI, CPI, EAC, ETC, VAC and TCPI, plus an interpretation in words. Practise until the formulas feel natural.

Recap: EVM compares PV (planned work), EV (budgeted value of work done) and AC (actual cost). SV = EV minus PV, CV = EV minus AC, SPI = EV / PV, CPI = EV / AC. EAC = BAC / CPI if trends continue, or AC + (BAC minus EV) for one-off variances; ETC = EAC minus AC; VAC = BAC minus EAC; TCPI = (BAC minus EV) / (BAC minus AC). DhakaEats in month 3: SV minus 2, CV minus 3, SPI 0.88, CPI 0.83, EAC about 43.2 lakh, TCPI about 1.17, an early warning that triggers action. Next lesson: identifying and analysing the risks that cause such variances.
key_points: PV is planned value, EV is the budgeted value of work actually done, AC is the actual cost; BAC is the total budget.
SV = EV minus PV and CV = EV minus AC; negative means behind schedule or over budget.
SPI = EV / PV and CPI = EV / AC; below 1 is worse than plan.
EAC = BAC / CPI if current efficiency continues; ETC = EAC minus AC; VAC = BAC minus EAC.
For one-off variances use EAC = AC + (BAC minus EV); for compounding problems divide by CPI x SPI.
TCPI = (BAC minus EV) / (BAC minus AC) shows the efficiency needed to finish on budget.
DhakaEats month 3: SPI 0.88, CPI 0.83, EAC about 43.2 lakh: act early.
Measure EV with objective rules (0/100, 50/50, milestones); EVM tracks plan progress, not quality.
lessons.tip: Remember one sentence: EV comes first and on top. Every variance starts with EV minus something, and every index is EV divided by something. If you write EV first, you will never flip a formula in the exam hall.
lessons.task: A project has BAC 50 lakh. At the review, PV is 20 lakh, EV is 18 lakh and AC is 24 lakh. Compute SV, CV, SPI, CPI, EAC (BAC / CPI), ETC, VAC and TCPI. Then write three sentences to the sponsor explaining what the numbers mean and one corrective action you would propose.

quiz.q: PV = 17, EV = 15, AC = 18 (lakh). What is the CPI?
quiz.explain: CPI = EV / AC = 15 / 18, about 0.83: over budget.

quiz.q: With the same numbers, what is the schedule variance?
quiz.explain: SV = EV minus PV = 15 minus 17 = minus 2 lakh: behind schedule.

quiz.q: BAC is 36 lakh and CPI is 0.833. Assuming the trend continues, EAC is about:
quiz.explain: EAC = BAC / CPI = 36 / 0.833, about 43.2 lakh.

quiz.q: A TCPI of 1.17 when the current CPI is 0.83 means:
options: The project will certainly finish under budget
The team must become far more efficient than so far to meet BAC, which is unrealistic
quiz.explain: Needing 1.17 value per taka after achieving only 0.83 signals the original budget is very unlikely to be met.

quiz.q: Under the 0/100 rule, a 2 lakh work package that has started but not finished earns:
quiz.explain: 0/100 gives no credit until the work package is complete.

lessons.title: Risk Management I: Identification and Analysis
lessons.content:
Before a long bus trip from Dhaka to Sylhet, a careful traveller thinks: the bus might be late, there might be a traffic jam at Bhairab, my phone might die, it might rain. So she carries a power bank and an umbrella, leaves early, and saves the bus company's number. She cannot stop the rain, but she has thought about it before it happened. That is risk management: thinking ahead about what might go wrong (or right), judging which possibilities matter most, and preparing. This lesson covers the first half: finding risks and analysing them. Lesson 16 covers what to do about them.

What a risk is: a risk is an uncertain event or condition that, if it occurs, has an effect on at least one project objective, such as scope, schedule, cost or quality. Two parts are essential: uncertainty (it may or may not happen) and impact (it would matter if it did). Something certain is not a risk; it is a fact to plan for. Something with no effect on objectives is not worth tracking.

Risk vs issue: a risk is something that might happen in the future. An issue is something that has already happened and must be dealt with now. If the payment provider's sandbox might be unreliable, that is a risk. If it has been down for three days, that is an issue. Good risk management turns fewer risks into issues, and when issues do come, they come with a prepared response.

Threats and opportunities: most people think of risks as bad things, called threats. But uncertainty can also be good: opportunities. MeghSoft might be able to reuse its grocery app's modules and save effort; a new cloud discount might cut hosting costs. Modern risk management treats both, because ignoring opportunities leaves value on the table.

Writing a good risk statement: vague risks like the project might be late cannot be managed. A useful format is cause, risk, effect: because of a cause, a risk event may occur, which would lead to an effect. Example: because only one developer knows the payment API, that developer might be unavailable during integration, which would delay payment integration by up to 3 weeks and push go-live. Now you can see what to do: train a second person.

Sources of software risk: Barry Boehm's well-known 1991 list of the top ten software risk items is still a good checklist: personnel shortfalls; unrealistic schedules and budgets; developing the wrong functions and properties; developing the wrong user interface; gold-plating; a continuing stream of requirements changes; shortfalls in externally furnished components; shortfalls in externally performed tasks; real-time performance shortfalls; and straining computer science capabilities, meaning trying technology at the edge of what is possible. Notice how many are about people, requirements and outside parties rather than code.

Risk categories: many organisations group risks with a risk breakdown structure, for example technical (new technology, performance, integration), external (vendors, regulators, market, weather), organisational (funding, priorities, staff), and project management (estimates, planning, communication). Walking through each category is a simple way to make sure you have not looked only where it is comfortable.

Identification techniques: brainstorming with the team and stakeholders; checklists from past projects and Boehm's list; interviews with experts; reviewing documents like the charter, scope statement and contracts; assumptions analysis, which asks for each assumption: what if it is false? (the client will supply restaurant data on time: what if they don't?); SWOT analysis of strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats; and a premortem, where the team imagines the project has failed one year from now and writes down why. The premortem is powerful because it gives people permission to voice worries they would otherwise keep quiet.

The risk register: identified risks go into a risk register, a table with one row per risk: an ID, the risk statement, category, probability, impact, a score, the owner, the planned response, triggers and status. Like the stakeholder register, it is a living document, reviewed regularly. A register created once and never opened again is one of the most common forms of pretend project management.

Qualitative analysis: with dozens of risks, you cannot study all deeply. Qualitative analysis ranks them quickly by rating probability and impact on simple scales, say 1 (very low) to 5 (very high), and multiplying for a score from 1 to 25. A probability-impact matrix colours the grid: high scores, say 15 and above, are red and need active responses; middle scores are amber and watched; low scores are green and just recorded. The organisation decides these thresholds based on its risk appetite: a bank may treat a security risk scored 8 as red, while a startup's marketing site may accept it.

A quick ranking: the payment sandbox might be unreliable: probability 4, impact 3, score 12. The only payment expert might leave: probability 2, impact 5, score 10. The app store might reject the app close to launch: probability 2, impact 4, score 8. Map API prices might rise: probability 2, impact 2, score 4. Ranking points the manager's attention to the sandbox and the single expert first. Watch out: multiplying ordinal scales like 1 to 5 is a convenient convention, not precise mathematics.

Quantitative analysis, risk exposure: for important risks, put numbers on probability and money on impact. Risk exposure, also called expected value of the risk, = probability x impact. For DhakaEats: R1 payment sandbox unreliable, probability 0.4, impact 3 lakh, exposure 1.2 lakh. R2 payment expert leaves, 0.1 x 5 lakh = 0.5 lakh. R3 client delays restaurant data, 0.3 x 2 lakh = 0.6 lakh. R4 map API price rise, 0.2 x 1.5 lakh = 0.3 lakh. R5 app store rejection delays launch, 0.2 x 4 lakh = 0.8 lakh. R6 performance problems at launch, 0.25 x 2.4 lakh = 0.6 lakh.

Where the probabilities come from: a probability of 0.4 sounds scientific, but usually it is a judgement. Make it as honest as possible: look at history (in MeghSoft's last five projects with outside payment providers, how many had sandbox trouble?), ask several people independently and compare, as in Wideband Delphi, and describe what the numbers mean in words so everyone uses the same scale, for example 0.1 means about one project in ten. Impacts should include all effects: extra effort at the loaded rate, delay costs such as penalties or lost revenue, and damage to reputation where it can be estimated.

From exposure to contingency: add the exposures: 1.2 + 0.5 + 0.6 + 0.3 + 0.8 + 0.6 = 4.0 lakh taka. This is where the 4 lakh contingency reserve in lesson 13 came from. The logic: not every risk will happen, but on average across many risks, the total cost of the ones that do happen should be near the sum of their exposures. It is an average, not a guarantee, which is why management reserve exists too.

Opportunities in the same table: reusing the grocery app's modules has probability 0.6 of saving 3 lakh, a positive exposure of 0.6 x 3 = 1.8 lakh. Opportunities are recorded with positive values and managed to increase their chance or size. Counting them prevents managers from building budgets that only expect bad news.

Expected monetary value and decision trees: when a decision involves risks, expected monetary value (EMV) helps compare options. EMV = sum of (probability x outcome) over the possible outcomes. A decision tree draws the decision as a square, then branches for options, then circles for chance events with probabilities, then outcomes. You calculate from the right: at each chance node, compute the EMV; at each decision node, choose the best option.

Decision tree worked, build or buy the payment module: Option Buy: a vendor SDK costs 3 lakh plus 1 lakh integration, 4 lakh total, with a 0.1 chance of compatibility problems costing an extra 2 lakh. Expected cost = 4 + 0.1 x 2 = 4.2 lakh. Option Build: in-house costs 2.5 lakh if all goes well, but there is a 0.4 chance of complications costing an extra 5 lakh. Expected cost = 2.5 + 0.4 x 5 = 4.5 lakh. Buy has the lower expected cost, 4.2 vs 4.5, and also a smaller worst case, 6 lakh vs 7.5 lakh. Build looks cheaper at first glance (2.5 vs 4), which is exactly the trap decision trees help you avoid.

Limits of EMV: EMV is an average over many repetitions. For a one-time decision where a bad outcome could sink the company, the worst case may matter more than the average. A small firm might reject an option with the best EMV if its worst case would bankrupt them. That attitude is called risk aversion, and it is perfectly rational.

Risk appetite, tolerance and threshold: risk appetite is how much uncertainty an organisation is willing to accept in pursuit of its goals. Risk tolerance is the acceptable range of variation for a specific objective, such as the budget may vary by plus or minus 5 percent. A risk threshold is the level beyond which a risk needs a response or escalation. A government health system and a games startup will set these very differently, and both can be right.

Real-life example 1, a hospital system upgrade: in a premortem, a nurse on the project team wrote: the project failed because we switched systems during the dengue season peak and staff had no time to learn. Nobody in the IT team had considered seasonality. The risk scored high on both probability and impact, so go-live was moved to a quieter month. A single sentence from a non-technical stakeholder saved the project.

Real-life example 2, a mobile game: a small studio in Dhaka listed a risk: because our game uses a new third-party advertising SDK, the SDK might crash on older Android phones, which are common among our users, causing bad reviews. They rated it high, tested early on cheap phones bought from a local market, found crashes, and switched SDKs before launch.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: writing vague risks without cause and effect; confusing risks with issues; ignoring opportunities; identifying risks once and never again; and treating risk scores as precise. Exams often ask you to define risk and distinguish it from an issue, list Boehm's top ten or other sources, describe identification techniques, compute risk exposure and EMV, draw and solve a decision tree, and explain the probability-impact matrix.

Recap: a risk is uncertain and affects objectives; an issue has already happened. Write risks as cause, risk, effect. Identify with checklists, brainstorming, assumptions analysis, SWOT and premortems, and record them in a living risk register. Rank qualitatively with a probability-impact matrix; quantify important ones with exposure = probability x impact. DhakaEats' six threats sum to 4 lakh of exposure, the basis of its contingency. Decision trees with EMV compare options: buying the payment module (4.2 lakh) beat building it (4.5 lakh). Next lesson: responding to risks and monitoring them.
key_points: A risk is an uncertain event that would affect an objective; an issue has already happened.
Risks can be threats or opportunities; manage both.
Write risks as cause, risk event, effect so the response becomes clear.
Identify risks with checklists (Boehm's top ten), brainstorming, assumptions analysis, SWOT and premortems.
Keep a living risk register with probability, impact, score, owner, response and triggers.
Qualitative analysis ranks risks with a probability-impact matrix; quantitative analysis uses exposure = probability x impact.
DhakaEats' threat exposures sum to 4 lakh, which sets the contingency reserve.
Decision trees compare options by EMV; buying the payment module (4.2 lakh) beat building it (4.5 lakh), but worst cases also matter.
lessons.tip: Run a ten-minute premortem with any group project: everyone writes, it is three months from now and our project failed; why? Read them out without discussion first. You will find risks that a normal planning meeting never surfaces.
lessons.task: Write six risks for a team building a Pohela Boishakh event-ticketing app, each in cause, risk, effect form. Rate each on probability (0 to 1) and impact in taka, compute exposures, and sum them to suggest a contingency reserve. Then draw a decision tree for one choice, such as using a paid or a free SMS service.

quiz.q: The payment sandbox has been down for three days. This is:
quiz.explain: It has already happened, so it is an issue to handle now, not an uncertain future risk.

quiz.q: A risk has probability 0.4 and impact 3 lakh. Its exposure is:
quiz.explain: Exposure = probability x impact = 0.4 x 3 = 1.2 lakh.

quiz.q: Building costs 2.5 lakh with a 0.4 chance of 5 lakh extra. Buying costs 4 lakh with a 0.1 chance of 2 lakh extra. Which has the lower EMV of cost?
quiz.explain: Build: 2.5 + 0.4 x 5 = 4.5. Buy: 4 + 0.1 x 2 = 4.2. Buy is cheaper on average.

quiz.q: In a premortem, the team:
options: Reviews a project after it has finished
Imagines the project has failed and lists the reasons
quiz.explain: A premortem imagines future failure to surface risks people might not otherwise mention.

quiz.q: Which is one of Boehm's top ten software risk items?
options: A continuing stream of requirements changes
quiz.explain: Requirements churn is on Boehm's list, along with personnel shortfalls, unrealistic schedules and gold-plating.

lessons.title: Risk Management II: Responses and Monitoring
lessons.content:
Every monsoon, Dhaka families face the risk of a flooded ground floor. Some move to a higher flat: they avoid the risk. Some raise the doorstep and keep sandbags: they reduce it. Some buy insurance for their furniture: they transfer the money loss to someone else. Some simply accept it and keep a plan ready to move things upstairs when the water rises. All four are sensible responses; the wrong response is to do nothing and then panic. Lesson 15 found and ranked DhakaEats' risks. This lesson decides what to do about each one, and how to keep watching them as the project moves.

Planning risk responses: for every important risk, the team chooses a strategy, defines concrete actions, assigns an owner, estimates the cost of the response, and records triggers that show the risk is about to happen or has happened. A response must be proportionate: spending 3 lakh to protect against a risk with 0.5 lakh exposure is usually wasteful, unless the worst case is unacceptable.

Avoid: avoiding a threat means changing the plan so the risk cannot happen, or cannot affect the project. If a brand-new framework might be unstable, use a mature one. If a feature depends on an unreliable government API, remove it from release 1. Avoidance is powerful but usually costs something: lost features, less innovation, or more time. Clarifying a vague requirement early is also a form of avoidance: the risk of building the wrong thing disappears.

Mitigate: mitigation reduces the probability, the impact, or both. Prototyping a risky screen reduces the chance of building the wrong UI. Load testing before launch reduces the chance of a crash at launch. Pair programming on the payment module reduces the impact of one person leaving. Most software risk responses are mitigations.

Transfer: transfer shifts the impact, usually the financial impact, to a third party, normally for a price. Examples: insurance, a fixed-price contract with a vendor (the vendor carries the cost overrun risk), warranties, performance bonds, or using a managed cloud service with an SLA instead of running your own servers. Transfer does not remove the risk: if the vendor fails, your schedule still suffers; you just get compensation or someone else pays the extra cost.

Accept: acceptance means deciding not to act unless the risk occurs. Passive acceptance just records the risk and deals with it if it happens. Active acceptance sets aside a contingency reserve of time or money and prepares a contingency plan. Low-exposure risks and risks with no cost-effective response are usually accepted. The map API price rise in DhakaEats, exposure 0.3 lakh, is actively accepted: the 4 lakh contingency covers it.

Escalate: newer PMBOK editions add escalation: if a risk is outside the project's scope or the project manager's authority, it is passed to the right level, such as the program, portfolio or sponsor, who then owns it. If DhakaEats discovers that a new central bank rule might affect all mobile-wallet apps the client runs, that is escalated to the client's management, not handled inside the project.

Opportunity responses: for good risks, the strategies mirror the threat ones. Exploit: make sure the opportunity happens, for example by assigning the developer who built the grocery app to DhakaEats so reuse actually works. Enhance: increase its probability or impact, for example by cleaning up the grocery modules first so more can be reused. Share: partner with someone better placed to capture it, such as a joint venture or revenue share. Accept: be willing to take it if it comes, without effort to chase it. Escalate also applies.

Worked mitigation with risk reduction leverage: R1, the payment sandbox might be unreliable, has probability 0.4 and impact 3 lakh, exposure 1.2 lakh. Mitigation: build a small mock payment server that imitates the provider, so the team can develop and test even when the sandbox is down, costing 0.4 lakh. Estimated new probability of a serious delay 0.15 and new impact 2 lakh, so new exposure 0.15 x 2 = 0.3 lakh. Boehm's risk reduction leverage, RRL = (exposure before minus exposure after) / cost of mitigation = (1.2 minus 0.3) / 0.4 = 0.9 / 0.4 = 2.25. Every taka spent removes 2.25 taka of expected loss: clearly worth doing.

A second calculation, and its limits: R2, the payment expert might leave, has probability 0.1 and impact 5 lakh, exposure 0.5 lakh. Mitigation by pairing a second developer costs about 0.6 lakh in slower progress and reduces impact to 1.5 lakh, so exposure becomes 0.1 x 1.5 = 0.15 lakh. RRL = (0.5 minus 0.15) / 0.6, about 0.58, which is below 1. On averages alone, not worth it. But the worst case, losing 5 lakh and missing launch, is very damaging, and pairing also improves code quality and spreads knowledge for future projects. The manager pairs anyway. RRL guides decisions; it does not replace judgement about worst cases.

Residual and secondary risks: after a response, some risk usually remains: residual risk. The mock server does not make sandbox problems impossible; residual exposure is 0.3 lakh. Responses can also create new risks: secondary risks. The mock server might behave differently from the real provider, so tests pass against the mock but fail in production. That secondary risk needs its own small response: run a full test against the real sandbox at least once a week.

Contingency and fallback plans: a contingency plan is what you will do if the risk occurs, decided in advance. For R5, app store rejection near launch: submit a build two weeks early, and if rejected, fix and resubmit using a prepared checklist of common rejection reasons. A fallback plan is plan B if the contingency plan itself fails: launch on Android first and iOS a week later, with the marketing campaign adjusted. A workaround, by contrast, is an unplanned response to a risk nobody identified; needing many workarounds is a sign that risk identification was weak.

Triggers and owners: a trigger is a warning sign that a risk is about to occur. For R1: the sandbox is down for more than 4 hours twice in one week. For R3: restaurant data not received by the agreed date. Every risk has an owner, the person who watches its triggers and runs its response. The owner is not necessarily the project manager; the backend lead owns R1, the client relationship manager owns R3.

Monitoring risks: risks change as the project moves: some disappear, some grow, new ones appear. Good practice is a short risk review in every weekly status meeting or sprint retrospective: are the triggers firing? Did the responses work? Any new risks? Risk audits occasionally check whether the risk process itself works. Agile teams often put top risks on a visible board and treat risk-reducing work, like a spike to test the payment API, as backlog items.

The risk burndown: plot the total risk exposure over time and you get a risk burndown chart. DhakaEats starts at 4.0 lakh of threat exposure. After the mock server (reducing R1 by 0.9) and pairing (reducing R2 by 0.35), exposure falls to 4.0 minus 0.9 minus 0.35 = 2.75 lakh. As risks pass, for example once the app is approved in both stores, their exposure drops to zero. A chart that is not falling as launch approaches is a warning sign in itself.

Using the reserves: when a planned risk occurs, its contingency plan runs and its cost is drawn from the contingency reserve, and the risk register records how much was used. If R1 happens despite the mock server and costs 1 lakh, the reserve drops from 4 to 3 lakh. Watching the remaining reserve against the remaining exposure tells the manager whether the project is still protected. If the reserve is being used faster than risks are retiring, it is time to raise the alarm, long before the money is gone.

Monte Carlo simulation, the idea: single-number estimates and even PERT can hide how uncertainties combine, especially at merges (lesson 11). Monte Carlo simulation runs the project many times on a computer, each time picking random durations or costs from each activity's range, and records the results. A tiny hand version: two tasks in sequence, X and Y. Run 1: X takes 4 weeks, Y 3, total 7. Run 2: 3 and 2, total 5. Run 3: 6 and 3, total 9. Run 4: 4 and 5, total 9. Run 5: 5 and 3, total 8. In 3 of 5 runs the total is 8 weeks or less, so the estimated chance of finishing within 8 weeks is about 60 percent. Real simulations use thousands of runs, so the percentages become stable, and they produce a full S-curve of probabilities, letting a manager say: we have an 80 percent chance of finishing by week 27.

Why merges matter, simply: if two independent paths must both finish before integration testing, and each has a 50 percent chance of being done by week 17, the chance that both are done by week 17 is only 0.5 x 0.5 = 25 percent. Monte Carlo captures this naturally; a single critical path calculation does not.

Real-life example 1, a payment switch migration: a bank planned to move its card transactions to a new switch over one weekend. Risks: transactions failing, data mismatch, long downtime. Responses: avoid by choosing a low-traffic weekend (not before Eid); mitigate with three full rehearsals; transfer with a vendor contract including penalties; and a contingency plan to roll back to the old switch within two hours, with a clear trigger: more than 1 percent failed transactions in the first hour. On the night, the trigger fired, they rolled back calmly, fixed the issue, and migrated successfully two weeks later.

Real-life example 2, a university fest app: student organisers identified the risk that campus Wi-Fi would collapse when thousands opened the app at once. They mitigated by making the schedule screen work offline after the first download, and prepared a fallback: printed schedules at the gate. On the day, the Wi-Fi did collapse; the app still worked, and the printed sheets handled the rest.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: choosing responses without costing them; thinking transfer removes the risk; forgetting residual and secondary risks; having no triggers or owners; and reviewing risks only at the start. Exams often ask you to list and explain the threat and opportunity strategies with examples, compute risk reduction leverage, distinguish contingency plans, fallback plans and workarounds, explain residual and secondary risks, and describe Monte Carlo simulation.

Recap: for threats, avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept or escalate; for opportunities, exploit, enhance, share, accept or escalate. Cost each response and check RRL = (exposure before minus after) / cost: the DhakaEats mock server scored 2.25. Record residual and secondary risks, contingency and fallback plans, triggers and owners. Review risks continuously and watch the risk burndown fall, from 4.0 to 2.75 lakh after two responses. Monte Carlo simulation reveals realistic probabilities when uncertainties combine. Next lesson: managing projects the agile way and choosing a life cycle.
key_points: Threat responses: avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept (passive or active) and escalate.
Opportunity responses: exploit, enhance, share, accept and escalate.
Transfer shifts financial impact to a third party for a price but does not remove the risk.
Risk reduction leverage = (exposure before minus exposure after) / cost of response; above 1 is usually worthwhile.
DhakaEats' mock payment server cut exposure from 1.2 to 0.3 lakh for 0.4 lakh: RRL 2.25.
Residual risk remains after a response; secondary risks are new risks created by the response.
Contingency plans are prepared responses, fallback plans are plan B, workarounds are unplanned fixes.
Monitor triggers and owners continuously; Monte Carlo simulation shows how uncertainties combine, especially at merges.
lessons.tip: For every red risk, force yourself to fill four boxes: strategy, action, owner, trigger. If any box is empty, the risk is not really being managed yet, it is only being worried about.
lessons.task: Take the six risks you wrote in the lesson 15 task. For each, choose a response strategy, write one concrete action, name an owner and a trigger, and estimate the cost of the response. Compute the risk reduction leverage for the two most important ones, and draw a simple risk burndown showing exposure before and after your responses.

quiz.q: Buying insurance against hardware loss is an example of:
quiz.explain: Insurance moves the financial impact to the insurer for a price; the risk event can still happen.

quiz.q: Exposure falls from 1.2 to 0.3 lakh after a response costing 0.4 lakh. The risk reduction leverage is:
A mock server makes tests pass that later fail against the real payment system. This new risk is a:
quiz.explain: A secondary risk is created by implementing a risk response.

quiz.q: Which response to an opportunity tries to make sure it definitely happens?
quiz.explain: Exploit acts to ensure the opportunity is realised; enhance only increases its probability or impact.

quiz.q: Two independent paths must both finish before testing. Each has a 50 percent chance of finishing by week 17. The chance both finish by week 17 is:
quiz.explain: For independent events, multiply: 0.5 x 0.5 = 0.25, which is why merges make schedules riskier.

lessons.title: Agile Project Management and Choosing a Life Cycle
lessons.content:
Planning a picnic for next Friday with friends is easy: you know the place, the food, the people. Planning how to run a brand-new street food stall for a whole year is different: you do not know which dishes will sell, what customers will ask for, or how the rent will change. For the picnic, a detailed plan made today works. For the stall, you are better off starting small, watching what sells each week, and adjusting. Software projects can look like either situation. This lesson explains agile project management, when it fits, and how to choose a life cycle for a given project.

Where agile came from: by the 1990s many software teams found that heavy, document-driven plans failed when requirements were uncertain and technology changed fast. In 2001, seventeen practitioners wrote the Agile Manifesto, valuing individuals and interactions, working software, customer collaboration and responding to change over processes and tools, comprehensive documentation, contract negotiation and following a plan. You studied the manifesto, XP and Scrum basics in Software Engineering (deep-cse-4-4, lessons 06 and 07). Here we look at what agile changes for the project manager.

The four life cycle types, revisited: lesson 02 named them. Predictive (Waterfall): scope, time and cost planned up front, change controlled tightly; good when requirements are stable and well understood, such as a regulatory report with a fixed format. Iterative: repeat cycles to refine a solution, good when the right solution is unclear. Incremental: deliver usable pieces one after another, good when early value matters. Adaptive or agile: both iterative and incremental, with short timeboxes and continuous re-planning, good when requirements are uncertain and feedback is valuable. Hybrid: a mix, often predictive around the edges (contracts, budgets, hardware, regulatory approvals) and agile inside (the software build).

Choosing with two questions: a simple way to choose, inspired by the Stacey matrix, is to ask two questions. How much do we agree on, and know about, the requirements? How certain is the technology and approach? If both are clear, a predictive approach is efficient. If either is uncertain, iterative and agile approaches are safer, because they turn assumptions into facts quickly. If both are very uncertain, start with short experiments, prototypes or spikes, before committing to a large plan. Other factors also matter: how easily can the client be involved, can the product be delivered in pieces, do contracts or regulators demand fixed scope, and how experienced is the team with agile practices.

DhakaEats: which life cycle? Requirements are partly known (ordering, payment, tracking) but details will change once real restaurants and riders use the app. The technology is mostly familiar, except the payment provider. The client wants a fixed launch date and budget. MeghSoft chooses a hybrid: a fixed overall budget and date with phase gates for the client (lesson 02), and two-week Scrum sprints inside, with scope as the flexible part. This is extremely common in real projects.

The inverted triangle: in a traditional project, scope is fixed and time and cost are estimated from it. Agile flips the triangle: time (the sprint and release dates) and cost (the team) are fixed, and scope is estimated and flexed. The question changes from how long will all these features take? to which most valuable features can we deliver by this date with this team? Quality is not supposed to flex: the definition of done stays firm.

Product vision and roadmap: agile planning works at several levels. The product vision is a short statement of who the product is for and why it matters: DhakaEats helps busy people in Dhaka get food from local restaurants quickly, while giving riders fair, trackable work. The product roadmap shows major themes or features over time, usually by quarter: Q1 ordering and payment, Q2 scheduled orders and loyalty, Q3 grocery. Roadmaps are intentions, not promises, and get more detailed for nearer periods, much like rolling wave planning.

Release planning: a release plan maps backlog items to upcoming sprints toward a release goal. For DhakaEats release 1, the product backlog holds 300 story points of user stories (lesson 14). With 13 two-week sprints before launch, the team needs an average of about 23 points per sprint. The release plan is updated after every sprint as actual velocity becomes known.

Velocity: velocity is the amount of work, usually in story points, a team completes per sprint, counting only items that meet the definition of done. It is a planning tool for the team, not a productivity score to compare teams, because story points are relative units each team defines for itself. Pushing teams to increase velocity tends to inflate estimates rather than speed up work.

Velocity forecasting, worked: after 5 sprints, the DhakaEats team's velocities were 16, 19, 21, 22 and 22, a total of 100 points. Velocity was low at first as the team learned the codebase, then stabilised. Using the last three sprints, the average is (21 + 22 + 22) / 3, about 21.7. Remaining backlog: 300 minus 100 = 200 points. Expected sprints needed: 200 / 21.7, about 9.2, so 10 sprints. Using the slowest recent velocity, 21: about 9.5, so 10 sprints. Using the fastest, 22: about 9.1, still 10 sprints. But only 8 sprints remain before launch.

What the forecast means: in 8 sprints at 21 to 22 points, the team can deliver about 168 to 176 more points, not 200. About 24 to 32 points will not fit. This is the same warning the EVM numbers gave in lesson 14 (SPI about 0.87), arriving through a different method, which builds confidence that it is real. The agile response is not to demand that the team simply work faster, but to choose what to leave out, using priorities agreed with the product owner.

MoSCoW prioritisation: MoSCoW sorts requirements into Must have (the release is useless or illegal without them), Should have (important but there is a workaround), Could have (nice if time allows), and Won't have this time (explicitly out of this release). The DSDM method, where MoSCoW comes from, recommends keeping Must haves to no more than about 60 percent of the effort, so that there is room to absorb problems by dropping Coulds and some Shoulds. For DhakaEats, rider ratings (8 points), restaurant sales reports (13 points) and saved favourite orders (8 points) are Could haves: 29 points, enough to close the gap. The client agrees to move them to release 1.1.

Burndown and burnup charts: a release burndown chart plots remaining work (points) on the vertical axis against sprints on the horizontal. A straight ideal line runs from the total at the start to zero at the release date; the actual line shows progress. If the actual line is above the ideal, the team is behind. A burnup chart plots completed work rising toward a separate line for total scope. Its advantage is that scope changes are visible: if the client adds 20 points, the scope line jumps up, instead of making it look as if the team did negative work, as a burndown would.

Reading a burnup: after 5 sprints, DhakaEats' completed line is at 100 and the scope line at 300. Extending the completed line at about 21.7 points per sprint shows it meeting the scope line during sprint 15, two sprints after the 13-sprint launch. When the Could haves move out, the scope line drops to 271, and the projection meets it at about sprint 13, right at the launch date with almost no slack, so the team guards its sprint goals carefully and keeps a couple of Should haves ready to drop if needed.

The planning onion: Mike Cohn, in his book Agile Estimating and Planning, describes agile planning as layers of an onion. The outer layers are strategy and portfolio, decided by senior management; then the product (vision and roadmap); then the release; then the iteration or sprint; and at the centre, the day, handled in the daily stand-up. Each inner layer is planned more often and in more detail than the one outside it. Agile teams therefore plan constantly, just in small pieces, which answers the common myth that agile means no planning.

What the project manager does in agile: in pure Scrum, there is no project manager role; responsibilities are spread among the Product Owner (what and in what order), the Developers (how, and their own sprint plan) and the Scrum Master (process and obstacles). In larger organisations, a project or delivery manager often still handles budgets, contracts, cross-team dependencies, vendor coordination, risk and reporting to governance, while respecting the team's self-management. Lesson 18 covers this in detail.

Agile contracts, briefly: fixed-price, fixed-scope contracts fit badly with agile. Common alternatives are time and materials with a budget cap, a fixed price per sprint with scope chosen sprint by sprint, or a fixed price for a fixed time with prioritised, flexible scope. MeghSoft's DhakaEats contract is the last type: fixed budget and date, scope ordered by MoSCoW, with a change process for anything new. Lesson 24 discusses contract types and risk.

Real-life example 1, a mobile banking app: a bank's first app was built Waterfall with an 18-month plan. By launch, competitors had already shipped features customers wanted and the bank's design felt dated. For version 2, the bank used a hybrid: quarterly roadmap, two-week sprints, monthly releases to a small group of customers. Feedback in the first month changed the order of three major features, and the most-used one turned out to be one that was not even in the original plan.

Real-life example 2, an exam result system: a board needed a system to publish results on a fixed, publicly announced date, with requirements fixed by regulation and no room for partial delivery. A mostly predictive approach with strong testing and rehearsal fitted well. Agile is not automatically better; the life cycle should follow the nature of the uncertainty.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: thinking agile means no planning or no documentation; using velocity to compare teams or as a target; letting Must haves fill 100 percent of capacity; reading a burndown without noticing scope changes; and forcing one life cycle on every project. Exams often ask you to compare predictive and adaptive life cycles, explain the inverted triangle, forecast a release with velocity, apply MoSCoW, interpret burndown and burnup charts, and recommend a life cycle for a scenario with reasons.

Recap: choose the life cycle by the uncertainty of requirements and technology, plus client involvement, deliverability in pieces and contractual constraints; hybrids are common. Agile fixes time and cost and flexes scope. Plan with vision, roadmap, release plan and sprints. Forecast with velocity from recent sprints: DhakaEats needed about 10 more sprints but had 8, so 29 Could-have points moved to release 1.1. MoSCoW keeps Musts to about 60 percent. Burnup charts show scope changes clearly. Next lesson: Scrum in depth from the project manager's point of view.
key_points: Life cycles: predictive, iterative, incremental, adaptive (agile) and hybrid; choose by requirement and technology uncertainty plus context.
Agile inverts the triangle: time and cost are fixed, scope flexes, quality stays fixed.
Plan at levels: vision, roadmap, release plan, sprint plan.
Velocity is completed story points per sprint, a team planning tool, not a productivity score.
DhakaEats: 200 points left at about 21.7 per sprint needed about 10 sprints but only 8 remained.
MoSCoW: Must, Should, Could, Won't this time; keep Musts to about 60 percent of effort.
Burnup charts show scope changes clearly; burndown charts show remaining work.
In agile, PM duties are shared among Product Owner, Developers and Scrum Master, with delivery managers handling budgets, vendors and governance.
lessons.tip: When you forecast with velocity, always give a range from the slowest and fastest recent sprints, never a single date. Saying 9 to 10 sprints is honest; saying sprint 14, day 3 is fiction.
lessons.task: Your team's last four sprint velocities were 18, 24, 20 and 22, and 150 points remain. Forecast the number of sprints using the average of the last three, the slowest and the fastest. If only 6 sprints remain, decide how many points to cut and list which kind of MoSCoW items you would move out.

quiz.q: In the agile inverted triangle, which is usually flexible?
quiz.explain: Agile fixes time and cost (sprints and team) and flexes scope; quality, via the definition of done, stays firm.

quiz.q: Recent velocities are 21, 22 and 22 and 200 points remain. About how many sprints are needed?
quiz.explain: Average about 21.7; 200 / 21.7 is about 9.2, so 10 sprints.

quiz.q: Why is a burnup chart better than a burndown chart when the client adds scope?
options: It does not use story points
It shows the scope line moving, so added work is visible
quiz.explain: A burnup has a separate scope line, so added scope appears as a jump instead of looking like negative progress.

quiz.q: Which project best fits a mostly predictive life cycle?
options: A new social app whose features depend on user feedback
A results system with requirements fixed by regulation and a fixed date
A research prototype using untested technology
A game whose fun factor must be discovered
quiz.explain: Stable, well-understood, fixed requirements suit predictive planning.

quiz.q: DSDM recommends keeping Must have items to about what share of the effort?
quiz.explain: About 60 percent, leaving room to absorb problems by dropping Could and some Should items.

lessons.title: Scrum for the Project Manager
lessons.content:
A cricket team does not plan the whole season ball by ball. It plans each match, reviews after the match, and practises what went wrong before the next one. During the match, the captain sets the field, the bowlers decide how to bowl each ball, and the coach watches from outside, helping the team improve without grabbing the ball. Scrum works in a similar way: short, fixed cycles, clear accountabilities, and regular moments to inspect and adapt. You met Scrum's basics in Software Engineering (deep-cse-4-4, lesson 07). This lesson looks at it from the manager's chair: what Scrum actually requires, where traditional project management fits, how to plan a sprint, and what goes wrong.

What Scrum is, precisely: Scrum is a lightweight framework, defined in the Scrum Guide by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, that helps people generate value through adaptive solutions for complex problems. It rests on empiricism (knowledge comes from experience and decisions are based on what is observed) and lean thinking (reduce waste, focus on essentials). Its three pillars are transparency, inspection and adaptation. The Guide is short on purpose; it says what Scrum is, not every practice a team should use. User stories, story points and burndown charts are popular complementary practices, not parts of the Scrum Guide itself.

The Scrum Team: the 2020 Scrum Guide describes one Scrum Team, typically 10 or fewer people, with no sub-teams or hierarchies, containing three accountabilities. The Product Owner is accountable for maximising the value of the product and for managing the Product Backlog: ordering it, making it visible and clear. The Product Owner is one person, not a committee. The Developers are the people who create the usable increment each sprint; they own the Sprint Backlog and how they do the work, and they are accountable for meeting the Definition of Done. The Scrum Master is accountable for the Scrum Team's effectiveness: teaching Scrum, coaching self-management, removing impediments, and helping the wider organisation understand Scrum.

Artifacts and commitments: Scrum has three artifacts, each with a commitment that gives focus. The Product Backlog is the ordered list of what is needed to improve the product; its commitment is the Product Goal, a future state of the product the team aims for. The Sprint Backlog is the Sprint Goal (why), the selected backlog items (what) and a plan for delivering them (how); its commitment is the Sprint Goal. The Increment is a usable step toward the Product Goal; its commitment is the Definition of Done, the shared quality standard every increment must meet. If an item does not meet the Definition of Done, it is not released and not counted.

The events and timeboxes: the Sprint is a container event of one month or less, during which all other events happen; a new sprint starts right after the previous one ends. Sprint Planning has a maximum of 8 hours for a one-month sprint. The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for the Developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt their plan. The Sprint Review is a maximum of 4 hours for a one-month sprint, where the team shows results to stakeholders and discusses what to do next. The Sprint Retrospective is a maximum of 3 hours for a one-month sprint, where the team inspects how it worked and plans improvements. For shorter sprints, the events are usually shorter.

Backlog refinement: refinement is an ongoing activity, not a formal event: the Product Owner and Developers break down, clarify and estimate upcoming backlog items so that they are ready for future sprints. Many teams spend up to about a tenth of their time on it. Without refinement, sprint planning turns into long, confused discussions.

Writing good backlog items: user stories often follow the template as a type of user, I want some goal, so that some reason: as a customer, I want to see my rider on a map, so that I know when to come downstairs. Bill Wake's INVEST checklist says good stories are Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small and Testable. Each story has acceptance criteria, often written as given, when, then: given an order is out for delivery, when I open the order screen, then I see the rider's location updated at least every 10 seconds.

Sprint planning in practice: sprint planning answers three questions: why is this sprint valuable (the Sprint Goal), what can be done (items selected from the top of the ordered backlog), and how will it be done (Developers break items into tasks). A team considers its past velocity and its capacity for this sprint. Example of capacity for a DhakaEats two-week sprint: 5 developers x 10 working days = 50 person-days. One developer has 2 days of leave, leaving 48. Scrum events and other meetings take about 1.25 days per person, 6.25 person-days, leaving about 41.75 person-days. If the team's recent velocity is 21 to 22 points and capacity is normal, it commits to a Sprint Goal with around 21 points of stories, not 30.

The Sprint Goal matters more than the list: a good Sprint Goal is a single objective, such as a customer can order and pay with a mobile wallet end to end. If the team discovers a task is harder than expected, it can negotiate scope with the Product Owner while still meeting the goal. Protecting the Sprint Goal from mid-sprint interruptions is one of the most practical things a manager can do. If the goal becomes obsolete, only the Product Owner can cancel the sprint.

Choosing the sprint length: the Guide allows any length up to one month, and most software teams pick one or two weeks. Shorter sprints give faster feedback and limit how much can go wrong before the next inspection, but the fixed cost of planning, review and retrospective takes a bigger share of the time. Longer sprints suit work that needs more time to produce a usable increment, but risks grow and plans drift. Whatever length is chosen, keep it consistent, because a steady rhythm is what makes velocity meaningful and forecasting possible. DhakaEats uses two weeks, which fits the client's wish to see a demo twice a month.

Where the project manager goes: the Scrum Guide has no project manager. Traditional PM duties are distributed: scope and priority go to the Product Owner; task planning and daily coordination go to the Developers; process improvement and impediment removal go to the Scrum Master. In real organisations, especially with contracts, budgets and many teams, someone still handles budget tracking, contracts and vendors, cross-team dependencies, release coordination, risk and governance reporting. Titles vary: delivery manager, programme manager, agile project manager. The key is to serve the team, not command it: never assign tasks inside a sprint, never turn the Daily Scrum into a status meeting for yourself, and get progress information from the Sprint Review and the team's visible boards.

Common role mistakes: making the Scrum Master the team's boss; appointing a Product Owner with no real authority, who must ask someone else for every decision (a proxy PO); having one person be both Product Owner and Scrum Master, which mixes what to build with how well the team works; and having a project manager who still assigns tasks, which kills self-management.

Scaling Scrum: when a product needs more people than one team, several approaches exist. A Scrum of Scrums is a simple practice where representatives of each team meet regularly to coordinate dependencies. Nexus, from Ken Schwaber's Scrum.org, is a framework for about 3 to 9 Scrum teams working on one product, with an integration team. LeSS (Large-Scale Scrum), by Craig Larman and Bas Vodde, keeps one Product Owner and one Product Backlog for many teams, with minimal extra roles. SAFe (Scaled Agile Framework), by Dean Leffingwell, adds more structure, including Agile Release Trains and regular Program Increment planning events where many teams plan together. Heavier frameworks add coordination but also overhead; the lighter ones demand more organisational change.

Common anti-patterns: water-scrum-fall, where analysis and design happen up front, Scrum is used only for coding, and testing happens at the end, keeping most of the old risks. Sprints with no usable increment, just progress on tasks. Carry-over every sprint, a sign of overcommitment or stories that are too big. No Definition of Done, so done means different things to different people. Retrospectives with no actions, or the same complaints every time. And using velocity as a target or a weapon. A good manager watches for these and raises them in retrospectives.

Metrics a manager can use in Scrum: sprint goal success rate (how often the goal is met), velocity trend (for forecasting, not judging), escaped defects (bugs found after release), cycle time from start to done for stories (lesson 19), the release burnup, and team happiness or engagement surveys. Combining a few of these gives a fair picture without pushing people to game a single number.

Real-life example 1, a fintech startup: a startup in Dhaka adopted Scrum but its founder joined every Daily Scrum and asked each developer, what did you do yesterday? The event became a 45-minute status report and people started inventing progress. The Scrum Master proposed that the founder attend the Sprint Review instead, where he could see working features and give feedback. The Daily Scrum went back to 15 minutes, focused on the Sprint Goal, and trust improved.

Real-life example 2, the DhakaEats sprint 7 review: in sprint 7, the Sprint Goal was customers can track their rider live. In the Sprint Review, the client's operations manager tried the feature on a cheap Android phone and noticed the map lagged badly on slow connections. The team added a story to send location updates less often on slow networks and placed it at the top of the backlog. Without a review with real stakeholders, the problem would have surfaced only after launch.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: calling Scrum a methodology that prescribes everything; thinking story points are part of the Scrum Guide; mixing up the commitments (Product Goal, Sprint Goal, Definition of Done) with the artifacts; forgetting the timebox limits; and believing Scrum has a project manager role. Exams often ask you to list Scrum accountabilities, artifacts and events with timeboxes, explain the commitments, write a user story with INVEST and acceptance criteria, calculate sprint capacity, describe how traditional PM duties are distributed, and compare scaling frameworks.

Recap: Scrum is a lightweight framework built on empiricism and lean thinking, with transparency, inspection and adaptation. One Scrum Team of usually 10 or fewer has a Product Owner, Developers and a Scrum Master. Three artifacts carry commitments: Product Backlog with Product Goal, Sprint Backlog with Sprint Goal, Increment with Definition of Done. Events: Sprint up to a month, Planning up to 8 hours, Daily Scrum 15 minutes, Review up to 4, Retrospective up to 3, for a one-month sprint. Plan sprints with velocity and capacity, protect the Sprint Goal, and serve rather than command. Scale with Scrum of Scrums, Nexus, LeSS or SAFe. Next lesson: Kanban, lean thinking and flow metrics.
key_points: Scrum is a lightweight framework based on empiricism and lean thinking, with transparency, inspection and adaptation.
One Scrum Team, typically 10 or fewer: Product Owner, Developers and Scrum Master.
Artifacts and commitments: Product Backlog with Product Goal, Sprint Backlog with Sprint Goal, Increment with Definition of Done.
Timeboxes for a one-month sprint: Planning up to 8 h, Daily Scrum 15 min, Review up to 4 h, Retrospective up to 3 h.
Good stories follow INVEST and have acceptance criteria such as given, when, then.
Plan sprints from recent velocity and real capacity, and protect the Sprint Goal.
Scrum has no project manager role; PM duties are distributed, and delivery managers serve rather than command.
Scaling options include Scrum of Scrums, Nexus, LeSS and SAFe; watch for anti-patterns like water-scrum-fall.
lessons.tip: If you ever manage a Scrum team, attend the Sprint Review, not the Daily Scrum. The Review shows you working software and real progress; the Daily Scrum belongs to the Developers.
