lessons.task: Write three user stories for a library app, each with INVEST in mind and two given-when-then acceptance criteria. Then calculate the capacity of a two-week sprint for a team of 4 developers where one has 3 days of leave and events take 1.25 days per person, and write a one-sentence Sprint Goal.

quiz.q: Which is the commitment attached to the Increment in the Scrum Guide?
quiz.explain: The Increment's commitment is the Definition of Done; the Product Backlog has the Product Goal and the Sprint Backlog has the Sprint Goal.

quiz.q: What is the timebox of the Daily Scrum?
quiz.explain: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for the Developers.

quiz.q: Who is accountable for ordering the Product Backlog?
quiz.explain: The Product Owner manages and orders the Product Backlog to maximise value.

quiz.q: In INVEST, the letter T stands for:
quiz.explain: INVEST: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable.

quiz.q: Doing analysis and design up front, Scrum only for coding, and testing at the end is called:
quiz.explain: Water-scrum-fall keeps most Waterfall risks while using Scrum only for the build phase.

lessons.title: Kanban, Lean and Flow Metrics
lessons.content:
Think of a busy fuchka stall near Dhanmondi Lake in the evening. If the seller starts twenty plates at once, half-filling each one, nobody gets a plate for ten minutes and some shells go soggy. If he finishes one or two plates at a time, every customer waits less and nothing is wasted. The stall serves the same number of plates per hour either way, but the customer's wait changes dramatically. That is the core idea of Kanban and lean thinking: stop starting, start finishing. This lesson explains lean principles, the Kanban method, and the flow metrics a project manager uses to see and improve how work moves.

Where lean came from: lean thinking grew out of the Toyota Production System, developed in Japan after the Second World War by Taiichi Ohno and others. Toyota aimed to produce exactly what customers needed, when they needed it, with the least waste. Kanban, Japanese for signboard or visual card, was Toyota's system of cards that signalled when to produce more parts, so that nothing was produced before it was needed. In 2003, Mary and Tom Poppendieck adapted lean ideas to software in their book Lean Software Development, and around 2007 David J. Anderson shaped the Kanban method for knowledge work.

The seven lean principles for software: the Poppendiecks listed seven principles: eliminate waste, build quality in, create knowledge (learn through experiments and feedback), defer commitment (decide at the last responsible moment, when you know more), deliver fast, respect people, and optimise the whole (improve the full flow from idea to customer, not one department's numbers).

The seven wastes of software: they also translated Toyota's wastes into software terms. Partially done work: code written but not tested or released, which has cost but gives no value yet. Extra features: things nobody uses; studies by the Standish Group famously suggested many features are rarely or never used. Relearning: rediscovering knowledge that was lost because it was not shared or written down. Handoffs: each time work passes between people, knowledge leaks. Delays: waiting for approvals, environments, answers or reviews. Task switching: jumping between many tasks costs focus time. Defects: bugs that must be found and fixed, more expensive the later they are found.

What Kanban is: the Kanban method is a way to improve the flow of work by starting with what you do now, not by introducing new roles or ceremonies. It has no fixed sprints. Work items move continuously across a board, and new work is pulled in only when there is capacity. Anderson's core practices are: visualise the workflow, limit work in progress, manage flow, make policies explicit, implement feedback loops, and improve collaboratively and evolve experimentally.

Visualising the work: a Kanban board has a column for each stage the work passes through, for example Ready, In Development, Code Review, Testing, Done. Each card is one work item, such as a user story or bug. Some columns are split into doing and done sub-columns, so you can see when an item has finished one stage but is waiting for the next. Swimlanes (horizontal rows) can separate types of work, such as urgent production bugs in an expedite lane. Simply putting everything on one visible board often reveals surprises: the DhakaEats team found 9 cards stuck in Code Review, waiting for one senior developer.

Limiting work in progress: a WIP limit is the maximum number of cards allowed in a column at once. If Code Review has a limit of 3 and already holds 3 cards, a developer who finishes coding cannot push another card in; instead, they help review. This is the pull system: work is pulled into a stage when there is room, not pushed in when the previous stage finishes. WIP limits expose bottlenecks quickly and push the team to swarm on stuck work. A common starting point is a limit a little below the current number of items in each stage, then adjust by experiment.

Little's law: the most important formula in flow is Little's law, proven by John Little in 1961 for stable queueing systems: average work in progress = average throughput x average cycle time. Rearranged, average cycle time = average WIP / average throughput. Throughput is how many items finish per unit of time. Cycle time is how long an item takes from start to finish.

Little's law, worked: the DhakaEats team usually has about 12 stories in progress and finishes about 6 stories a week. Average cycle time = 12 / 6 = 2 weeks. A customer-facing request entering the system therefore takes about two weeks to come out. Now the team introduces WIP limits and brings work in progress down to 6 stories, while throughput stays about 6 per week, because the same people are doing the same total amount of work. Average cycle time = 6 / 6 = 1 week. Nobody worked harder, but each story now reaches customers twice as fast. In practice, throughput often rises a little too, because less task switching means less waste.

The conditions behind Little's law: the law holds for long-run averages when the system is stable: items that start eventually finish, the average WIP is about the same at the start and end of the period, and the average age of WIP is not growing. It is not a tool to predict one particular item's cycle time; it tells you about averages, and why limiting WIP shortens waiting.

Lead time and cycle time: definitions vary between organisations, so always state yours. A common convention: lead time is measured from when the customer requests something (or it is committed) to when it is delivered; cycle time is measured from when work actually starts to when it is finished. A story can wait three weeks in the backlog before anyone starts it, so lead time can be much longer than cycle time. Customers feel lead time; teams usually control cycle time more directly.

Flow efficiency: flow efficiency = active work time / total lead time x 100 percent. If a DhakaEats story takes 10 days from start to delivery but only 2 days of that is someone actually working on it, flow efficiency is 2 / 10 = 20 percent. The other 80 percent is waiting: for review, for a test environment, for a question to be answered. Many knowledge-work teams measure flow efficiency of 15 percent or less. The lesson for managers is powerful: making people type faster helps little; removing waiting helps a lot.

Percentiles and service level expectations: averages hide the long waits that annoy customers. Suppose the last 20 DhakaEats stories had cycle times of 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, 6, 6, 7, 7, 8, 8, 9, 10, 12 and 15 days. The total is 129 days, so the average is 6.45 days. Sorted, the 17th value of 20 is 9 days, so about 85 percent of stories finished in 9 days or less. A team can then publish a service level expectation: 85 percent of stories finish within 9 days of starting. That is far more useful to a client than an average, because it states how often the promise holds.

The cumulative flow diagram: a cumulative flow diagram (CFD) plots, for each day, the cumulative number of items that have reached each stage, as stacked coloured bands. The vertical thickness of a band at any day shows the WIP in that stage; the horizontal distance between the top band and the Done band roughly shows average cycle time; the slope of the Done band shows throughput. A band that keeps getting thicker shows a bottleneck building up. Bands that are flat for days show work stuck. A healthy CFD has bands of steady thickness rising smoothly.

Kanban metrics for forecasting: instead of story points and velocity, Kanban teams often forecast by counting items. If throughput has ranged from 4 to 8 stories per week and 60 stories remain, a simple range is 60 / 8 = 7.5 weeks to 60 / 4 = 15 weeks. Monte Carlo simulation (lesson 16) improves this by sampling past weekly throughputs thousands of times, giving answers like an 85 percent chance of finishing within 11 weeks. This works well when items are broken down to roughly similar size.

Kanban or Scrum: Scrum uses fixed sprints, defined roles and sprint commitments; Kanban uses continuous flow, WIP limits and no required roles. Scrum suits product development with a steady rhythm of planned increments. Kanban suits work that arrives unpredictably, such as support, operations, bug fixing and maintenance. Many teams combine them, sometimes called Scrumban: sprints and reviews for rhythm, plus a board with WIP limits and flow metrics. After launch, the DhakaEats support team will use pure Kanban, with an expedite lane for payment outages.

Value stream mapping: a value stream map draws every step from a customer request to delivery, with the working time and waiting time of each step. For the DhakaEats release process: development 3 days, waiting for review 2 days, review half a day, waiting for the test environment 3 days, testing 1 day, waiting for the weekly release 3 days. Total about 12.5 days, of which only 4.5 are work. The biggest wins are clear: a second test environment and more frequent releases, not faster coding.

Real-life example 1, a telecom support team: a mobile operator's IT support team kept a shared spreadsheet of tickets and every engineer worked on 6 or 7 tickets at once. Customers complained that simple requests took weeks. The team moved to a Kanban board with a WIP limit of 2 per engineer and a daily look at blocked cards. Throughput stayed almost the same, but average cycle time dropped from about 15 days to about 5, exactly what Little's law predicts when WIP falls by about two thirds.

Real-life example 2, a newspaper's website team: a Dhaka newspaper's small web team was pulled between editors wanting new features, ad sales wanting campaign pages, and urgent breaking-news fixes. Sprints kept breaking because of urgent work. They switched to Kanban with three swimlanes, breaking news (expedite, limit 1), ads (limit 2) and features (limit 3), with explicit policies about which lane wins. Arguments about priorities dropped because the rules were written on the board.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: putting cards on a board without WIP limits, which gives a pretty board but no flow improvement; treating WIP limits as optional when they feel inconvenient; using averages only and ignoring long tails; confusing lead time and cycle time; and blaming individuals for slow flow instead of fixing the system. Exams often ask you to list lean principles and the seven wastes, explain Kanban practices, apply Little's law, calculate flow efficiency, interpret a cumulative flow diagram, and compare Kanban with Scrum.

Recap: lean, from Toyota and adapted to software by the Poppendiecks, aims to eliminate waste and optimise the whole flow. Kanban visualises work, limits WIP and manages flow without fixed sprints. Little's law: cycle time = WIP / throughput; DhakaEats halved cycle time from 2 weeks to 1 by cutting WIP from 12 to 6. Flow efficiency shows how much of the lead time is real work, 20 percent in our example. Use percentiles for promises, such as 85 percent within 9 days, and read cumulative flow diagrams to spot bottlenecks. Next lesson: managing the people and teams who do all this work.
key_points: Lean comes from the Toyota Production System; the Poppendiecks adapted it to software with seven principles.
Seven software wastes: partially done work, extra features, relearning, handoffs, delays, task switching, defects.
Kanban practices: visualise, limit WIP, manage flow, explicit policies, feedback loops, evolve experimentally.
Little's law: average cycle time = average WIP / average throughput; 12 / 6 = 2 weeks, 6 / 6 = 1 week.
Lead time starts at the request; cycle time starts when work begins.
Flow efficiency = active time / lead time; 2 of 10 days is 20 percent.
Use percentiles for service level expectations: 85 percent of stories within 9 days.
A cumulative flow diagram shows WIP, cycle time and throughput; widening bands reveal bottlenecks.
lessons.tip: When a team says it is too busy, count the cards in progress before adding people. Very often the fix is to start fewer things, not to hire more hands.
lessons.task: Draw a Kanban board for a task you do regularly, such as group assignments or household chores, with at least four columns. Set a WIP limit for each column. For one week, record how many items finish and the average number in progress, then use Little's law to compute the average cycle time, and suggest one waste to remove.

quiz.q: A team averages 12 items in progress and finishes 4 items per week. By Little's law, average cycle time is:
quiz.explain: Cycle time = WIP / throughput = 12 / 4 = 3 weeks.

quiz.q: A story takes 10 days from start to delivery, but only 2 days are active work. Flow efficiency is:
quiz.explain: Flow efficiency = 2 / 10 = 20 percent; the rest is waiting.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the seven wastes of software listed by the Poppendiecks?
quiz.explain: Refactoring improves code quality; the wastes are partially done work, extra features, relearning, handoffs, delays, task switching and defects.

quiz.q: In a cumulative flow diagram, a band that keeps getting thicker indicates:
options: A growing bottleneck in that stage
quiz.explain: Band thickness is the WIP in that stage; growing thickness means work is piling up there.

quiz.q: Which kind of work suits Kanban better than fixed sprints?
options: A brand-new product with a planned roadmap
Support and operations work that arrives unpredictably
quiz.explain: Kanban's continuous flow handles unpredictable arrivals, such as support tickets, better than fixed sprint commitments.

lessons.title: Managing People and Teams
lessons.content:
Put eleven star players in a cricket team who do not talk to each other, and a less famous but united team will often beat them. The same is true in software. A project plan, a budget and an EVM chart do not write code; people do. Most failed projects that look like technical failures turn out, when you dig, to be people failures: unclear roles, unresolved conflicts, burned-out developers, or one key person quietly leaving. This lesson covers how teams form, what motivates people, how to lead and resolve conflict, and how a project manager builds a team that can actually deliver DhakaEats.

Acquiring the team: before managing a team you need one. The project manager usually negotiates with functional or resource managers for people with the right skills, sometimes recruits, and sometimes uses contractors (lesson 24). A skills matrix lists the skills the project needs, such as Flutter, backend, payment integration, testing and UI design, against each available person, rated from 0 (none) to 3 (expert). Gaps show where to hire, train or partner. For DhakaEats, the matrix showed only one person rated 3 in payment integration, the bus factor problem from lesson 15, so a second developer was paired with her.

Tuckman's stages of team development: in 1965 Bruce Tuckman described stages that teams pass through: forming (polite, unsure, depending on the leader), storming (conflicts about roles, approaches and authority), norming (agreeing on how to work together), and performing (working effectively with little supervision). In 1977 he added adjourning, when the team disbands at the end. A manager's style should change with the stage: give clear direction while forming, facilitate and resolve conflict during storming, step back and support while norming and performing. Storming is normal; a team that never disagrees is usually avoiding important conversations.

Maslow's hierarchy of needs: Abraham Maslow suggested in 1943 that people satisfy needs in a rough order: physiological (food, rest), safety (job security, fair pay), belonging (being part of the team), esteem (recognition, respect), and self-actualisation (growth, doing meaningful work). A developer worried about unpaid salary will not be motivated by a certificate of appreciation. The hierarchy is a simplification and later research questions the strict order, but it reminds managers to fix basic needs first.

Herzberg's two-factor theory: Frederick Herzberg found in 1959 that the things that cause dissatisfaction are different from the things that create motivation. Hygiene factors, such as salary, working conditions, company policy and job security, cause dissatisfaction when poor, but improving them only removes dissatisfaction. Motivators, such as achievement, recognition, interesting work, responsibility and growth, actually create motivation. For a manager: a working air conditioner and a decent laptop are hygiene; letting a developer own the rider-tracking feature from design to launch is a motivator.

McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y: Douglas McGregor in 1960 described two sets of manager assumptions. Theory X assumes people dislike work, avoid responsibility and must be controlled and pushed. Theory Y assumes people can enjoy work, seek responsibility when conditions are right, and can direct themselves toward goals they believe in. Managers' assumptions tend to become self-fulfilling: treat people as untrustworthy and they stop taking initiative. Agile self-managing teams are built on Theory Y assumptions.

Autonomy, mastery and purpose: Daniel Pink's 2009 book Drive summarised research suggesting that for creative, thinking work, the strongest motivators are autonomy (control over how to do the work), mastery (getting better at something that matters) and purpose (feeling the work serves something larger). Big rewards tied to narrow targets can even reduce creativity on complex tasks. For a software manager this means: give clear goals, let the team decide how, invest in learning, and connect the work to real users, such as showing the team a video of a rider using their app.

The job characteristics model, worked: Hackman and Oldham's model (1976) says a job is motivating when it has skill variety, task identity (doing a whole, identifiable piece of work), task significance, autonomy and feedback. They combine these, each rated 1 to 7, into a motivating potential score: MPS = ((skill variety + task identity + task significance) / 3) x autonomy x feedback. A DhakaEats tester who only runs scripts written by others, never sees the whole feature, and gets no feedback might score skill variety 3, task identity 2, task significance 5, autonomy 2, feedback 3: MPS = (10 / 3) x 2 x 3 = 20. Redesign the role so she designs test strategies for the full payment flow, chooses her own tools, and sees defect trends weekly: skill variety 5, identity 5, significance 5, autonomy 4, feedback 5, giving MPS = 5 x 4 x 5 = 100. Notice that autonomy and feedback multiply: if either is very low, the whole score collapses.

Team charter and working agreements: early in forming, a good manager helps the team write a short team charter: its purpose, values, decision rules (who decides what, and how disagreements are settled), communication norms (core hours, response times, which channel for what) and the definition of done. Agreements written by the team itself are followed far better than rules handed down. The DhakaEats team agreed, for example, that core hours are 11 am to 4 pm, urgent issues go to a phone call rather than chat, and nobody merges code without one review.

Belbin team roles: Meredith Belbin's research found that effective teams have a balance of behavioural roles, not only technical skills. His nine roles include the Plant (creative ideas), Shaper (drive), Monitor Evaluator (careful judgement), Implementer (turns ideas into action), Completer Finisher (polishes and checks details), Coordinator, Teamworker, Resource Investigator and Specialist. A team of five Plants produces brilliant ideas but ships nothing; a team with no Completer Finisher ships buggy releases.

Leadership styles: there is no single best style. Situational leadership, from Paul Hersey and Ken Blanchard, matches style to the person's competence and commitment for a particular task: directing (clear instructions) for an enthusiastic beginner, coaching (direction plus support) for someone struggling, supporting (encouragement, shared decisions) for a capable but unsure person, and delegating for a skilled, confident person. A new junior developer on the DhakaEats team needs directing on the payment code, while the senior Flutter developer needs delegating. Servant leadership, important in agile, puts the leader's job as removing obstacles and helping the team grow, not giving orders.

Power: a project manager often has little formal authority over team members who report to functional managers. French and Raven's bases of power help: legitimate (position), reward, coercive (punishment), expert (knowledge) and referent (respect and likeability). Project managers who rely on expert and referent power usually get better long-term cooperation than those who rely on coercion.

Conflict and how to resolve it: conflict in projects most often comes from schedules, priorities and resources, followed by technical opinions, procedures, costs and personalities. The Thomas-Kilmann model describes five modes, based on how assertive and how cooperative you are. Competing (forcing): win-lose, useful in emergencies. Accommodating (smoothing): give way to keep peace, useful when the issue matters more to the other side. Avoiding (withdrawing): postpone, useful when tempers are high or the issue is trivial. Compromising: each side gives up something, a quick middle ground. Collaborating (problem-solving): find a solution that fully satisfies both, best for important issues when there is time, because it builds lasting agreement.

A conflict, worked: the DhakaEats backend lead wants two more weeks to refactor the order service; the client relationship manager wants new features shown at the next demo. Forcing either side damages trust. Collaborating, the manager brings both together with data: the order service causes 40 percent of current bugs. They agree to refactor in small slices across three sprints, each sprint also delivering one visible feature. Both goals are met, and the decision is owned by both.

Psychological safety: Amy Edmondson defined psychological safety as a shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking: you can admit a mistake, ask a basic question or challenge an idea without being humiliated. Google's Project Aristotle study of its teams, published in 2015, found psychological safety was the most important factor separating effective teams. In a team without it, bugs get hidden and bad news arrives late. Managers build it by admitting their own mistakes, thanking people for raising problems, and running blameless post-mortems.

Sustainable pace and overtime: crunch, long periods of overtime before a deadline, is common in software and especially in games. Short bursts can help, but long crunch raises error rates, burnout and resignations, and the extra hours are often lost to rework. XP's practice of a sustainable pace and the agile principle that teams should be able to maintain a constant pace indefinitely both reflect this. When DhakaEats fell behind, the manager cut scope (lesson 17) rather than demanding 60-hour weeks for two months.

Developing the team: managers should plan training, mentoring and pairing; give regular one-to-one meetings; provide specific feedback, both positive and corrective; recognise contributions publicly; and think about career paths. Team-building is not only picnics: shared goals, clear roles and early wins build a team more than any game. Co-located teams can use a shared room; remote and hybrid teams need deliberate effort, such as cameras-on stand-ups, written decisions and occasional in-person meetups.

Real-life example 1, a Bangladeshi outsourcing firm: a Dhaka company building software for European clients lost about a third of its developers in a year. Exit interviews showed that salary was acceptable but people felt they never learned anything new and never saw the end users. The company started rotating developers across projects, funding certifications, and inviting clients to demo days. Within a year, resignations roughly halved. These were Herzberg's motivators, not hygiene factors.

Real-life example 2, the hero developer: in one startup a single brilliant developer fixed every crisis at night. Management praised him constantly. The rest of the team stopped learning the core code, and when he burned out and left, the company could not release for two months. Rewarding heroics over shared ownership created a single point of failure. Pairing, code reviews and documentation would have spread knowledge.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: treating people as interchangeable resources; using money as the only motivator; avoiding all conflict; one leadership style for everyone; and praising overtime and heroics. Exams often ask you to explain Tuckman's stages, compare Maslow and Herzberg, contrast Theory X and Y, compute a motivating potential score, describe situational leadership, list conflict resolution modes with when to use each, and explain psychological safety.

Recap: build the team with a skills matrix and fix single points of failure. Teams go through forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning. Fix hygiene factors, then use motivators: autonomy, mastery, purpose, recognition and growth. The MPS formula showed redesigning a tester's role raising her score from 20 to 100. Match leadership style to each person and task, prefer expert and referent power, use collaboration for important conflicts, protect psychological safety and a sustainable pace. Next lesson: communication management, keeping everyone informed.
key_points: A skills matrix shows gaps and single points of failure before work starts.
Tuckman: forming, storming, norming, performing, adjourning; the manager's style should change with the stage.
Herzberg: hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction; motivators such as achievement and growth create motivation.
Theory X assumes people must be controlled; Theory Y assumes they can self-direct, the basis of agile teams.
MPS = ((skill variety + task identity + task significance) / 3) x autonomy x feedback; redesign raised a role from 20 to 100.
Situational leadership: directing, coaching, supporting, delegating, matched to competence and commitment.
Conflict modes: competing, accommodating, avoiding, compromising, collaborating; collaborate on important issues.
Psychological safety and a sustainable pace make teams effective; heroics create single points of failure.
lessons.tip: Hold a short one-to-one with every team member at least every two weeks and ask one question: what is getting in your way? You will hear about most problems weeks before they reach a status report.
lessons.task: Rate a job you know (a part-time job, a club role or a group project role) on the five job characteristics from 1 to 7 and compute its MPS. Then suggest two changes that would raise the lowest factor, and recompute. Also describe one conflict you have seen and which Thomas-Kilmann mode was used.

quiz.q: A team argues about roles and approaches after its first few weeks. Which Tuckman stage is this?
quiz.explain: Storming is the stage of conflict about roles, approaches and authority.

quiz.q: According to Herzberg, which is a motivator rather than a hygiene factor?
quiz.explain: Recognition and achievement are motivators; salary, conditions and policy are hygiene factors.

quiz.q: Skill variety 3, task identity 2, task significance 5, autonomy 2, feedback 3. The MPS is:
Which conflict mode looks for a solution that fully satisfies both sides?
quiz.explain: Collaborating (problem-solving) seeks a win-win; compromising has each side give something up.

quiz.q: Google's Project Aristotle found the most important factor in team effectiveness was:
quiz.explain: Psychological safety, the belief that it is safe to take interpersonal risks, stood out above the other factors.

lessons.title: Communication Management
lessons.content:
Remember the game of passing a whispered message around a circle of friends? By the time it reaches the last person, buy two kilos of potatoes has become fly to Cox's Bazar on Tuesday. Projects play that game every day. The client tells the account manager, who tells the project manager, who tells the team lead, who tells a developer, and the feature that gets built is not quite what anyone wanted. Studies of project managers often estimate that they spend most of their time, sometimes quoted as around 90 percent, communicating. This lesson covers how to plan communication so that the right people get the right information, in the right form, at the right time.

What communication management is: in PMBOK terms it has three parts: plan communications management (decide who needs what, when, how and from whom), manage communications (create, collect, distribute and store the information) and monitor communications (check that it is working and adjust). It works hand in hand with stakeholder management from lesson 04: the stakeholder register says who matters and how much; the communication plan says how to keep each of them informed and engaged.

The basic communication model: a sender encodes a message (into words, a chart, a demo), sends it through a medium (email, meeting, chat, document), and the receiver decodes it. Noise is anything that interferes: jargon, a bad phone line, different first languages, distractions, or simply assumptions. Feedback from the receiver confirms whether the message was understood. The sender is responsible for making the message clear; the receiver is responsible for confirming understanding. When a DhakaEats developer says the API is done, the client may hear the feature is ready to use, while the developer means the code is written but not tested. A shared definition of done removes that noise.

Communication channels, worked: every pair of people who might need to talk is a potential communication channel. With n people, the number of channels is n(n minus 1) / 2. A team of 3 has 3 channels. The DhakaEats core team of 6 has 6 x 5 / 2 = 15 channels. Add the client's product owner, the operations manager and the payment provider's contact, and 9 people give 9 x 8 / 2 = 36 channels. At 12 people, 66 channels. Channels grow roughly with the square of team size, which is why large teams need structure: smaller sub-teams, clear interfaces, and agreed points of contact. It also explains part of Brooks's law from lesson 12.

Push, pull and interactive communication: push communication is sent to specific people: emails, status reports, memos. It ensures the message was sent, not that it was read or understood. Pull communication is placed where people can access it when they want: a wiki, a shared drive, a project dashboard, a Jira board. It works for large audiences and reference information. Interactive communication is real-time, two-way exchange: meetings, calls, video conferences, workshops. It is best for resolving ambiguity, making decisions and handling sensitive topics. A good plan uses all three deliberately.

Formal and informal, written and verbal: formal written communication includes contracts, the project charter, change requests and status reports; it must be precise and is kept as a record. Informal written includes chat messages and quick emails. Formal verbal includes presentations and steering committee briefings. Informal verbal includes hallway conversations and quick calls. Important decisions made informally should be confirmed in writing, for example a short email after a call: as discussed, we will move rider ratings to release 1.1.

The communication management plan: for each stakeholder or group, the plan records what information they need, why, how often, in what format, through which method, who sends it, and how to escalate. A small part of the DhakaEats plan: the client sponsor receives a one-page status report every two weeks by email from the project manager, plus a monthly steering meeting. The client's product owner attends every Sprint Review and has daily access to the board. The development team holds a 15-minute Daily Scrum and uses one chat channel per area. The payment provider's contact gets a weekly technical call during integration. Restaurant partners receive a short newsletter every month and a training session before launch.

Status reports that are actually read: a good status report fits on one page. It states overall status, often as RAG: green (on track), amber (at risk but manageable), red (needs help or a decision). It shows key metrics, such as SPI, CPI, burnup progress and risk exposure; achievements since the last report; plans for the next period; top risks and issues; and decisions needed, with dates. The DhakaEats month 3 report, using the numbers from lesson 14, says: overall amber; SPI 0.88, CPI 0.83; payment integration delayed by sandbox problems; decision needed by 15th: approve moving 29 points of Could haves to release 1.1. Never make a red project look green. Watermelon reporting, green outside and red inside, destroys trust when the truth comes out.

Meetings and what they cost: meetings are expensive. Using the DhakaEats loaded rate of 1 lakh per person-month and about 160 working hours per month, one person-hour costs about 625 taka. A one-hour weekly meeting with 8 people costs 8 x 625 = 5,000 taka per week, or 5,000 x 26 = 1.3 lakh over the 26-week project. That is worth it if the meeting makes decisions or prevents mistakes, and wasteful if it only reads out updates that could be an email. Every meeting should have a clear purpose, an agenda sent in advance, only the people needed, a timebox, and written decisions and action items with owners and dates afterwards.

Information radiators and dashboards: an information radiator is a large, visible display of project information, such as a physical board, a burnup chart on the wall, or a TV showing the build status. Alistair Cockburn coined the term. Radiators make information pull-based and always current, which reduces the need for status meetings. For DhakaEats, a dashboard shows sprint burndown, release burnup, open bugs by severity, build status and the top five risks, and the client has a link to it.

Delivering bad news: every project has bad news. The rule is: early, honest, with options. Telling the client in month 3 that the 6-month launch needs 29 points cut, with two alternative options and their costs, is respectful and gives them choices. Telling them in month 6 that the launch will slip by a month gives them no choices. Use the facts (SPI, velocity forecast), explain the cause briefly without blaming, present options, recommend one, and ask for a decision by a date. Bad news is best delivered interactively, by call or meeting, then confirmed in writing.

Escalation paths: the plan should say how issues rise when they cannot be solved at the current level: for example, team lead within 2 days, project manager within 1 week, steering committee at the next monthly meeting, or immediately for anything that threatens the launch date or budget by more than 10 percent. Clear escalation prevents both silence and panic.

Monitoring communications: a plan is only useful if it works. Ways to check: ask stakeholders every month or two whether they get the information they need, in a quick two-question survey; watch for signs of failure, such as the same question asked repeatedly, decisions being revisited, or people surprised in reviews; and track simple numbers, such as how many action items close on time. When the DhakaEats restaurant partners kept phoning the support line about menu updates, the team realised the monthly newsletter was not being read and switched to a short WhatsApp video message, which worked far better.

Project documentation and knowledge: written records outlive conversations. Keep a decision log (what was decided, when, by whom, and why), meeting notes, architecture decision records and a project wiki. When a developer joins in month 4, these let her catch up in days rather than weeks, and they protect the project when people leave.

Remote, cultural and language issues: distributed teams lose the casual information that flows in an office, so they need more deliberate communication: written decisions, recorded demos, overlapping core hours, and occasional face-to-face meetings. Cultural differences matter too. In some cultures, including much of South Asia, saying no directly to a senior person or a client can feel rude, so problems may be described softly, such as it may be a little difficult. A good manager learns to ask open questions, like what would need to be true for this date to work?, and makes it safe to say no. Language also matters: a Bangla-speaking team serving a Swedish client may need written summaries after every call to catch misunderstandings.

Conway's law: in 1968 Melvin Conway observed that organisations design systems whose structure mirrors their own communication structure. If the DhakaEats customer app, rider app and backend are built by three teams who rarely talk, the system will tend to have three loosely connected parts with awkward interfaces between them. Managers can use this deliberately, the so-called inverse Conway manoeuvre: arrange teams and their communication paths to match the architecture you want.

Real-life example 1, a government e-service: a project to put a land records service online had weekly meetings with more than 20 people, including officials from several departments. Meetings lasted three hours and decisions were rarely recorded. The new project manager split them into a 30-minute steering meeting for decisions with 6 people, plus a shared dashboard and a written weekly summary for everyone else. Decisions that used to take a month were made in a week.

Real-life example 2, the misunderstood requirement: a client of a Dhaka software firm said in a call that reports should be real time. The team built a complex streaming system. At the demo, it turned out the client meant updated every morning instead of every month. One clarifying question with an example would have saved weeks of work. Write requirements down with examples and confirm them; the receiver's feedback step is not optional.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: assuming that sending an email means the message was understood; one-size-fits-all reports for every stakeholder; long status meetings with no decisions; hiding bad news; and ignoring cultural communication styles. Exams often ask you to calculate communication channels, explain the sender-receiver model and noise, compare push, pull and interactive communication, describe the contents of a communication management plan, and design a status report.

Recap: plan who needs what, when, how and from whom; manage the flow; monitor whether it works. Channels grow as n(n minus 1) / 2: 15 for 6 people, 36 for 9, 66 for 12. Use push, pull and interactive methods on purpose. Keep status reports to one page with honest RAG status and clear decisions needed. A weekly 8-person hour-long meeting costs DhakaEats about 1.3 lakh over the project, so make meetings count. Deliver bad news early, honestly, with options. Next lesson: managing software quality.
key_points: Communication management: plan, manage and monitor communications, alongside stakeholder management.
Sender, encoding, medium, decoding, noise and feedback; the receiver must confirm understanding.
Communication channels = n(n minus 1) / 2: 6 people give 15 channels, 9 give 36, 12 give 66.
Push (email, reports), pull (wiki, dashboards) and interactive (meetings, calls) each have their place.
A communication plan records who needs what, why, when, how, from whom and how to escalate.
One-page status reports with honest RAG status, key metrics and decisions needed; avoid watermelon reporting.
Meetings cost money: 8 people for 1 hour weekly is about 1.3 lakh over 26 weeks at DhakaEats rates.
Deliver bad news early with options; Conway's law links team communication to system structure.
lessons.tip: End every meeting by reading the decisions and action items aloud, each with an owner and a date, and send them in writing within the hour. Half of all meeting value is lost when nobody records what was agreed.
lessons.task: Write a one-page communication plan for a group project with at least five stakeholders (for example teammates, supervisor, users and lab staff). For each, give the information, frequency, method and sender. Calculate the number of communication channels in your group, and draft a one-page RAG status report for the current week.

Putting project documents on a shared wiki for people to read when they need them is:
quiz.explain: Pull communication places information where people can access it on their own schedule.

options: A project reported green while it is really red inside
Reports that use too many colours
quiz.explain: Green outside, red inside: hiding real problems, which destroys trust when exposed.

quiz.q: Which method is best for resolving an ambiguous requirement quickly?
quiz.explain: Interactive, two-way communication lets both sides ask questions and confirm understanding immediately.

options: Adding people to a late project makes it later
Work expands to fill the time available
Systems mirror the communication structure of the organisation that builds them
Cycle time equals WIP divided by throughput

lessons.title: Software Quality Management
lessons.content:
A good biryani cook in Old Dhaka does not wait until the guests complain to check whether the rice is salty. She buys good rice, measures the spices, tastes while cooking, and only then serves. If she skips all that and a hundred wedding guests get bland biryani, no apology can fix it. Software quality works the same way: quality is built in through the whole process, checked along the way, and costs far more to fix once it reaches the customer. You studied testing techniques in Software Engineering (deep-cse-4-4) and in depth in Software Testing and QA. This lesson looks at quality from the project manager's side: planning it, paying for it, measuring it, and improving the process that produces it.

What quality means: there are several useful definitions. Philip Crosby defined quality as conformance to requirements. Joseph Juran called it fitness for use. ISO 9000 defines it as the degree to which a set of inherent characteristics fulfils requirements. For software, the ISO/IEC 25010 product quality model lists characteristics such as functional suitability, performance efficiency, compatibility, usability (called interaction capability in the 2023 revision), reliability, security, maintainability and portability. A DhakaEats app that has every feature but crashes on cheap phones is not high quality, because reliability and performance are part of quality.

Quality versus grade: grade is a category of features, quality is how well requirements are met. A simple food delivery app with few features can be high quality (low grade, high quality) if it works reliably. A feature-packed app full of bugs is high grade, low quality. Low grade may be acceptable; low quality never is.

The three processes: in PMBOK terms, plan quality management decides which standards apply and how to meet and check them; manage quality (often called quality assurance) makes sure the processes being used will produce quality, for example through process audits, coding standards and reviews; control quality checks the actual products against requirements, for example through testing and inspections, and records the results. Assurance is about the process, control is about the product. Prevention through good process is cheaper than inspection.

The quality management plan: for DhakaEats, the plan defines quality goals with numbers: crash-free sessions above 99.5 percent, order placement under 3 seconds on a 4G connection, no open critical or high-severity defects at release, unit test coverage of at least 70 percent on payment and order logic, and every pull request reviewed by one other developer. It names tools (a static analysis tool, automated tests in the build pipeline, crash reporting), responsibilities, and when audits happen. Measurable goals let everyone know when quality is good enough.

Cost of quality, the four categories: cost of quality divides quality-related spending into the cost of conformance (prevention and appraisal) and the cost of non-conformance (internal and external failure). Prevention costs: training, coding standards, design reviews, tooling. Appraisal costs: testing, code reviews, inspections, audits. Internal failure costs: fixing defects found before release, rework, retesting. External failure costs: defects found by customers: support calls, hotfixes, refunds, lost customers, damaged reputation.

Cost of quality, worked: halfway through, the DhakaEats manager estimates quality-related costs: prevention 1.0 lakh, appraisal 2.5 lakh, internal failure 2.0 lakh, and external failure from a pilot with 20 restaurants 1.5 lakh. Total cost of quality = 1.0 + 2.5 + 2.0 + 1.5 = 7.0 lakh, about 19 percent of the 36 lakh of planned work. The manager invests an extra 0.5 lakh in prevention: a payment design review and a short secure coding course. For the rest of the project the estimates become prevention 1.5, appraisal 2.3, internal failure 1.5, external failure 0.8, a total of 6.1 lakh. Spending 0.5 more on prevention saved 0.9 lakh overall. This is the classic lesson: money moved earlier saves more money later.

Why late defects cost more: a defect in a requirement found during requirements review may take minutes to fix. The same misunderstanding found after release can mean redesign, recoding, retesting, redeploying, data repair and angry customers. Barry Boehm's studies are often summarised as showing that fixing a defect in production can cost many times, sometimes quoted as up to 100 times for large systems, more than fixing it at requirements time. The exact ratio varies, but the direction is reliable.

Defect removal efficiency: DRE measures how well the team finds defects before release: DRE = defects found before release / (defects found before release + defects found after release) x 100 percent. DhakaEats found 180 defects before release and users reported 20 in the first 90 days after. DRE = 180 / (180 + 20) = 180 / 200 = 90 percent. Capers Jones, who studied thousands of projects, reported that average projects remove roughly 85 percent of defects before release and the best exceed 95 percent; the precise figures vary by study and year.

Defect density: defect density = defects / size, often per KLOC or per function point. With 20 post-release defects in about 9.8 KLOC (lesson 08), DhakaEats has about 20 / 9.8 = 2.04 post-release defects per KLOC. Comparing defect density across modules shows where quality is weakest; comparing across releases shows whether the process is improving. As with all metrics, do not use it to punish individuals, or people will stop reporting bugs.

The seven basic quality tools: Kaoru Ishikawa popularised seven simple tools: cause-and-effect (fishbone or Ishikawa) diagrams, check sheets, histograms, Pareto charts, scatter diagrams, control charts, and flowcharts (some lists use stratification instead). Two of them are especially useful to software managers: Pareto charts and control charts.

Pareto analysis, worked: the Pareto principle, named after the economist Vilfredo Pareto and popularised in quality by Juran, says that a few causes produce most of the effects, often roughly 80/20. DhakaEats' 200 defects by module: payment 70, order 50, menu 30, tracking 25, others 25. Sorted from largest, payment and order together have 120 of 200, which is 60 percent; adding menu gives 150, which is 75 percent. A Pareto chart, bars in descending order plus a cumulative percentage line, makes it obvious that the payment and order modules deserve extra reviews and tests first.

Control charts, worked: a control chart plots a process measurement over time with a centre line (the mean) and control limits, usually 3 standard deviations above and below. Points inside the limits show normal, common-cause variation; a point outside shows a special cause worth investigating. Defects found per week in DhakaEats testing for 8 weeks were 12, 15, 11, 14, 13, 16, 12 and 15. Mean = 13.5, standard deviation about 1.66, so the upper control limit is about 13.5 + 3 x 1.66 = 18.5 and the lower about 8.5. In week 9, testers found 30 defects, far above the limit. Investigation found a special cause: a new module had been merged without its unit tests. Reacting to normal variation (like 16 versus 12) is tampering; reacting to a special cause is good management.

Quality gates and the definition of done: a quality gate is a checkpoint that work must pass before moving on. In a build pipeline, a gate might block a merge if any test fails, coverage drops below the target, or static analysis finds a critical issue. Before release, a gate might require zero open critical defects and a passing performance test. In agile teams, the definition of done plays the same role for each story: code reviewed, tests written and passing, acceptance criteria met, documentation updated. Gates turn quality goals from wishes into rules.

Technical debt: Ward Cunningham coined the term technical debt for shortcuts taken to deliver faster, such as skipping tests or copying code instead of designing it properly. Like a loan, it can be useful in the short term, but it charges interest: every later change becomes slower and riskier. A project manager should make debt visible, for example as backlog items, and plan regular repayment, perhaps 10 to 20 percent of each sprint, instead of letting it grow until the code cannot be changed safely.

Reviews and inspections: reviews are among the most cost-effective quality activities, because they find defects before any testing. Michael Fagan's formal inspections, developed at IBM in the 1970s, use defined roles (moderator, author, reader, recorder, inspectors), preparation, a meeting and follow-up. Lighter forms include walkthroughs, pair programming and pull-request code reviews. For DhakaEats, every pull request needs one reviewer, and the payment module gets a formal design inspection.

Process improvement frameworks: W. Edwards Deming promoted the Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle (PDCA) for continuous improvement: plan a change, try it, check the results, and act by adopting or adjusting it. ISO 9001 is a standard for quality management systems that organisations can be certified against. CMMI (Capability Maturity Model Integration), developed at Carnegie Mellon's Software Engineering Institute, describes maturity levels from 1 (initial, ad hoc) to 5 (optimising, continuous improvement); some Bangladeshi software firms have been appraised at CMMI levels to win international clients. Six Sigma, started at Motorola, uses the DMAIC cycle (define, measure, analyse, improve, control) to reduce variation; its name comes from a target of about 3.4 defects per million opportunities.

Real-life example 1, a ride-sharing app's crash: a ride-sharing app released an update on a Friday evening without enough testing on older Android versions. It crashed on startup for many users over the weekend, and the team spent days on hotfixes, refunds and social media apologies. Afterwards they added automated tests on a set of popular low-cost phones and a staged rollout to 5 percent of users first. Their external failure costs fell sharply.

Real-life example 2, a bank's Pareto analysis: a bank's software team analysed six months of production incidents and found that two integration points, with the card switch and the SMS gateway, caused over half of them. Instead of spreading testing effort evenly, they built contract tests and monitoring for those two points. Incidents fell by roughly half within a quarter.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: thinking quality means only testing; cutting reviews and tests when the schedule is tight, which moves costs into expensive external failures; confusing quality and grade; confusing assurance (process) and control (product); and using defect metrics to blame people. Exams often ask you to define quality and the cost of quality categories, compute DRE and defect density, draw and interpret Pareto and control charts, compare QA and QC, and describe CMMI levels, ISO 9001, Six Sigma or PDCA.

Recap: quality is conformance to requirements and fitness for use, measured with characteristics like reliability and performance. Plan quality with measurable goals, assure the process, control the product. Cost of quality has prevention, appraisal, internal failure and external failure; at DhakaEats, 0.5 lakh more in prevention saved 0.9 lakh. DRE was 90 percent, defect density about 2.04 per KLOC. Pareto showed two modules caused 60 percent of defects; a control chart flagged week 9 as a special cause. Improve the process with reviews, PDCA, CMMI, ISO 9001 and Six Sigma. Next lesson: configuration, change control and release management.
key_points: Quality is conformance to requirements and fitness for use; ISO/IEC 25010 lists product quality characteristics.
Grade is the feature category; low grade can be fine, low quality never is.
Quality assurance improves the process; quality control checks the product.
Cost of quality: prevention, appraisal, internal failure, external failure; DhakaEats saved 0.9 lakh by adding 0.5 in prevention.
DRE = defects before release / all defects; 180 / 200 = 90 percent.
Pareto: payment and order modules caused 60 percent of 200 defects.
Control chart limits at mean plus or minus 3 standard deviations; week 9 with 30 defects was a special cause.
Process improvement: Fagan inspections, Deming's PDCA, ISO 9001, CMMI levels 1 to 5, Six Sigma DMAIC.
lessons.tip: When the schedule gets tight, never cut code reviews first. They are one of the cheapest ways to find defects, and every defect they miss tends to come back later at a much higher price.
lessons.task: Collect the bugs from any project you have worked on, or invent 30 realistic ones, and group them by cause or module. Draw a Pareto chart with cumulative percentages, identify the vital few causes, and propose one prevention action and one appraisal action for each. Then compute the DRE if 4 more bugs are found after release.

quiz.q: Before release 180 defects were found and 20 after release. The DRE is:
Training developers in secure coding is which cost of quality category?
quiz.explain: Training prevents defects from being created, so it is a prevention cost.

quiz.q: Which activity is quality assurance rather than quality control?
options: Auditing whether the team follows its coding standards
Running the test suite on a build
Inspecting a finished screen against its requirements
Counting defects found in system testing
quiz.explain: Assurance checks the process; the others check the product, which is quality control.

quiz.q: A control chart has mean 13.5 and standard deviation about 1.66. Which weekly value signals a special cause?
quiz.explain: The upper control limit is about 13.5 + 3 x 1.66 = 18.5; 30 is far above it.

quiz.q: A simple, reliable app with few features is best described as:
quiz.explain: Few features means low grade; reliability and meeting requirements means high quality.

lessons.title: Configuration, Change Control and Release Management
lessons.content:
Imagine five friends writing one group assignment by emailing a Word file back and forth. Soon there are files called final.docx, final2.docx, final_really_final.docx and final_fixed_by_Rahim.docx. Nobody knows which one has the latest introduction, someone's changes vanish, and on submission day the wrong version is uploaded. Software teams face the same chaos, multiplied by thousands of files and dozens of people. This lesson covers the three disciplines that keep it under control: configuration management (knowing exactly what we have), change control (deciding carefully what we change) and release management (delivering changes safely to users).

Software configuration management: SCM is the discipline of identifying the items that make up a system, controlling changes to them, recording their status and checking that they are correct and complete. IEEE and ISO standards on configuration management describe four classic activities: configuration identification, configuration control, configuration status accounting, and configuration audits. You used version control tools in Software Engineering (deep-cse-4-4); here we focus on the management side.

Configuration items and baselines: a configuration item (CI) is anything placed under configuration control: source code, but also requirements documents, designs, test cases, build scripts, database schemas, infrastructure configuration and third-party library versions. Each CI has a unique identifier and version. A baseline is an agreed, reviewed snapshot of a set of CIs that can only be changed through formal change control. Typical baselines are the requirements baseline, the design baseline and the product baseline for each release. For DhakaEats, the scope baseline from lesson 05 and the release 1.0 code tag are both baselines.

Version control and branching: version control systems such as Git record every change with who made it, when and why, and allow any past version to be restored. Teams choose a branching strategy. In trunk-based development, everyone commits small changes to one main branch at least daily, with unfinished features hidden behind feature flags; it keeps integration pain low and suits continuous delivery. GitFlow uses long-lived develop and main branches plus feature, release and hotfix branches; it gives more control over scheduled releases but can create large, painful merges. DhakaEats uses short-lived feature branches merged into main within two days, after one code review and a passing build.

Status accounting and audits: configuration status accounting records and reports the state of CIs: which version is in which environment, which change requests are open, approved or implemented, and which defects are fixed in which build. A configuration audit checks that a release matches its documentation. A functional configuration audit checks that the item does what its requirements say, usually through test results. A physical configuration audit checks that what is shipped matches what was recorded: the right versions of code, libraries, documents and settings. Audits catch problems like a debug setting accidentally left on in production.

Environments and reproducible builds: most teams keep several environments: development, where developers try things; test or QA, where testers work; staging, a close copy of production used for final checks; and production, which real users touch. A change should move through them in order, and the same build package should be promoted from one to the next rather than rebuilt each time, so that what was tested is exactly what is released. Reproducible builds, where the same source and settings always produce the same output, depend on pinning library versions and keeping build scripts under version control. Infrastructure as code, describing servers and networks in versioned files, brings the same discipline to environments.

The configuration management plan: a short plan states which items are CIs, how they are named and versioned, the branching strategy, who may approve merges and baselines, the change control procedure and thresholds, how releases are tagged, and how audits are done. For DhakaEats it is two pages, but it settles dozens of questions before they become arguments.

Why change control: every project changes; uncontrolled change is scope creep (lesson 05). Change control does not mean refusing change. It means every proposed change is recorded, its impact on scope, schedule, cost, quality and risk is analysed, the right people decide, and the plans and baselines are updated if it is approved. In agile teams, small changes are handled by the product owner reordering the backlog; formal change control is kept for changes that affect contract, budget, release dates or baselines.

The change control process: first, someone submits a change request describing what and why. Second, the change is logged with an ID in the change log. Third, the team performs an impact analysis. Fourth, a change control board (CCB) or the authorised person approves, rejects or defers it. Fifth, if approved, baselines and plans are updated and the change is implemented. Sixth, it is verified and the requester is informed. The CCB for DhakaEats is the client's product owner, MeghSoft's project manager and the technical lead, meeting weekly; changes under 5 story points can be approved by the product owner alone.

Change request, worked: in month 4, the client asks to bring scheduled orders, planned for Q2, into release 1. The team estimates 34 story points. At the recent velocity of about 21.7 points per sprint, that is 34 / 21.7, about 1.6 sprints. One sprint of the 5-developer team is 5 x half a month = 2.5 person-months, about 2.5 lakh at the loaded rate, so the change costs about 1.6 x 2.5, roughly 3.9 lakh. Remember that DhakaEats already had to move 29 Could-have points out to make the date (lesson 17). The impact analysis gives the CCB three options: A, reject and keep scheduled orders in Q2; B, accept and swap out 34 points of Should-have items of equal size; C, accept, add about 3.9 lakh and move launch by about 3 weeks, which exceeds the 2 lakh management reserve and needs sponsor approval. The CCB chooses B after the client confirms that two Should-have reports can wait. The decision, the reasons and the updated backlog are recorded.

Release management: release management plans, schedules and controls the movement of releases into test and production environments. It covers release planning (what goes into which release and when), building and packaging, testing in staging, approvals, deployment, communication to users and support teams, and post-release monitoring. For mobile apps it also includes app store submission and review time, which can take from hours to several days.

Semantic versioning: many teams name releases with semantic versioning, MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Increase PATCH for backward-compatible bug fixes: 1.4.2 becomes 1.4.3. Increase MINOR for new backward-compatible features: 1.4.3 becomes 1.5.0. Increase MAJOR for changes that break compatibility, such as removing an API field other apps depend on: 1.5.0 becomes 2.0.0. The DhakaEats API follows semantic versioning, so the restaurant panel's developers know immediately whether an update is safe.

Continuous integration and delivery: continuous integration means every change is merged into the main branch often and automatically built and tested, so integration problems are found within minutes. Continuous delivery extends this so that every change that passes the pipeline could be released at any time with the push of a button; continuous deployment goes one step further and releases every passing change automatically. These practices make releases small, frequent and boring, which is exactly what you want.

Safer rollout strategies: a canary or staged rollout releases the new version to a small share of users first, watches error and crash rates, and expands only if the numbers are healthy. Blue-green deployment keeps two identical production environments and switches traffic from the old (blue) to the new (green), allowing instant switch-back. Feature flags let code be deployed while a feature stays hidden, so the feature can be turned on gradually or switched off without redeploying. Both Google Play and Apple's App Store support phased releases for mobile apps.

Staged rollout, worked: DhakaEats has about 50,000 users when version 1.2 is ready. The team releases it to 5 percent first, which is 2,500 users. The normal crash rate is 0.3 percent of users, about 7 or 8 people out of 2,500. Within hours, crash reporting shows 1.2 percent, which is 30 users, four times the normal rate. The team halts the rollout and fixes the bug. Had they released to everyone, about 50,000 x 1.2 percent = 600 users would have hit the crash. The staged rollout limited the damage to 30.

Rollback and release checklists: every release needs a tested way back. For the backend, that may mean redeploying the previous version and having database migrations that can be reversed or are backward compatible. For mobile apps, you cannot pull an installed version back from users' phones, so feature flags and server-side switches are the main safety net. A release checklist for DhakaEats includes: all quality gates passed, release notes written, support team briefed, monitoring dashboards ready, rollback plan tested, and the release not scheduled for a Friday night or just before Eid, when traffic peaks and staff are away.

Real-life example 1, Knight Capital: in 2012 the US trading firm Knight Capital deployed new software to its servers, but one of eight servers did not get the update, and old, unused code was accidentally reactivated through a reused flag. In about 45 minutes, the system sent millions of unintended orders and the firm lost around 440 million dollars, which nearly destroyed it. Weak deployment checks, no configuration audit and dead code behind an old flag combined into one of the most expensive release failures ever recorded.

Real-life example 2, a university's result portal: a university updated its results portal the night before results were announced, directly on the live server, with no version control. A typo broke the login page and nobody could tell which file had changed. The fix took four hours while thousands of students waited. Next semester, they used Git, a staging server and a rehearsal one week before, and the release took ten minutes.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: putting only code under version control and not configuration or database schemas; approving changes without impact analysis; letting the CCB become a slow bureaucracy for tiny changes; big-bang releases with no rollback plan; and releasing at the riskiest times. Exams often ask you to define configuration items and baselines, list the four SCM activities, describe the change control process and the CCB, explain semantic versioning, compare deployment strategies such as blue-green and canary, and analyse a change request.

Recap: configuration management identifies CIs and baselines, controls their changes, accounts for their status and audits them. Use version control for everything and a branching strategy that keeps integration frequent. Change control records, analyses, decides and updates: the DhakaEats scheduled-orders request cost about 1.6 sprints or 3.9 lakh, and the CCB swapped equal-sized Should-haves. Release with semantic versions, CI/CD, staged rollouts and tested rollback; a 5 percent canary limited one crash to 30 users instead of 600. Next lesson: procurement, contracts and outsourcing.
key_points: SCM activities: configuration identification, configuration control, status accounting and audits.
Configuration items include code, requirements, designs, tests, scripts, schemas and library versions; baselines change only through change control.
Trunk-based development keeps integration frequent; GitFlow uses long-lived branches for scheduled releases.
Change control: submit, log, analyse impact, decide (CCB), update baselines, implement, verify.
DhakaEats change: 34 points at about 21.7 per sprint is about 1.6 sprints or 3.9 lakh; the CCB swapped equal-sized Should-haves.
Semantic versioning MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: patch for fixes, minor for compatible features, major for breaking changes.
CI, continuous delivery and continuous deployment make releases small and frequent.
Staged rollouts, blue-green deployment and feature flags limit damage; a 5 percent canary limited a crash to 30 users instead of 600.
lessons.tip: Never ask whether we can make a change; ask what it will cost in scope, time, money and risk, and who decides. Turning every change request into those four numbers ends most arguments quickly.
lessons.task: Your team's velocity is 20 points per sprint and one sprint costs 2 lakh. A client asks for a 30-point feature in the current release. Write a one-page change request with impact analysis and three options for the change control board. Then give the next version number after 2.3.4 for a bug fix, a new compatible feature and a breaking API change.

options: An agreed, reviewed snapshot that can change only through formal change control
The first line of code in a project

quiz.explain: A backward-compatible feature increases MINOR and resets PATCH: 1.5.0.

quiz.q: Which SCM activity checks that what is shipped matches what was recorded?
quiz.explain: A physical configuration audit compares the actual release contents against the recorded configuration.

quiz.explain: 5 percent of 50,000 is 2,500; 1.2 percent of 2,500 is 30.
