quiz.explain: Blue-green deployment switches traffic from the old environment to the new one and allows instant switch-back.

lessons.title: Procurement, Contracts and Outsourcing
lessons.content:
When a family in Dhaka builds a house, they rarely do everything themselves. They hire a contractor, buy bricks and rods from suppliers, maybe pay an electrician by the day. How they write each deal matters enormously. A fixed price for the whole house protects the family if costs rise, but the contractor may cut corners. Paying the electrician by the day is flexible, but the bill can grow if he works slowly. Software projects make the same choices constantly: buy a payment service or build one, hire a vendor at a fixed price or by the hour, outsource testing or keep it in-house. This lesson covers procurement management: deciding what to buy, choosing sellers, writing contracts that share risk sensibly, and managing vendors and outsourcing.

What procurement management is: procurement management covers the processes to buy products, services or results from outside the project team. In PMBOK terms: plan procurement management (decide what to buy, how, and with which contract type), conduct procurements (get responses, select sellers, sign contracts) and control procurements (manage the relationship, monitor performance, handle changes and close contracts). For MeghSoft, DhakaEats involves at least four procurements: a payment gateway service, a map and routing service, an SMS gateway for one-time passwords, and cloud hosting. MeghSoft is also itself a seller, because the client bought DhakaEats from MeghSoft under a contract.

Make-or-buy analysis: the first question is whether to build in-house or buy from outside. Reasons to buy: the item is not your core strength, a mature product exists, you need it quickly, or a vendor offers economies of scale. Reasons to make: it is your competitive advantage, you need full control, no suitable product exists, or long-term costs are lower. Hidden costs on both sides must be included: maintenance, upgrades, security, staff time to integrate and manage vendors.

Make-or-buy, worked: DhakaEats needs an SMS gateway for login codes. Building one with a direct connection to mobile operators would cost about 3 lakh up front plus 0.2 lakh per month for maintenance and operator fees. Buying from an SMS service provider costs about 0.35 lakh per month. Break-even: 3 + 0.2m = 0.35m, so 0.15m = 3 and m = 20 months. Over 12 months, building costs 3 + 0.2 x 12 = 5.4 lakh and buying costs 0.35 x 12 = 4.2 lakh, so buying is cheaper. Over 36 months, building costs 3 + 0.2 x 36 = 10.2 lakh and buying 0.35 x 36 = 12.6 lakh, so building becomes cheaper. But building also brings operator negotiations and reliability risk that are not MeghSoft's strength. MeghSoft buys now and reviews after two years.

Procurement documents: a request for information (RFI) asks the market what solutions exist. A request for quotation (RFQ) asks for prices on a clearly specified item, where price is the main factor. A request for proposal (RFP) asks vendors to propose how they would solve a problem, with price as one of several factors. The statement of work (SOW) describes in detail what the seller must deliver: scope, deliverables, acceptance criteria, schedule and reporting. A vague SOW is the most common root of vendor disputes, just as a vague scope is for projects.

Source selection with weighted scoring: to choose between vendors fairly, agree on criteria and weights before reading proposals, then score each vendor. For the DhakaEats map and routing service, the criteria are technical fit 40 percent, price 30 percent, experience in Bangladesh 20 percent and support 10 percent, each scored from 1 to 10. Vendor A scores 8, 6, 8, 7: 0.4 x 8 + 0.3 x 6 + 0.2 x 8 + 0.1 x 7 = 3.2 + 1.8 + 1.6 + 0.7 = 7.3. Vendor B scores 7, 9, 6, 8: 2.8 + 2.7 + 1.2 + 0.8 = 7.5. Vendor C scores 9, 5, 7, 9: 3.6 + 1.5 + 1.4 + 0.9 = 7.4. Vendor B wins narrowly. Because the scores are so close, the team also checks sensitivity: if technical fit were weighted 50 percent and price 20 percent, would the winner change? Close results call for reference checks and perhaps a short proof of concept before signing. Many organisations also set screening criteria, such as data stored inside Bangladesh, that any vendor must pass before scoring.

Contract types and risk: the contract type decides who carries the cost risk. In fixed-price contracts the seller carries most of it; in cost-reimbursable contracts the buyer does; time and materials sits in between. Choose based on how well the scope is known: a clear scope suits fixed price; an unclear scope suits cost-reimbursable or time and materials.

Fixed-price contracts: firm fixed price (FFP): one price for the defined scope, whatever it actually costs the seller. Best for the buyer when scope is clear; sellers add risk margins and push back hard on any change. Fixed price incentive fee (FPIF): a target cost, target profit and target price, a sharing ratio for overruns and underruns, and a ceiling price above which the seller pays all extra cost. Fixed price with economic price adjustment (FP-EPA): used for long contracts where prices can change with inflation or exchange rates, for example a three-year support contract priced partly in dollars.

FPIF, worked: target cost 20 lakh, target profit 2 lakh, so target price 22 lakh; sharing ratio 70/30 (buyer/seller); ceiling price 25 lakh. If the actual cost is 23 lakh, the overrun is 3 lakh; the seller bears 30 percent, 0.9 lakh, so profit becomes 2 minus 0.9 = 1.1 lakh and the price is 23 + 1.1 = 24.1 lakh, below the ceiling. The point of total assumption (PTA), where the seller starts to bear all extra cost, is (ceiling price minus target price) / buyer share + target cost = (25 minus 22) / 0.7 + 20, about 24.29 lakh. If the actual cost is 26 lakh, above the PTA, the buyer pays only the ceiling of 25 lakh and the seller loses 1 lakh.

Cost-reimbursable contracts: the buyer pays the seller's actual allowable costs plus a fee. Cost plus fixed fee (CPFF): the fee is fixed regardless of cost. Cost plus incentive fee (CPIF): the fee changes with performance against a target cost, using a sharing ratio. Cost plus award fee (CPAF): the fee is awarded based on the buyer's judgement of performance against agreed criteria. These suit research or unclear scope, but the buyer must monitor costs closely.

CPIF, worked: target cost 20 lakh, target fee 2 lakh, sharing ratio 80/20 (buyer/seller). If the actual cost is 24 lakh, the overrun is 4 lakh; the seller's share is 20 percent, 0.8 lakh, so the fee drops to 2 minus 0.8 = 1.2 lakh and the buyer pays 24 + 1.2 = 25.2 lakh. If the actual cost is 18 lakh, the underrun is 2 lakh; the seller gains 0.4, so the fee is 2.4 lakh and the buyer pays 18 + 2.4 = 20.4 lakh. Both sides benefit from saving money.

Time and materials: T&M contracts pay an agreed rate per hour or day per role, plus materials. They are quick to set up and flexible, ideal for staff augmentation or small, unclear work, but without a cap the cost can grow without limit. A not-to-exceed amount and regular timesheet reviews protect the buyer. As lesson 17 noted, agile work often uses T&M with a cap or a fixed price per sprint.

Service level agreements: for ongoing services, a service level agreement (SLA) defines measurable targets and consequences: for example, 99.9 percent monthly availability for the payment gateway, response to critical incidents within 15 minutes, and service credits if targets are missed. Remember the arithmetic: 99.9 percent of a 30-day month allows about 43 minutes of downtime; 99 percent allows about 7.2 hours. Read the SLA's exclusions carefully: scheduled maintenance often does not count.

Outsourcing models and Bangladesh: onshore outsourcing uses vendors in the same country, nearshore in nearby countries and time zones, offshore in distant ones. Bangladesh has a large and growing software and IT-enabled services export industry, represented by BASIS (Bangladesh Association of Software and Information Services), and many Dhaka firms work as offshore vendors for clients in Europe, North America and Japan. Freelancing platforms are also a major source of income for Bangladeshi developers. Benefits for clients include lower cost and access to talent; risks include communication gaps, time-zone delays, quality variation, intellectual property and data protection concerns.

Protecting the buyer: important contract clauses include ownership of intellectual property and source code, confidentiality, data protection and data location, warranty periods for defects, acceptance criteria and procedures, payment milestones tied to accepted deliverables, change procedures, penalties or liquidated damages for late delivery, termination rights, dispute resolution and governing law. Source code escrow places the code with a neutral third party, released to the buyer if the vendor goes out of business. In Bangladesh, government buying follows the Public Procurement Act 2006 and Public Procurement Rules 2008, and most government tenders now run through the electronic government procurement (e-GP) system.

Controlling procurements: after signing, the buyer monitors the seller's performance against the SOW and SLA, reviews deliverables, approves payments, manages changes through the contract change process, keeps records of all communication, and handles claims and disputes, preferably by negotiation. At the end, procurement closure confirms all deliverables were accepted, final payments made, and lessons recorded for future vendor choices.

Real-life example 1, the cheapest bid: a government agency awarded a website project to the lowest bidder under a firm fixed price. The SOW said only modern, responsive website. The vendor delivered a template site; the agency expected custom features. Months of arguments followed, because nothing in the SOW defined what was promised. The next tender used a detailed SOW with acceptance tests, and weighted scoring that gave technical quality 60 percent.

Real-life example 2, a Dhaka vendor for a Danish client: a Dhaka software company won a long-term contract from a Danish logistics firm, starting with a three-month T&M pilot with a cap. The pilot built trust and showed real velocity, after which the parties signed a fixed price per quarter with a prioritised backlog and an SLA for production support. Starting small and moving to a more structured contract once both sides understood the work reduced risk for both.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: choosing vendors on price alone; vague statements of work; the wrong contract type for the level of scope certainty; ignoring hidden costs in make-or-buy; and assuming outsourcing removes responsibility, when the buyer still owns the project's outcome. Exams often ask you to perform a make-or-buy analysis, compare contract types and their risk to buyer and seller, calculate CPIF fees or the FPIF point of total assumption, apply weighted scoring, and list important contract clauses.

Recap: procurement plans what to buy, selects sellers and controls contracts. Make-or-buy compares total costs over time: the SMS gateway breaks even at 20 months, so buying wins for now. Use RFI, RFQ, RFP and a clear SOW. Weighted scoring picked vendor B at 7.5. Fixed price puts risk on the seller, cost-reimbursable on the buyer, T&M in between; in our FPIF example the PTA was about 24.29 lakh, and in CPIF a 24 lakh cost meant a 25.2 lakh bill. Protect yourself with SLAs, IP clauses and escrow. Next lesson: monitoring, closing the project and the capstone.
key_points: Procurement: plan what to buy, conduct procurements to select sellers, control procurements through closure.
Make-or-buy: the SMS gateway breaks even at 3 / (0.35 minus 0.2) = 20 months; buying wins over 12 months.
RFI explores the market, RFQ asks for prices, RFP asks for proposed solutions; the SOW defines exactly what the seller delivers.
Weighted scoring with weights set in advance: vendor B 7.5, C 7.4, A 7.3; close scores need reference checks.
Fixed price puts cost risk on the seller, cost-reimbursable on the buyer, time and materials in between.
FPIF point of total assumption = (ceiling minus target price) / buyer share + target cost: about 24.29 lakh.
CPIF: a 4 lakh overrun at 80/20 cuts the seller's fee from 2 to 1.2 lakh; the buyer pays 25.2 lakh.
SLAs, IP ownership, escrow and acceptance criteria protect the buyer; the buyer still owns the outcome.
lessons.tip: Before signing any vendor contract, read the statement of work and ask: could a stranger tell, from this page alone, whether the vendor delivered? If not, rewrite it with deliverables and acceptance tests.
lessons.task: Your team must choose a cloud hosting provider. Define four criteria with weights adding up to 100 percent, score three real or imaginary providers from 1 to 10, and calculate the weighted totals. Then do a make-or-buy comparison for hosting your own server (1.5 lakh up front plus 0.1 lakh per month) versus cloud (0.2 lakh per month) and find the break-even month.

quiz.explain: 3 + 0.2m = 0.35m, so 0.15m = 3 and m = 20 months.

quiz.q: Which contract type puts the most cost risk on the seller?
quiz.explain: Under firm fixed price the seller must deliver the defined scope for the agreed price whatever it costs.

quiz.explain: The overrun of 4 cuts the fee by 20 percent of 4 = 0.8, so fee 1.2 and total 24 + 1.2 = 25.2 lakh.

quiz.explain: A request for proposal asks for solution proposals; an RFQ asks mainly for prices on a clearly specified item.

quiz.explain: Escrow protects the buyer by giving access to the code if the vendor goes out of business.

lessons.title: Monitoring, Closure and the Capstone
lessons.content:
A pilot flying from Dhaka to Chattogram does not set the autopilot at take-off and go to sleep. Every few minutes the crew checks position, speed, fuel and weather, compares them with the flight plan, and makes small corrections. At landing, they do not just walk off: they hand the aircraft over, complete the logbook, and report anything that went wrong so the next flight is safer. Projects need the same discipline at the end as at the start. This final lesson ties the course together: the monitoring and controlling loop that runs through the whole project, how to recover a project in trouble, how to close a project properly, and the complete DhakaEats story from idea to launch as a recap. It ends with careers and what to study next.

The monitoring and controlling loop: monitoring and controlling runs alongside every other process group (lesson 02). The loop is simple: measure actual performance, compare it with the baselines for scope, schedule and cost, analyse variances and trends, decide on corrective or preventive action, and update forecasts and plans. Corrective action fixes a problem that has happened; preventive action reduces the chance of a future one. Without baselines there is nothing to compare against, which is why planning matters even in agile projects.

A project dashboard: a good dashboard shows a few numbers that together give an honest picture, each with a trend and a threshold. Schedule: SPI or SPI(t) from earned schedule, milestone status and the release burnup (lessons 14 and 17). Cost: CPI, EAC and remaining reserve (lessons 13 and 14). Scope: approved changes and backlog size (lesson 23). Quality: defect trends, DRE and crash-free rate (lesson 22). Flow: cycle time percentiles and WIP (lesson 19). Risk: total exposure and the risk burndown (lesson 16). People: team health survey results and attrition (lesson 20). Each metric should have a defined threshold: for DhakaEats, CPI or SPI below 0.9 turns amber and below 0.8 red.

The DORA idea: the DevOps Research and Assessment (DORA) programme, known through the book Accelerate by Nicole Forsgren, Jez Humble and Gene Kim and the yearly State of DevOps reports, identified four key metrics of software delivery performance. Deployment frequency: how often you release to production. Lead time for changes: how long from code committed to code running in production. Change failure rate: the share of deployments that cause a failure needing a fix. Time to restore service: how long it takes to recover from a failure. Their research found that high performers do well on speed and stability together; they are not a trade-off. In the month after launch, DhakaEats deployed 40 times and 3 deployments caused incidents, so the change failure rate was 3 / 40 = 7.5 percent.

Integrated change control: changes in one area ripple into others. A scope change affects schedule, cost, quality, risk, resources and contracts. Integrated change control means every change is assessed across all of these before approval, and all affected baselines and plans are updated together. The scheduled-orders request in lesson 23 is an example: the CCB looked at points, sprints, cost, reserve and the client's priorities in one decision.

Project recovery: when indicators turn red, a manager must act quickly and calmly. Steps: first, stop and assess honestly: what is the real status, what is the root cause (unclear scope, bad estimates, wrong people, technical problems, unmanaged risks)? Second, decide whether the project is still worth finishing; sometimes the business case (lesson 03) no longer holds and the right answer is to stop. Third, re-plan with options: cut or defer scope, add time, add money or experienced people early (remembering Brooks's law, lesson 12), reduce technical risk with spikes, or change the approach. Fourth, get stakeholder agreement on a new baseline. Fifth, monitor more frequently until stable. TCPI from lesson 14 tells you whether finishing within the original budget is realistic: at DhakaEats in month 3 it was 1.17, a warning that the original budget needed help.

Kill decisions and sunk costs: money already spent is a sunk cost and cannot be recovered whatever you decide. Decisions should be based only on future costs and benefits. If finishing a failing project will cost 20 lakh more and bring 10 lakh of benefits, it should be stopped even if 50 lakh has already been spent. Managers often keep pouring money in because stopping feels like admitting failure; this is the sunk cost fallacy. Stage gates make such decisions normal and less personal.

Closing a project: closure is a real process, not an afterthought. It includes obtaining formal acceptance of the deliverables from the client against the acceptance criteria; handing over to operations and support, with documentation, training, runbooks and access; closing contracts with vendors (lesson 24), confirming that all deliverables were received and final payments made; final financial reporting; archiving project records; releasing team members with recognition and feedback; and celebrating. Projects that end abruptly, with people moved away overnight, lose knowledge and leave operational teams struggling. Projects that are cancelled early also need closure, so that lessons and assets are not lost.

Lessons learned and blameless post-mortems: lessons learned should be collected throughout the project, not only at the end, when people have forgotten or left. A retrospective at project close asks: what went well, what did not, what would we do differently, and what should we recommend to future projects? A blameless post-mortem, common in operations after incidents, focuses on how the system and process allowed the problem, not on who to punish, because people hide information when they fear blame. Lessons must be stored somewhere future teams will actually find them, and someone should be responsible for acting on the top few.

The DhakaEats story, part 1: it started with a business case (lesson 03): a 60 lakh project with a payback of about 2.29 years, ROI around 41.7 percent and an NPV of 9.27 lakh at 10 percent. A charter named the sponsor and the project manager, and a stakeholder register mapped the client, restaurants, riders and the payment provider (lesson 04). Scope was defined and split into a WBS of about 130 person-weeks (lessons 05 and 06). Estimates were triangulated: about 196 function points at 6.5 FP per person-month gave about 30 person-months, and COCOMO gave 26 to 36 person-months, warning that six months was tight (lessons 07 to 09).

The DhakaEats story, part 2: the network diagram showed a 26-week critical path A-B-E-G-H-I, and crashing E and G could buy 2 weeks for 3 lakh (lessons 10 and 11). Resource levelling and Brooks's law shaped the team of six (lesson 12). The budget was built up from 30 lakh of labour and 6 lakh of non-labour costs to a 40 lakh cost baseline with 4 lakh contingency and 42 lakh total with management reserve (lesson 13). In month 3, EVM showed SPI 0.88 and CPI 0.83 with an EAC of 43.2 lakh (lesson 14). Risk management had already matched the 4 lakh contingency to the expected exposure and the mock payment server cut R1's exposure from 1.2 to 0.3 lakh (lessons 15 and 16).

The DhakaEats story, part 3: velocity forecasting confirmed the problem, so 29 Could-have points moved to release 1.1, and later the CCB swapped scheduled orders in for equal-sized Should-haves (lessons 17 and 23). WIP limits halved cycle time from 2 weeks to 1 (lesson 19). Pareto analysis focused testing on the payment and order modules, and DRE reached 90 percent (lesson 22). A 5 percent staged rollout caught a crash affecting 30 users instead of 600 (lesson 23). DhakaEats launched on the planned date with 271 of the original 300 points, about 90 percent of the planned scope and all the Must haves. The final actual cost was 39.5 lakh, within the 40 lakh cost baseline but above the 36 lakh of planned work, about 1.1 times it. Against the 60 lakh contract price, MeghSoft's gross margin was 60 minus 39.5 = 20.5 lakh, about 34 percent. Release 1.1 shipped the deferred features six weeks later.

DhakaEats' lessons learned: start payment integration earlier, because external dependencies were the biggest source of delay. Put WIP limits in place from the first sprint, not the fifth. Keep a test environment per team. Agree the MoSCoW split with the client at the start, so that cutting scope is a planned move rather than a crisis. And keep reporting honest: the amber status in month 3, with options, is what made the client trust MeghSoft for the next project.

Careers in project management: software project management roles include project coordinator, project manager, delivery manager, programme manager, Scrum Master, product owner and product manager, as well as engineering manager on the technical side. Many people move into these roles after a few years as developers, testers or business analysts, because understanding the technical work earns the team's respect. In Bangladesh, software firms, banks, telecom operators, NGOs running digital programmes and outsourcing companies all hire project managers.

Certifications: the PMP (Project Management Professional) from the Project Management Institute (PMI) is widely recognised and requires several years of project experience plus formal training; PMI's CAPM is an entry-level option. PRINCE2, popular in the UK, Europe and with some government and development projects, has Foundation and Practitioner levels. For agile, Scrum.org offers the PSM (Professional Scrum Master) and PSPO, and the Scrum Alliance offers the CSM (Certified ScrumMaster); PMI also offers the PMI-ACP for agile practitioners. Certifications help with job applications, but employers value real project experience and results more.

What to study next: if you are working on your final year project, the Final Year Project and Thesis course (deep-cse-6-7) shows how to plan, run and write up a long project, a perfect place to use this course's WBS, schedule and risk tools on yourself. System Design (deep-cse-6-13) covers the architecture decisions behind systems like DhakaEats, so you can estimate and plan technical work with more confidence. Beyond the courses, the best practice is real: manage a club event, a hackathon team or an open source contribution as a small project, with a charter, a backlog, a risk list and a retrospective.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: monitoring without baselines or thresholds; waiting too long to start recovery; continuing failing projects because of sunk costs; skipping formal acceptance and handover; and collecting lessons learned that nobody reads. Exams often ask you to describe the monitoring and controlling loop, design a project dashboard, explain integrated change control, outline project recovery steps, list closure activities, explain lessons learned and blameless post-mortems, and describe the DORA metrics.

Recap: monitor continuously against baselines with a small honest dashboard covering schedule, cost, scope, quality, flow, risk and people. DORA's four keys measure delivery speed and stability; DhakaEats' change failure rate was 7.5 percent. Use integrated change control, recover early with honest options, and ignore sunk costs. Close projects properly with acceptance, handover, contract closure, recognition and lessons learned. DhakaEats launched on time with about 90 percent of the planned scope, cost 39.5 lakh against a 40 lakh baseline, and earned a 34 percent margin, because problems were seen early and handled with data. That is what software project management is for: turning uncertainty into decisions, one honest number at a time.
key_points: Monitoring and controlling: measure, compare with baselines, analyse, act (corrective or preventive), and update forecasts.
A dashboard covers schedule, cost, scope, quality, flow, risk and people, each with thresholds.
DORA's four keys: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, time to restore; 3 of 40 deployments failing is 7.5 percent.
Integrated change control assesses every change across scope, time, cost, quality, risk and contracts together.
Project recovery: assess honestly, check the business case, re-plan with options, re-baseline, monitor closely; ignore sunk costs.
Closure: formal acceptance, handover, contract closure, final reports, archiving, releasing and recognising people.
Lessons learned are collected throughout; blameless post-mortems focus on systems, not blame.
DhakaEats launched on time with about 90 percent of scope, 39.5 lakh actual cost and a 34 percent margin.
lessons.tip: Keep a running lessons-learned page from day one and add one line every sprint retrospective. At closure you will have a real record instead of a vague memory, and the next project starts smarter.
lessons.task: Pick a project you have finished, such as a course project, event or hackathon. Write a one-page closure report: what was delivered versus planned, final cost or effort versus estimate, three things that went well, three that did not, and three recommendations. Then design a six-metric dashboard you would use if you ran it again, with a threshold for each metric.

quiz.q: A team deployed 40 times in a month and 3 deployments caused incidents. The change failure rate is:
quiz.explain: Change failure rate = 3 / 40 = 7.5 percent.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the four DORA key metrics?
quiz.explain: The four keys are deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service.

quiz.q: A failing project has spent 50 lakh, needs 20 lakh more and will bring 10 lakh of benefit. The rational decision, ignoring other factors, is to:
options: Stop, because future cost exceeds future benefit
Continue, because 50 lakh has already been spent
quiz.explain: The 50 lakh is a sunk cost; only the future 20 lakh cost versus 10 lakh benefit matters.

quiz.q: A blameless post-mortem focuses on:
options: How the system and process allowed the problem
quiz.explain: Blameless post-mortems examine systems and processes so that people share information openly.

quiz.q: Which activity belongs to project closure?
options: Obtaining formal acceptance and handing over to operations
quiz.explain: Closure includes formal acceptance, handover, contract closure, archiving and releasing the team.
